Remote Has Changes? ↓ Yes ↓ git pull ↓ Local Repository Updated OR Remote Has No New Changes ↓ git pull ↓ Already Up to Date
Step 6: After pulling, check the repository status again:
git status
Step 7: Practice the complete team workflow:
git pull ↓ Modify File ↓ git add . ↓ git commit -m "Your message" ↓ git push
Final Understanding Check:

1. What does git pull do? 2. What is the direction of git pull? 3. What is the difference between git pull and git push? 4. What does git pull origin main mean? 5. What happens if there are no new remote changes? 6. Can git pull result in a merge conflict? 7. What should you check before pulling? 8. What common workflow comes after pulling the latest changes?
Practice Goal: You should understand how to bring remote changes into your local branch using git pull origin main or git pull when an upstream relationship is configured.

qna.q: Q1. What does git pull do?
qna.a: It gets changes from a remote repository and integrates them into the current local branch.

qna.q: Q2. What is the common command to pull changes from the main branch of origin?
qna.a: git pull origin main

qna.q: Q3. What does origin represent in git pull origin main?
qna.a: It represents the remote name.

qna.q: Q4. What does main represent in git pull origin main?
qna.a: It represents the remote branch from which changes are pulled.

qna.q: Q5. What is the direction of git pull?
qna.a: Remote repository to local repository.

qna.q: Q6. What is the direction of git push?
qna.a: Local repository to remote repository.

qna.q: Q7. What is the difference between git pull and git push?
qna.a: git pull gets remote changes into the local repository, while git push sends local commits to the remote repository.

qna.q: Q8. What can git pull conceptually be understood as doing?
qna.a: Getting remote changes and then integrating them into the current branch.

qna.q: Q9. What happens if there are no new changes on the remote?
qna.a: Git does not need to bring in new commits, and the branch remains up to date.

qna.q: Q10. Can git pull result in a merge conflict?
qna.a: Yes. A conflict can occur if local and remote changes cannot be automatically integrated.

qna.q: Q11. Which command is useful to check your local working state before pulling?
qna.a: git status

qna.q: Q12. Complete the common workflow: Pull → Work → Add → Commit → ______.
qna.a: Push

items.title: Clone a Repository
explanation: Simple Meaning
git clone creates a local copy of an existing remote Git repository on your computer.
Remote Repository ↓ git clone ↓ Your Computer ↓ Local Repository Created
Simple Definition: git clone downloads an existing Git repository and creates a local working copy on your computer.
Why Do We Need git clone? ⭐
Sometimes a repository already exists on a remote server. Instead of creating a new local repository with git init, you can copy the existing repository to your computer using git clone.
Existing Remote Repository ↓ Want to work on it? ↓ git clone ↓ Local Copy Created
Basic Command ⭐
git clone repository-address
You provide the address of the existing remote repository that you want to copy.
Understand Each Part
git clone repository-address

PartMeaning
gitRun a Git command
cloneCopy an existing repository
repository-addressThe location of the remote repository
Simple Example

Remote Repository │ ├── index.html ├── style.css ├── README.md └── Git History ↓ git clone repository-address ↓ Your Computer │ └── Project Folder ├── index.html ├── style.css ├── README.md └── Git History
What Does git clone Create? ⭐
Cloning does more than simply copy the visible project files. Git creates a local Git repository containing the project files and repository history.
git clone ↓ Project Files Created + Local Git Repository Created + Repository History Available + Remote Connection Configured
This is why git clone is different from manually downloading and copying project files.
Clone vs Download Files ⭐

ActionResult
Download filesGets file contents
git cloneCreates project files plus a local Git repository with history
Download ↓ Files ──────────────────── git clone ↓ Files + Git Repository + Commit History + Remote Connection
What Happens During Cloning?
Step 1 Provide Repository Address ↓ Step 2 Git Connects to Remote Repository ↓ Step 3 Repository Data Is Copied ↓ Step 4 Project Folder Is Created ↓ Step 5 Local Git Repository Is Ready
Clone Creates a Folder ⭐
When you clone a repository, Git normally creates a new folder for the project.
Before Clone Projects/ ↓ git clone repository-address ↓ After Clone Projects/ └── project-name/ ├── Files └── .git/
You can then move into that folder:
cd project-name
Important: You Do Not Need git init After Cloning ⚠️
A cloned repository is already a Git repository. Therefore, you normally do not need to run git init after git clone.
git clone ↓ Local Git Repository Already Created ✅ Then: git init ↓ Usually Not Needed ❌
git init vs git clone ⭐

CommandWhen UsedResult
git initStarting a new Git repository locallyCreates a new empty Git repository structure
git cloneGetting an existing repositoryCreates a local copy of an existing repository
Starting New Project? ↓ git init ──────────────────── Existing Remote Project? ↓ git clone
Clone Automatically Connects the Remote ⭐
When you clone a repository, Git normally configures the source repository as a remote named origin.
Remote Repository ↓ git clone ↓ Local Repository Created ↓ origin Automatically Configured ↓ You Can Check Using: git remote -v
This means you normally do not need to manually run git remote add origin ... immediately after cloning the repository.
Clone vs Add Remote

ActionPurpose
git cloneCreate a local copy of an existing remote repository
git remote addConnect an existing local repository to a remote
Existing Remote Repository ↓ Need Local Copy? ↓ git clone ──────────────────── Existing Local Repository ↓ Need Remote Connection? ↓ git remote add
Complete Clone Workflow ⭐
Find Existing Repository ↓ Copy Repository Address ↓ Open Terminal ↓ Move to Desired Parent Folder ↓ git clone repository-address ↓ Project Folder Created ↓ cd project-name ↓ Start Working
Example After Cloning
After cloning, you can check the repository status:
git status
You can also check the configured remote:
git remote -v
And view the commit history:
git log
git clone ↓ cd project-name ↓ git status ↓ git remote -v ↓ git log
Common Team Workflow
Remote Repository Already Exists ↓ New Developer Joins Project ↓ Copies Repository Address ↓ git clone ↓ Gets Local Repository ↓ git pull ↓ Make Changes ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ git push
Clone and Future Pull/Push
After cloning, the repository is ready for normal Git workflows. You can get later remote changes and send your own commits using the appropriate Git commands.
git clone ↓ Get Initial Local Copy Later: git pull ↓ Get New Remote Changes Make Changes ↓ git commit ↓ git push ↓ Send Your Commits
Where Should You Run git clone?
Run git clone from the parent folder where you want Git to create the new project folder.
Example Projects/ ↓ Open Terminal Here ↓ git clone repository-address ↓ Projects/ └── project-name/
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Run git init after cloning Correct ✅ Clone already creates a Git repository ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Clone only copies visible files Correct ✅ Clone also gets Git repository data and history ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Run git remote add origin immediately after cloning Correct ✅ The cloned source is normally already configured as origin ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Clone and pull are the same Correct ✅ Clone gets the initial local copy of a repository Pull gets later changes for an existing local repository ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Use git clone inside a repository when you want to update it Correct ✅ For an existing local repository, use appropriate commands such as git pull to get later changes
git clone vs git pull ⭐

CommandMain Purpose
git cloneCreate the initial local copy of an existing repository
git pullGet later remote changes for an existing local repository
First Time Getting Repository? ↓ git clone ──────────────────── Already Have Local Repository? Need Latest Changes? ↓ git pull
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
CLONE First Copy Remote → New Local Repository ──────────────────── PULL Later Updates Remote → Existing Local Repository ──────────────────── PUSH Send Your Changes Local → Remote
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
git cloneCreate a local copy of an existing repository
git clone repository-addressClone the repository at that address
Project FolderNormally created during cloning
Local Git RepositoryCreated automatically
Git HistoryAvailable in the cloned repository
originNormally configured for the cloned source
git init after cloneNormally not needed
git pullGet later changes for an existing local repository

Final Definition: git clone creates a local copy of an existing remote Git repository. It normally creates the project folder, local Git repository, repository history, and a remote connection to the cloned source.
practice: Choose an existing remote repository that you want to copy to your computer.
Step 1: Open Terminal or Command Prompt.
Step 2: Move to the parent folder where you want the project to be created.
cd path-to-parent-folder
Step 3: Clone the repository:
git clone repository-address
Replace repository-address with the address of the repository you want to clone.
Step 4: Check that a new project folder was created.
Step 5: Move into the cloned project folder:
cd project-name
Step 6: Verify that it is already a Git repository:
git status
Step 7: Check the remote connection:
git remote -v
Step 8: View the existing commit history:
git log
Choose Repository ↓ Copy Address ↓ git clone ↓ New Project Folder ↓ cd project-name ↓ git status ↓ Check Remote and History
Final Understanding Check:

1. What does git clone do? 2. Does cloning create a local Git repository? 3. Do you need git init after cloning? 4. What is normally created as the remote name after cloning? 5. What is the difference between git clone and git pull? 6. What is the difference between git clone and git remote add? 7. Which command checks the remote after cloning? 8. Which command shows the repository history?

Practice Goal: You should be able to clone an existing remote repository, enter the newly created project folder, verify the Git repository, and understand why git clone differs from git init, git pull, and git remote add.

qna.q: Q1. What does git clone do?
qna.a: It creates a local copy of an existing remote Git repository.

qna.q: Q2. What is the basic git clone command?
qna.a: git clone repository-address

qna.q: Q3. What should repository-address represent?
qna.a: It should represent the location of the existing remote repository.

qna.q: Q4. Does git clone normally create a project folder?
qna.a: Yes. Git normally creates a new folder for the cloned project.

qna.q: Q5. Does git clone create a local Git repository?
qna.a: Yes. The cloned project is already a Git repository.

qna.q: Q6. Do you normally need to run git init after git clone?
qna.a: No. git clone already creates the local Git repository.

qna.q: Q7. What is normally configured as the remote name after cloning?
qna.a: origin

qna.q: Q8. What is the difference between git clone and git pull?
qna.a: git clone creates the initial local copy of an existing repository, while git pull gets later remote changes for an existing local repository.

qna.q: Q9. What is the difference between git clone and git remote add?
qna.a: git clone creates a local copy from an existing remote repository, while git remote add connects an existing local repository to a remote.

qna.q: Q10. Which command can you use to check the configured remote after cloning?
qna.a: git remote -v

qna.q: Q11. Which command can you use to view the commit history after cloning?
qna.a: git log

qna.q: Q12. Complete the rule: First time getting an existing repository → ______. Getting later changes for an existing local repository → ______.
qna.a: git clone; git pull.

items.title: Fetch Changes
explanation: Simple Meaning
git fetch downloads the latest changes and information from a remote repository but does not automatically merge those changes into your current working branch.
Remote Repository ↓ git fetch ↓ Remote Changes Downloaded ↓ Local Working Branch Not Automatically Changed
Simple Definition: git fetch gets the latest changes from a remote repository and updates your remote-tracking information without automatically integrating those changes into your current branch.
Why Do We Need git fetch? ⭐
Sometimes you want to check what has changed on the remote repository before bringing those changes into your local branch. git fetch allows you to get that information first.
Remote Has New Changes ↓ You Want to Check First ↓ git fetch ↓ Remote Information Updated ↓ Review Changes ↓ Decide Whether to Merge or Rebase
Basic Command ⭐
git fetch
This commonly fetches updates from the configured remote for your repository.
You can also explicitly specify a remote:
git fetch origin
Understand git fetch

Before Fetch Local main ● Commit A origin/main ● Commit A ● Commit B Your local remote information may be outdated ↓ git fetch ↓ Remote Information Updated Local main ● Commit A origin/main ● Commit A ● Commit B
Important: Your Current Branch Does Not Automatically Change ⭐

This is the most important difference to understand. After git fetch, remote changes may be available locally as remote-tracking information, but your current branch is not automatically updated with those commits.
git fetch ↓ Get Remote Changes ↓ Update origin/main Information ↓ Current local main remains unchanged
Example
Suppose another developer pushes a new commit to the remote repository.

Before Another Developer Pushes Local main origin/main ● Commit A ● Commit A ↓ Another Developer Pushes Commit B Remote Repository ● Commit A ● Commit B ↓ You Run git fetch ↓ Local main origin/main ● Commit A ● Commit A ● Commit B Your current main branch still has only Commit A
What Is a Remote-Tracking Branch?
A remote-tracking branch is Git's local reference to the state of a branch on a remote repository.
For example:
origin/main
Usually represents your local knowledge of the main branch on the remote named origin.
origin/main │ │ │ └── Remote branch name │ └── Remote name
git fetch vs git pull ⭐

CommandWhat It Does
git fetchGets remote changes but does not automatically integrate them into your current branch
git pullGets remote changes and integrates them into your current branch

git fetch Remote Repository ↓ Download Changes ↓ Update Remote-Tracking Information ↓ Review First ──────────────────── git pull Remote Repository ↓ Get Changes ↓ Integrate Changes ↓ Current Branch Updated
Easy Example: Fetch First, Merge Later ⭐
Step 1 Remote Has New Changes ↓ Step 2 git fetch ↓ Step 3 Review Changes ↓ Step 4 Decide to Integrate ↓ Step 5 git merge origin/main ↓ Local main Updated
This gives you more control because you can inspect incoming changes before integrating them into your working branch.
Complete Fetch Workflow
git fetch ↓ Get Latest Remote Information ↓ Check Remote-Tracking Branches ↓ Review Incoming Changes ↓ Choose What to Do ↓ Merge / Rebase / Continue Working
Fetch Does Not Modify Your Working Files Automatically ⭐
Because fetching does not automatically integrate the fetched commits into your current branch, your working project files do not automatically change just because you ran git fetch.
Before Fetch index.html = Old Version ↓ git fetch ↓ After Fetch index.html = Still Current Local Version Remote changes are available for review
How to See Incoming Changes
After fetching, you can compare your current branch with the remote-tracking branch.
git log main..origin/main
This can show commits that exist in origin/main but not in your local main branch.
You can also compare file changes:
git diff main origin/main
git fetch ↓ git log main..origin/main ↓ Check New Commits OR git diff main origin/main ↓ Check File Differences
Fetch from a Specific Remote
git fetch origin
Here, origin is the name of the remote from which Git should fetch changes.
Fetch a Specific Branch
git fetch origin main
This explicitly fetches information related to the main branch from the remote named origin.

CommandPurpose
git fetchFetch from configured remotes according to repository configuration
git fetch originFetch from the remote named origin
git fetch origin mainFetch the specified main branch from origin
Fetch vs Pull Visual Comparison ⭐
FETCH Remote main ● A ● B ↓ git fetch ↓ origin/main knows about A + B Local main ● A ──────────────────── PULL Remote main ● A ● B ↓ git pull ↓ Local main ● A ● B
When Is git fetch Useful?

Want to see latest remote changes? ↓ git fetch Want to review before integration? ↓ git fetch Want to update remote-tracking information? ↓ git fetch Want to immediately get and integrate changes? ↓ git pull
Common Team Workflow ⭐
Other Developers Push Changes ↓ Remote Repository Updated ↓ You Run git fetch ↓ Check New Commits ↓ Review Differences ↓ Everything Looks Good? ↓ Yes ↓ Merge or Rebase Changes
Fetch → Review → Integrate
FETCH Get information ↓ REVIEW Understand changes ↓ DECIDE Choose what to do ↓ INTEGRATE Merge or rebase when needed
git fetch vs git clone

CommandPurpose
git cloneCreate the initial local copy of an existing repository
git fetchGet updated information for an existing local repository
First Time Getting Repository? ↓ git clone ──────────────────── Already Have Repository? Want Latest Remote Information? ↓ git fetch
git fetch vs git pull vs git push ⭐

CommandDirectionPurpose
git fetchRemote → Local Git dataGet updates without automatically integrating into current branch
git pullRemote → LocalGet and integrate remote changes
git pushLocal → RemoteSend local commits to remote
FETCH Remote → Remote-Tracking Information No automatic integration ──────────────────── PULL Remote → Current Local Branch Get + Integrate ──────────────────── PUSH Local Commits → Remote
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ git fetch updates my current branch Correct ✅ Fetch gets remote information but does not automatically integrate it into your current branch ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ git fetch and git pull are exactly the same Correct ✅ Fetch does not automatically integrate changes Pull gets and integrates changes ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ git fetch automatically changes my working files Correct ✅ Fetching alone does not automatically update your working branch files ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ git fetch is only for the first time Correct ✅ git clone is for the initial copy; fetch is used later to get remote updates ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ After git fetch, my local main must contain all remote commits Correct ✅ Remote commits may be visible through origin/main while local main remains unchanged until integration
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
FETCH Get changes and check PULL Get changes and use them PUSH Send your changes
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
git fetchGets remote changes and updates remote-tracking information
Current branchNot automatically integrated with fetched changes
Working filesNot automatically changed by fetch alone
origin/mainRemote-tracking reference for main on origin
git fetch originFetch from origin
git fetch origin mainFetch main from origin
git pullGet and integrate remote changes
git pushSend local commits to remote

Final Definition: git fetch downloads the latest changes and repository information from a remote and updates remote-tracking references such as origin/main, without automatically integrating those changes into your current local branch.
practice: Use a local repository that is already connected to a remote repository.
Step 1: Check your current branch:
git branch
Step 2: Check the configured remote:
git remote -v
Step 3: Fetch the latest remote information:
git fetch
You can explicitly fetch from origin:
git fetch origin
Step 4: Check whether the remote has commits that your local main branch does not have:
git log main..origin/main
Step 5: Compare file differences between your local branch and the fetched remote-tracking branch:
git diff main origin/main
Step 6: Remember that running git fetch alone does not automatically merge those changes into your current branch.
Remote Changes ↓ git fetch ↓ origin/main Updated ↓ Review Commits ↓ Review Differences ↓ Choose Whether to Integrate
Step 7: If you want to practice integrating fetched changes, you can merge the remote-tracking branch when appropriate:
git merge origin/main
Final Understanding Check:

1. What does git fetch do? 2. Does git fetch automatically update your current branch? 3. Does git fetch automatically change your working files? 4. What does origin/main represent? 5. What is the difference between git fetch and git pull? 6. Which command fetches from origin? 7. Which command can show commits in origin/main that are missing from main? 8. Complete the workflow: Fetch → Review → ______.

Practice Goal: You should understand how to use git fetch to get remote updates, inspect incoming commits and changes, and understand why fetching does not automatically integrate those changes into your current branch.

qna.q: Q1. What does git fetch do?
qna.a: It downloads changes and repository information from a remote and updates remote-tracking information without automatically integrating those changes into the current branch.

qna.q: Q2. Does git fetch automatically update your current local branch with fetched commits?
qna.a: No. It does not automatically integrate fetched changes into your current branch.

qna.q: Q3. Does git fetch automatically modify your working project files?
qna.a: No. Fetching alone does not automatically update the files of your current working branch.

qna.q: Q4. What does origin/main generally represent?
qna.a: It is a remote-tracking reference representing your local knowledge of the main branch on the remote named origin.

qna.q: Q5. What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
qna.a: git fetch gets remote changes without automatically integrating them into your current branch, while git pull gets and integrates remote changes.

qna.q: Q6. Which command explicitly fetches changes from the remote named origin?
qna.a: git fetch origin

qna.q: Q7. Which command can explicitly fetch the main branch from origin?
qna.a: git fetch origin main

qna.q: Q8. Which command can show commits that exist in origin/main but not in local main?
qna.a: git log main..origin/main

qna.q: Q9. Which command can compare file differences between main and origin/main?
qna.a: git diff main origin/main

qna.q: Q10. Complete the rule: Fetch → Review → ______.
qna.a: Integrate.

qna.q: Q11. Which command is generally used for the initial local copy of an existing repository?
qna.a: git clone

qna.q: Q12. Complete the comparison: Fetch = get and inspect, Pull = get and ______, Push = ______ changes.
qna.a: integrate; send.

items.title: Fork vs Clone
explanation: Simple Meaning
Fork and Clone are both used when you want to work with an existing repository, but they create copies in different places and for different purposes.

Simple Rule: Fork = Copy a repository to your own account.
Clone = Copy a repository to your own computer.
The Main Difference ⭐
FORK Existing Repository ↓ Copy to Your GitHub Account ↓ Your Own Remote Repository ──────────────────── CLONE Remote Repository ↓ Copy to Your Computer ↓ Local Repository
What Is Forking?
A fork creates your own copy of an existing repository on the remote hosting platform under your account.
Original Repository ↓ Click Fork ↓ Your Account ↓ Your Forked Repository
The important point is that the fork is another remote repository associated with your account.
What Is Cloning?
Cloning creates a local copy of a repository on your computer.
Remote Repository ↓ git clone ↓ Your Computer ↓ Local Repository
Fork Location vs Clone Location ⭐

ActionCopy Is Created Where?
ForkOn the remote hosting platform, under your account
CloneOn your local computer
Fork Cloud / Remote Clone Your Computer / Local
Simple Example
Suppose there is an existing repository called project.
Original Repository owner/project ↓ You Fork It ↓ Your Remote Copy your-account/project
Now you want to work with your fork on your computer.
your-account/project ↓ git clone ↓ Your Computer └── project/ ├── Files └── .git/
Fork and Clone Are Often Used Together ⭐
Forking and cloning are not always alternatives. A common workflow is to fork a repository first and then clone your fork to your computer.
Original Repository ↓ FORK ↓ Your Remote Repository ↓ CLONE ↓ Your Local Repository ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit ↓ Push
Why Would You Fork a Repository?
Forking is commonly useful when you want your own remote copy of a project, especially when you do not directly work on the original repository.
Original Repository ↓ No Direct Changes to Original ↓ Fork Repository ↓ Your Own Remote Copy ↓ Make Your Changes
Why Would You Clone a Repository?
You clone a repository when you want to get a working copy of that repository onto your computer.
Repository Exists Remotely ↓ Need to Work Locally ↓ git clone ↓ Repository Available on Computer
Fork vs Clone Step by Step ⭐
FORK PROCESS Original Remote Repository ↓ Create Fork ↓ Your Remote Repository ──────────────────── CLONE PROCESS Remote Repository ↓ git clone repository-address ↓ Your Local Repository
Example: Clone the Original Repository
Original Remote Repository ↓ git clone ↓ Local Repository ↓ Work Locally
This is useful when you have the appropriate access to work directly with that repository.
Example: Fork Then Clone ⭐
Original Repository ↓ Fork ↓ Your Remote Fork ↓ git clone ↓ Your Local Copy ↓ Make Changes ↓ git push ↓ Your Remote Fork
Important: Fork Does Not Mean Local Copy ⚠️
A common beginner mistake is thinking that a fork automatically downloads the repository to your computer.
FORK ❌ Does Not Automatically Create A Local Folder on Your Computer FORK ✅ Creates Your Own Remote Copy Need Local Copy? ↓ Use git clone
Important: Clone Does Not Create a Fork ⚠️
Another common mistake is thinking that git clone creates a separate remote repository under your account.
git clone ❌ Does Not Automatically Create Your Own Remote Repository git clone ✅ Creates a Local Copy On Your Computer
Fork vs Clone Comparison ⭐

FeatureForkClone
Where is the copy created?Remote hosting platformYour computer
Creates local folder?NoYes
Creates another remote repository?YesNo
Git command required?No Git command like git fork is used in normal workflowYes, git clone
Main purposeCreate your own remote copyWork with a repository locally
Fork Is Different from a Git Command
git clone is a Git command that you run in your terminal. Forking is generally performed through the repository hosting platform's interface.
CLONE Terminal Command git clone repository-address ──────────────────── FORK Hosting Platform Action Repository → Fork
Remote Relationships
After cloning a repository, the repository you cloned from is normally configured as origin.
git clone ↓ Local Repository ↓ origin ↓ Points to the Repository You Cloned
When working with a fork, developers may later configure another remote pointing to the original repository. This is commonly called upstream.
Original Repository ↑ upstream │ Your Local Repository │ origin ↓ Your Fork
This naming convention helps distinguish your fork from the original repository.
origin vs upstream

NameCommon Meaning in a Fork Workflow
originYour fork, usually the repository you cloned from
upstreamThe original repository that your fork came from
Original Project ↓ Fork ↓ Your Fork ↓ Clone ↓ Your Computer origin → Your Fork upstream → Original Repository
Typical Contribution Workflow ⭐
1. Find Original Repository ↓ 2. Fork It ↓ 3. Clone Your Fork ↓ 4. Create a Branch ↓ 5. Make Changes ↓ 6. git add ↓ 7. git commit ↓ 8. git push ↓ 9. Request Your Changes to Be Reviewed
Fork vs Clone vs Pull

ActionMain Purpose
ForkCreate your own remote copy
git cloneCreate the initial local copy
git pullGet and integrate later remote changes
FORK Original Remote → Your Remote ──────────────────── CLONE Remote → New Local Repository ──────────────────── PULL Remote → Existing Local Repository
Easy Real-World Analogy 🧠
Original Book in a Library ↓ FORK = Create Your Own Copy In Another Library CLONE = Bring a Copy To Your Own Desk PULL = Get the Latest Updates For the Copy on Your Desk
When Should You Use Which?
Need Your Own Remote Copy? ↓ FORK Need Repository on Your Computer? ↓ CLONE Already Have Local Repository? Need Latest Changes? ↓ PULL
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Fork creates a local repository Correct ✅ Fork creates your own remote copy ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ git clone creates a fork Correct ✅ git clone creates a local copy ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Fork and clone are exactly the same Correct ✅ They create copies in different places ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ After forking, the project is already on my computer Correct ✅ You normally clone the fork to work locally ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Fork replaces clone Correct ✅ A common workflow is Fork → Clone
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
FORK Your Own Remote Copy CLONE Your Own Local Copy PULL Get Later Remote Updates PUSH Send Local Commits to Remote
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
ForkCreate your own remote copy of an existing repository
git cloneCreate a local copy of a remote repository
Fork locationRemote hosting platform
Clone locationYour computer
Fork → CloneCommon workflow for working on your own copy of another project
originCommonly points to the repository you cloned from
upstreamCommon name for the original repository in a fork workflow

Final Definition: Forking creates your own remote copy of a repository, while cloning creates a local copy of a repository on your computer. A common workflow is Fork → Clone → Make Changes → Commit → Push.
practice: For this practice, choose an existing repository that you want to understand as an example.
Step 1: Identify the original repository.
Original Repository ↓ Owned by Someone Else
Step 2: Fork the repository using the remote hosting platform interface. This creates your own remote copy.
Original Repository ↓ Fork ↓ Your Remote Repository
Step 3: Copy the address of your fork.
Step 4: Open Terminal in the parent folder where you want the project to be created.
Step 5: Clone your fork:
git clone repository-address
Step 6: Move into the project folder:
cd project-name
Step 7: Check the configured remote:
git remote -v
Step 8: Understand the result:
Your Local Repository ↓ origin ↓ Your Remote Fork
Step 9: Make a small change, then practice the normal workflow:
git add .
git commit -m "Update project"
git push
Fork ↓ Clone ↓ Create Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Add ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Changes Sent to Your Fork
Final Understanding Check:

1. Where does a fork create a copy? 2. Where does git clone create a copy? 3. Does forking automatically create a local folder? 4. Does git clone automatically create your own remote repository? 5. What is a common workflow using both? 6. What does origin commonly point to after cloning your fork? 7. What does upstream commonly represent in a fork workflow? 8. Complete the workflow: Fork → Clone → ______ → Commit → Push.
Practice Goal: You should clearly understand that Fork creates your own remote copy, git clone creates a local copy, and both can be used together in a common contribution workflow.

qna.q: Q1. What is the main difference between fork and clone?
qna.a: A fork creates your own remote copy of a repository, while git clone creates a local copy on your computer.

qna.q: Q2. Where is a fork normally created?
qna.a: On the remote hosting platform under your account.

qna.q: Q3. Where does git clone create a copy?
qna.a: On your local computer.

qna.q: Q4. Does forking automatically create a local project folder on your computer?
qna.a: No. A fork creates a remote copy. You normally use git clone to get a local copy.

qna.q: Q5. Does git clone automatically create your own separate remote repository?
qna.a: No. git clone creates a local copy of the repository.

qna.q: Q6. What is a common workflow when contributing through your own copy?
qna.a: Fork → Clone → Make Changes → Commit → Push.

qna.q: Q7. What does origin commonly represent after cloning your fork?
qna.a: It commonly points to the remote repository you cloned, which is usually your fork.

qna.q: Q8. What does upstream commonly represent in a fork workflow?
qna.a: It commonly represents the original repository from which the fork was created.

qna.q: Q9. Which action creates the initial local copy of a repository?
qna.a: git clone

qna.q: Q10. Which action creates your own remote copy of an existing repository?
qna.a: Fork

qna.q: Q11. Complete the rule: Fork = own ______ copy, Clone = own ______ copy.
qna.a: remote; local.

qna.q: Q12. Complete the workflow: Original Repository → Fork → Your Remote Copy → ______ → Your Local Copy.
qna.a: Clone.

items.title: What is a Pull Request?
explanation: Simple Meaning
A Pull Request (PR) is a request to review and merge your changes from one branch or repository into another branch or repository.
Your Changes ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Others Review Changes ↓ Discussion / Approval ↓ Merge Changes
Simple Definition: A Pull Request is a feature provided by repository hosting platforms that lets developers propose changes, review them, discuss them, and merge them into a target branch.
Why Is It Called a Pull Request?
You are requesting that the target repository or branch pull in your changes. In simple words, you are saying: “Please review my changes and merge them into this project.”
Your Branch New Changes ↓ Request ↓ Target Branch “Please pull these changes”
Simple Example ⭐
Suppose you are working on a new login feature.
main │ └── Create feature/login branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit Changes ↓ Push Branch ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Request: feature/login → main
Pull Request Is Not a Git Command ⚠️
There is no normal Git command such as git pull-request. A Pull Request is generally a feature provided by repository hosting platforms.
Git Commands git add git commit git push git pull ──────────────────── Hosting Platform Feature Pull Request
Typical Pull Request Workflow ⭐
1. Create a Branch ↓ 2. Make Changes ↓ 3. git add ↓ 4. git commit ↓ 5. git push ↓ 6. Create Pull Request ↓ 7. Review Changes ↓ 8. Discuss / Request Changes ↓ 9. Approve ↓ 10. Merge
Source Branch and Target Branch
A Pull Request usually has two important branches:

BranchMeaning
Source BranchThe branch containing your proposed changes
Target BranchThe branch where you want those changes to be merged
Source Branch feature/login Contains Your Changes │ │ Pull Request ↓ Target Branch main Receives Changes After Merge
Pull Request Does Not Immediately Merge Changes ⭐
Creating a Pull Request does not automatically merge your changes. It first creates a request for review and discussion.
Create Pull Request ↓ Changes Are Proposed ↓ Review Happens ↓ Approved? ↙ ↘ No Yes ↓ ↓ Fix Changes Merge
Why Do Teams Use Pull Requests?
Pull Requests Help With: ✓ Code Review ✓ Finding Bugs ✓ Discussing Changes ✓ Maintaining Code Quality ✓ Team Collaboration ✓ Approval Before Merge ✓ Tracking Why Changes Were Made
Code Review
Other developers can inspect the changes before they are merged. They can review modified files, comment on specific lines, ask questions, and suggest improvements.
Developer A Makes Changes ↓ Pull Request ↓ Developer B Reviews Code ↓ Comments / Suggestions ↓ Developer A Updates Code
Pull Request Example
Imagine the main branch contains the current stable application.
main ● Stable Application │ └── feature/payment ● Add Payment Page ● Add Validation ● Fix Payment Bug ↓ Pull Request ↓ feature/payment ↓ main
The team can review all the changes from feature/payment before merging them into main.
Pull Request After Forking ⭐
Pull Requests are also commonly used when contributing changes from a fork back to the original repository.
Original Repository ↓ Fork ↓ Your Repository ↓ Clone ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit + Push ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Original Repository Reviews Changes
Branch Pull Request vs Fork Pull Request

TypeExample
Same Repository PRfeature/login → main
Fork PRYour fork branch → Original repository branch
Same Repository feature/login ↓ PR main ──────────────────── Fork Workflow Your Fork feature/fix ↓ PR Original Repository main
What Happens After Review?
Pull Request Created ↓ Reviewer Checks Code ↓ Decision ├── Needs Changes │ ↓ │ Update Code │ ↓ │ Push Again │ ↓ │ Pull Request Updates │ └── Approved ↓ Merge
Push New Changes to an Existing Pull Request ⭐
If you make additional commits on the same source branch and push them, the existing Pull Request can automatically include those new commits.
feature/login ↓ Commit 1 ↓ Push ↓ Create PR ↓ Reviewer Requests Changes ↓ Commit 2 ↓ Push ↓ Same PR Updated
You usually do not need to create a completely new Pull Request every time you make a correction on the same branch.
Pull Request vs Merge ⭐

ConceptMeaning
Pull RequestRequest to review and propose changes for integration
MergeGit operation that combines changes into a branch
Pull Request ↓ Propose + Review Changes ↓ Approval ↓ Merge ↓ Changes Become Part of Target Branch
Pull Request vs git pull ⚠️
These two concepts are different.

ConceptPurpose
Pull RequestPropose changes for review and merging
git pullGet and integrate changes from a remote repository into your local branch
PULL REQUEST “Please review and merge my changes.” ──────────────────── git pull “Get remote changes into my local branch.”
Common Pull Request Statuses
Open Changes are waiting for review Approved Review conditions are satisfied Changes Requested Reviewer wants updates Merged Changes were integrated Closed Request was closed without merging
What Should a Good Pull Request Contain?

PartPurpose
Clear TitleQuickly explains the change
DescriptionExplains what and why
Relevant ChangesKeeps the PR focused
ReviewersAllows appropriate people to review

Good PR Example:
Title: Add login validation
Description: Adds validation for empty username and password fields.
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Pull Request = git pull Correct ✅ They are different concepts ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Creating a PR automatically merges code Correct ✅ A PR proposes changes for review first ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Pull Request is a normal Git command Correct ✅ It is generally a repository hosting platform feature ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Need a new PR for every correction Correct ✅ New commits pushed to the same PR branch can update the existing PR ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ A Pull Request and merge are the same Correct ✅ PR = propose/review process Merge = combine changes
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
COMMIT Save changes locally PUSH Send commits to remote PULL REQUEST Ask for review and merge MERGE Combine approved changes
Complete Workflow ⭐
Create Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Add ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Changes Needed? ↙ ↘ Yes No ↓ ↓ Fix + Push Approve ↓ ↓ PR Updates Merge ↘ ↙ Updated Target Branch
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
Pull RequestRequest to review and merge proposed changes
Source BranchContains your changes
Target BranchReceives changes after merge
Code ReviewOthers inspect and comment on changes
ApprovalReview conditions are satisfied
MergeCombines changes into the target branch
git pullDifferent from a Pull Request

Final Definition: A Pull Request (PR) is a repository hosting platform feature used to propose changes from a source branch or repository to a target branch or repository. It allows changes to be reviewed, discussed, approved, and then merged.
practice: Use a repository where you have permission to push a branch.
Step 1: Start from your main branch:
git switch main
Step 2: Create a new feature branch:
git switch -c feature/pr-practice
Step 3: Make a small change to any project file.
Step 4: Check the changes:
git status
Step 5: Stage the changes:
git add .
Step 6: Create a commit:
git commit -m "Add PR practice change"
Step 7: Push the branch to the remote repository:
git push -u origin feature/pr-practice
Step 8: Open your repository hosting platform and create a Pull Request.
Source Branch: feature/pr-practice
Target Branch: main
feature/pr-practice ↓ Contains Your Commit ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ main ↓ Review Proposed Changes
Step 9: Give the Pull Request a clear title and description.
Step 10: Make another small change on the same feature branch and push it to understand how an existing PR can update.
git add .
git commit -m "Update PR practice change"
git push
Step 11: Observe that the additional commit is included in the same Pull Request when it is pushed to the PR's source branch.
Create Branch ↓ Make Change ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Create PR ↓ Review ↓ Fix Needed? ↓ Yes Make Another Commit ↓ Push ↓ Same PR Updates
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is a Pull Request? 2. Is a Pull Request the same as git pull? 3. Does creating a PR automatically merge changes? 4. What is the source branch? 5. What is the target branch? 6. What happens when a reviewer requests changes? 7. Can new commits update an existing PR? 8. Complete the workflow: Commit → Push → PR → Review → ______.
Practice Goal: You should be able to create a feature branch, commit and push changes, create a Pull Request from that branch to main, and understand the review → update → approval → merge workflow.

qna.q: Q1. What is a Pull Request?
qna.a: A Pull Request is a request to review and merge proposed changes from a source branch or repository into a target branch or repository.

qna.q: Q2. Is a Pull Request the same as git pull?
qna.a: No. A Pull Request proposes changes for review and merging, while git pull gets and integrates remote changes into a local branch.

qna.q: Q3. Does creating a Pull Request automatically merge the changes?
qna.a: No. A Pull Request first proposes the changes for review and discussion.

qna.q: Q4. What is a source branch?
qna.a: It is the branch containing the proposed changes.

qna.q: Q5. What is a target branch?
qna.a: It is the branch where the proposed changes are intended to be merged.

qna.q: Q6. Is a Pull Request a normal Git command?
qna.a: No. It is generally a feature provided by repository hosting platforms.

qna.q: Q7. What happens if a reviewer requests changes?
qna.a: You update the code, commit the changes, and push them to the same source branch. The existing Pull Request can then include those new commits.

qna.q: Q8. What is the difference between a Pull Request and a merge?
qna.a: A Pull Request is the process of proposing and reviewing changes, while a merge is the operation that combines changes into a branch.

qna.q: Q9. Why do teams use Pull Requests?
qna.a: They help with code review, discussion, collaboration, finding issues, approvals, and maintaining code quality.

qna.q: Q10. Can a Pull Request be created from one branch to another branch in the same repository?
qna.a: Yes. For example, feature/login can create a Pull Request targeting main.

qna.q: Q11. Can Pull Requests also be used with forks?
qna.a: Yes. Changes from a branch in your fork can be proposed to a branch in the original repository.

qna.q: Q12. Complete the workflow: Create Branch → Make Changes → Commit → Push → ______ → Review → Merge.
qna.a: Create Pull Request.

items.title: Create a Feature Branch
explanation: Simple Meaning
A feature branch is a separate branch created to develop a specific feature without directly changing the main branch.
main │ └── Create Feature Branch ↓ feature/login ↓ Develop Feature ↓ Test Changes ↓ Pull Request ↓ Merge into main
Simple Definition: A feature branch is a Git branch created for developing one specific feature, improvement, or task separately from the main branch.
Why Do We Need a Feature Branch? ⭐
The main branch usually represents the primary version of the project. Instead of making unfinished changes directly on main, developers create a separate branch and work safely there.
Without Feature Branch ❌ main ↓ Unfinished Changes ↓ Risk of Affecting Main Code ──────────────────── With Feature Branch ✅ main ↓ Create feature branch ↓ Work Separately ↓ Test ↓ Merge When Ready
Basic Command ⭐
You can create and switch to a new feature branch using:
git switch -c feature/login
This command does two things:
git switch -c feature/login ↓ 1. Create feature/login ↓ 2. Switch to feature/login
Older Alternative Command
git checkout -b feature/login
This also creates the branch and switches to it.

CommandPurpose
git switch -c feature/loginCreate and switch to a new branch
git checkout -b feature/loginOlder alternative to create and switch
Recommended Naming Style ⭐
Use meaningful branch names that clearly explain the work being done.
Good Examples ✅ feature/login feature/payment feature/user-profile feature/add-search Avoid ❌ branch1 newbranch test123 abc
Step-by-Step: Create a Feature Branch ⭐
Step 1: Check your current branch.
git branch
The branch with * is your current branch.
* main develop
Step 2: Switch to main if you want to create the feature branch from the latest main branch.
git switch main
Step 3: Create the feature branch.
git switch -c feature/login
Git creates the new branch from your current commit and immediately switches you to it.
Before main ● A ● B ↑ Current Branch ↓ git switch -c feature/login ↓ main feature/login ● A ● A ● B ● B ↑ Current Branch
Check That the Branch Was Created
git branch
Example output:
main * feature/login
The * means you are currently working on feature/login.
Make Changes on the Feature Branch ⭐
Once you are on the feature branch, you can make changes related to that feature.
feature/login ↓ Add Login Page ↓ Add Validation ↓ Fix Login Issues ↓ Commit Changes
Your commits are now created on the feature branch, not directly on main.
Example Workflow
git switch main git switch -c feature/login
Now make changes to your project files.
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Add login feature"
main ● A ● B feature/login ● A ● B ● C Add login feature
Feature Branch and Main Branch Are Separate ⭐
Changes committed on feature/login do not automatically appear on main.
main ● A ● B feature/login ● A ● B ● C ● D Commits C and D are not yet part of main
The feature branch changes become part of main only after they are integrated, for example through a merge.
Switch Between Branches
git switch main
Switch back to the main branch.
git switch feature/login
Switch back to the feature branch.
feature/login ↓ git switch main ↓ main ↓ git switch feature/login ↓ feature/login
Push the Feature Branch to Remote ⭐
After creating commits locally, you can push the feature branch to the remote repository.
git push -u origin feature/login
The -u option sets the upstream tracking relationship, so later you can usually use a simpler command:
git push
Local feature/login ↓ git push -u origin feature/login ↓ Remote Repository ↓ feature/login Created Remotely
Complete Feature Branch Workflow ⭐
main ↓ Switch to main ↓ Create feature branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ Test Changes ↓ git push ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Merge into main
Feature Branch Example with Pull Request
main │ ├── ● A └── ● B │ └── feature/login │ ├── ● C Add login page ├── ● D Add validation └── ● E Fix login bug ↓ Pull Request ↓ main
One Feature, One Branch
A good practice is to keep a feature branch focused on a specific piece of work.
feature/login ✓ Login-related changes feature/payment ✓ Payment-related changes feature/search ✓ Search-related changes
Avoid mixing many unrelated changes into one branch when possible.
Avoid ❌ feature/login + Login feature + Payment system + Database migration + Unrelated UI redesign Better ✅ feature/login feature/payment feature/database-update feature/ui-redesign
What Happens to main While You Work?
The main branch remains unchanged by commits made only on your feature branch.
Start main ● A ● B Create feature branch ↓ feature/login ● A ● B ↓ Make commits ↓ ● C ● D main still ● A ● B
After the Feature Is Complete
Feature Complete ↓ Test Changes ↓ Push Feature Branch ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Code Review ↓ Approved ↓ Merge into main
Feature Branch vs Main Branch ⭐

Feature BranchMain Branch
Used for specific development workPrimary project branch
Contains feature-specific commitsContains integrated project changes
Usually temporaryUsually long-lived
Can be merged when readyReceives completed changes
Common Commands

CommandPurpose
git branchView local branches
git switch mainSwitch to main
git switch -c feature/loginCreate and switch to a feature branch
git checkout -b feature/loginOlder alternative
git push -u origin feature/loginPush the new branch and set upstream
git pushPush later commits after upstream is configured
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Creating the branch but continuing to work on main Correct ✅ Check git branch and ensure * is on your feature branch ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Feature branch changes automatically appear on main Correct ✅ They remain separate until integrated ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ A feature branch must be created from main every time Correct ✅ It can be created from the appropriate current branch depending on the workflow ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Creating a feature branch automatically creates it on the remote Correct ✅ The branch is local until you push it ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ One branch should contain every type of change Correct ✅ Keep branches focused when possible
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
MAIN Primary Project Branch FEATURE BRANCH Develop One Specific Feature PULL REQUEST Request Review MERGE Bring Completed Feature into Main
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
Feature BranchSeparate branch for a specific feature or task
git switch -c feature/loginCreate and switch to the branch
git checkout -b feature/loginOlder alternative
* in git branchShows the current branch
Feature commitsRemain separate from main until integrated
git push -u origin feature/loginPush the feature branch to remote
Typical final stepCreate a Pull Request and merge when approved

Final Definition: A feature branch is a separate Git branch used to develop a specific feature or task independently from the main branch. After the work is complete, it can be reviewed and merged into the target branch.
practice: Use an existing Git repository for this practice.
Step 1: Check your current branch:
git branch
Step 2: Switch to main:
git switch main
Step 3: Create and switch to a feature branch:
git switch -c feature/practice
Step 4: Verify that you are on the new branch:
git branch
You should see something similar to:
main * feature/practice
Step 5: Make a small change to a project file.
Step 6: Check the modified files:
git status
Step 7: Stage the changes:
git add .
Step 8: Commit the feature change:
git commit -m "Add practice feature"
Step 9: Push the feature branch:
git push -u origin feature/practice
Step 10: Switch back to main and check that the feature commit is not automatically part of main.
git switch main git log --oneline
Step 11: Switch back to your feature branch:
git switch feature/practice
Step 12: Create a Pull Request from feature/practice to main when you are ready to propose the changes for review.
main ↓ Create feature/practice ↓ Make Changes ↓ Add ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Merge into main
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is a feature branch? 2. Which command creates and switches to feature/login? 3. Which symbol shows the current branch in git branch output? 4. Do feature branch commits automatically appear on main? 5. Does creating a branch locally automatically create it on the remote? 6. Which command pushes feature/login and sets upstream? 7. What usually happens after the feature is complete? 8. Complete: Feature Branch → Develop → Commit → Push → ______ → Merge.

Practice Goal: You should be able to create a feature branch, make and commit changes independently from main, push the branch to a remote repository, and understand how it is later used in a Pull Request workflow.

qna.q: Q1. What is a feature branch?
qna.a: A feature branch is a separate branch used to develop a specific feature, improvement, or task independently from the main branch.

qna.q: Q2. Which command creates and switches to a new feature branch?
qna.a: git switch -c feature/login

qna.q: Q3. What is the older alternative command?
qna.a: git checkout -b feature/login

qna.q: Q4. What does the * symbol mean in git branch output?
qna.a: It shows the branch you are currently working on.

qna.q: Q5. Do commits made on a feature branch automatically appear on main?
qna.a: No. The commits remain separate until the branches are integrated.

qna.q: Q6. Does creating a local feature branch automatically create the branch on the remote repository?
qna.a: No. You need to push the branch to the remote.

qna.q: Q7. Which command pushes feature/login and sets its upstream tracking relationship?
qna.a: git push -u origin feature/login

qna.q: Q8. Why are feature branches useful?
qna.a: They allow specific work to be developed and tested separately without directly changing the main branch.

qna.q: Q9. What is a good branch name for adding a login feature?
qna.a: feature/login

qna.q: Q10. What usually happens after a feature branch is ready?
qna.a: The changes are pushed, reviewed through a Pull Request or another workflow, and then merged into the target branch when approved.

qna.q: Q11. Complete the command: git switch -c ______
qna.a: feature/login

qna.q: Q12. Complete the workflow: Feature Branch → Make Changes → Commit → Push → ______ → Merge.
qna.a: Pull Request.

items.title: Push Branch to GitHub
explanation: Simple Meaning
After creating a branch and making commits locally, you need to push the branch to GitHub so that the branch is also available in the remote repository.
Your Computer Local Branch feature/login ↓ git push ↓ GitHub Remote Branch feature/login
Simple Definition: Pushing a branch sends your local commits and branch information to a remote repository such as GitHub.
Why Push a Branch to GitHub? ⭐
A branch created using Git exists only on your local computer initially. Other developers cannot see or access that branch until you push it to the remote repository.
Create Branch Locally ↓ feature/login ↓ Only on Your Computer ❌ ──────────────────── git push ↓ feature/login ↓ Available on GitHub ✅
Before Pushing a Branch
Normally, you should already have a remote repository configured and have at least one commit ready to push.
Local Repository ↓ Remote Configured? ↓ Yes Create Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit Changes ↓ Push Branch
Check Your Current Branch
Before pushing, check which branch you are currently working on:
git branch
Example:
main * feature/login
The * means that feature/login is your current branch.
Push a New Branch for the First Time ⭐
When pushing a branch for the first time, use:
git push -u origin feature/login
Let's understand each part:

PartMeaning
git pushSend local commits to a remote repository
-uSet the upstream tracking relationship
originThe remote repository name
feature/loginThe branch being pushed
git push -u origin feature/login git push ↓ Send commits -u ↓ Remember tracking relationship origin ↓ Remote repository feature/login ↓ Branch to push
What Happens After the First Push?
GitHub receives your local commits and creates the remote branch if it does not already exist.
Before Push Local: feature/login ● A ● B ● C GitHub: feature/login ❌ ↓ git push -u origin feature/login ↓ After Push Local: feature/login ● A ● B ● C GitHub: feature/login ● A ● B ● C
What Does -u Do? ⭐
The -u option, also written as --set-upstream, connects your local branch with its corresponding remote branch.
Local Branch feature/login │ │ tracks ↓ Remote Branch origin/feature/login
After this relationship is configured, you can usually push future commits with:
git push
You do not need to repeatedly type the complete branch name in the usual workflow.
Push Later Changes ⭐
After the branch has already been pushed and upstream tracking is configured, the normal workflow becomes:
Make Changes ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ git push
Example:
git add . git commit -m "Add password validation" git push
New Local Commit ↓ git push ↓ GitHub Branch Updated
Complete Example ⭐
Suppose you want to create and push a branch called feature/login.
Step 1: Switch to the branch from which you want to start.
git switch main
Step 2: Create and switch to the feature branch.
git switch -c feature/login
Step 3: Make changes to your project files.
Step 4: Check the changes.
git status
Step 5: Stage the changes.
git add .
Step 6: Commit the changes.
git commit -m "Add login feature"
Step 7: Push the new branch to GitHub.
git push -u origin feature/login
main ↓ Create feature/login ↓ Make Changes ↓ Add ↓ Commit ↓ Push to GitHub ↓ Remote feature/login Created
Local Branch vs Remote Branch ⭐

TypeExampleLocation
Local Branchfeature/loginYour computer
Remote Branchorigin/feature/loginRemote repository
Your Computer feature/login ↓ git push GitHub origin/feature/login
How to View Local and Remote Branches
To view only local branches:
git branch
To view remote branches:
git branch -r
To view both local and remote branches:
git branch -a
git branch Local branches only ──────────────────── git branch -r Remote branches only ──────────────────── git branch -a Local + Remote branches
Example Output After Pushing
git branch -a * feature/login main remotes/origin/feature/login remotes/origin/main
This shows that the local branch and the corresponding remote branch are both available.
Push a Different Branch
You can push any local branch by specifying its name.
git push -u origin feature/payment
Local feature/payment ↓ git push -u origin feature/payment ↓ GitHub feature/payment
Push the Current Branch Using -u
If you are currently on the branch you want to push, Git can also use the current branch name automatically:
git push -u origin HEAD
HEAD represents your current checked-out branch in this context.
Current Branch feature/login ↓ HEAD ↓ git push -u origin HEAD ↓ Push Current Branch
Verify That the Branch Was Pushed
Check the remote branches:
git branch -r
You may see:
origin/main origin/feature/login
You can also check the repository page on GitHub and view the available branches.
Push Branch Before Creating a Pull Request ⭐
In a typical workflow, the branch needs to be available on the remote repository before you can create a Pull Request using the remote hosting platform.
Create Feature Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit ↓ Push Branch ↓ GitHub ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Merge
Important: Commit Before Push ⚠️
git push sends commits. If you modify a file but do not commit the change, that uncommitted modification is not sent by git push.
Modify File ↓ Uncommitted Changes ↓ git push ❌ Does Not Push Those Changes ──────────────────── Modify File ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ git push ✅ Changes Sent to Remote
Push Does Not Automatically Merge into main ⚠️
Pushing feature/login only updates the remote feature/login branch. It does not automatically put those changes into main.
git push origin feature/login ↓ Updates origin/feature/login Does NOT automatically update origin/main
To integrate the feature into main, a separate merge or Pull Request workflow is required.
Common Errors
Error: No remote configured
git push ↓ Error: No Remote
Check configured remotes:
git remote -v
If needed, add the remote repository:
git remote add origin repository-address
Error: Branch name does not exist
Trying to Push feature/login ↓ But Local Branch Does Not Exist ↓ Error
Check your branches:
git branch
Error: Authentication or permission denied
This can happen when your account does not have permission to push to the remote repository or authentication is not configured correctly.
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Creating a branch locally means it is already on GitHub Correct ✅ Use git push to send it to GitHub ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ git push sends uncommitted file changes Correct ✅ Commit changes first ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Pushing a feature branch updates main Correct ✅ Only the pushed branch is updated ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Need to use the full push command every time Correct ✅ After setting upstream, git push is usually enough ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Local branch and remote branch are the same thing Correct ✅ They exist in different locations and are connected through a remote relationship
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
CREATE Create Branch Locally COMMIT Save Changes in Local Git PUSH Send Commits + Branch to GitHub PULL REQUEST Request Review and Merge
Quick Summary

CommandPurpose
git push -u origin feature/loginPush a new branch and set upstream
git pushPush later commits after tracking is configured
git branchView local branches
git branch -rView remote branches
git branch -aView all branches
git remote -vView configured remotes

Final Definition: Pushing a branch to GitHub sends your local commits to the remote repository and makes the branch available remotely. For the first push, a common command is git push -u origin branch-name. After upstream tracking is configured, you can usually use git push for later commits.
practice: Use a Git repository that already has a remote repository configured.
Step 1: Check the configured remote:
git remote -v
You should normally see origin pointing to your remote repository.
Step 2: Check your current branch:
git branch
Step 3: Create and switch to a practice branch:
git switch -c feature/push-practice
Step 4: Make a small change to any project file.
Step 5: Check the change:
git status
Step 6: Stage the change:
git add .
Step 7: Commit the change:
git commit -m "Add push branch practice"
Step 8: Push the branch to GitHub for the first time:
git push -u origin feature/push-practice
Local feature/push-practice ↓ First Push ↓ GitHub origin/feature/push-practice
Step 9: Verify the remote branch:
git branch -r
Look for origin/feature/push-practice.
Step 10: Make one more small change.
Step 11: Commit it:
git add . git commit -m "Update push practice"
Step 12: Push again using the shorter command:
git push
First Push git push -u origin feature/push-practice ↓ Upstream Configured ↓ Later Commits ↓ git push
Final Understanding Check:

1. Where does a newly created local branch exist initially? 2. Which command pushes a new branch and sets upstream? 3. What does -u do? 4. After the first push, which command is usually enough? 5. Does git push send uncommitted changes? 6. Does pushing feature/login automatically update main? 7. Which command shows remote branches? 8. Complete: Create Branch → Commit → ______ → Pull Request.
Practice Goal: You should be able to create a local branch, commit changes, push it to GitHub using git push -u origin branch-name, verify the remote branch, and push later commits using git push.

qna.q: Q1. What does pushing a branch do?
qna.a: It sends the local branch commits to a remote repository and makes the branch available remotely.

qna.q: Q2. Which command is commonly used to push a new branch for the first time?
qna.a: git push -u origin feature/login

qna.q: Q3. What does the -u option do?
qna.a: It sets the upstream tracking relationship between the local branch and the remote branch.

qna.q: Q4. What can you usually use after the upstream relationship is configured?
qna.a: git push

qna.q: Q5. Does git push send uncommitted changes?
qna.a: No. Normally, changes need to be committed before they can be pushed.

qna.q: Q6. Does pushing feature/login automatically merge it into main?
qna.a: No. It updates the remote feature/login branch. Merging into main is a separate process.

qna.q: Q7. Which command shows remote branches?
qna.a: git branch -r

qna.q: Q8. Which command shows both local and remote branches?
qna.a: git branch -a

qna.q: Q9. What does origin/feature/login represent?
qna.a: It represents the remote-tracking reference for the feature/login branch on the origin remote.

qna.q: Q10. Which command can check configured remote repositories?
qna.a: git remote -v

qna.q: Q11. Where does a newly created branch exist before it is pushed?
qna.a: On your local computer.

qna.q: Q12. Complete the workflow: Create Branch → Make Changes → Commit → ______ → Create Pull Request.
qna.a: Push the branch.

items.title: Create a Pull Request
explanation: Simple Meaning
After pushing your feature branch to GitHub, you can create a Pull Request (PR) to propose merging your changes into another branch, usually main.
feature/login Contains Your Changes ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ main Target Branch ↓ Review ↓ Merge
Simple Definition: Creating a Pull Request means proposing changes from a source branch to a target branch for review, discussion, and possible merging.
Where Does a Pull Request Fit? ⭐
Create Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ git push ↓ CREATE PULL REQUEST ⭐ ↓ Code Review ↓ Approve ↓ Merge
A Pull Request is normally created after your branch has been pushed to the remote repository.
Before Creating a Pull Request
You should normally have:
✓ Git repository ✓ Remote repository configured ✓ Feature branch created ✓ Changes committed ✓ Feature branch pushed ✓ Ready to propose changes
Example Situation
Suppose you created a branch called feature/login and made several commits.
main ● A ● B feature/login ● A ● B ● C Add login page ● D Add validation ● E Fix login issue
Now you want to bring commits C, D, and E into main. Instead of merging immediately, you can first create a Pull Request.
feature/login ● C ● D ● E ↓ Pull Request ↓ main
Step 1: Push Your Branch ⭐
First, ensure your feature branch is available on GitHub.
git push -u origin feature/login
After the first push and upstream configuration, later changes can usually be pushed using:
git push
Local Branch feature/login ↓ git push ↓ GitHub feature/login
Step 2: Open the Repository on GitHub
Open the repository where you pushed the feature branch. GitHub may show an option to compare your recently pushed branch and create a Pull Request.
GitHub Repository ↓ feature/login Available ↓ Compare Changes ↓ Create Pull Request
Step 3: Select the Branches ⭐
A Pull Request compares two branches.

BranchExampleMeaning
Base / Target BranchmainBranch that will receive the changes
Compare / Source Branchfeature/loginBranch containing your proposed changes
Base Branch / Target main ↑ │ Proposed Changes │ Compare Branch / Source feature/login
In this example, the Pull Request direction is:
feature/login → main
Important: Check the Direction ⚠️
Before creating the Pull Request, carefully check which branch is the source and which branch is the target.
Correct Example ✅ feature/login ↓ Pull Request ↓ main ──────────────────── Wrong Direction ❌ main ↓ Pull Request ↓ feature/login
Normally, your feature branch contains the new work, while main is the branch intended to receive that work.
Step 4: Review the Changes
Before submitting the Pull Request, review the commits and file changes being proposed.
Pull Request Comparison ↓ Commits ↓ Changed Files ↓ Added Lines ↓ Removed Lines ↓ Check Everything
This helps you verify that only the intended changes are included.
Step 5: Add a Clear Pull Request Title ⭐
The title should clearly describe the main change.
Good Titles ✅ Add login validation Fix payment calculation issue Add user profile page Update search functionality ──────────────────── Poor Titles ❌ Changes Update Fix New work
Step 6: Add a Description
A description helps reviewers understand what changed and why.

Example:
Title: Add login validation

Description:
Added validation for empty username and password fields and improved error messages.
Step 7: Create the Pull Request ⭐
After checking the source branch, target branch, commits, changed files, title, and description, submit the Pull Request.
Select Source Branch ↓ Select Target Branch ↓ Review Changes ↓ Add Title ↓ Add Description ↓ Create Pull Request
The Pull Request is now open and ready for review.
What Happens After Creating the Pull Request?
Pull Request Open ↓ Reviewer Checks Changes ↓ Decision ├── Request Changes │ ↓ │ Update Code │ ↓ │ Commit + Push │ ↓ │ Same PR Updates │ └── Approve ↓ Merge
Request Changes and Update the Same PR ⭐
If a reviewer asks you to make changes, you usually continue working on the same source branch.
PR: feature/login → main ↓ Reviewer Requests Changes ↓ Update feature/login ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ git push ↓ Existing Pull Request Updates
You normally do not need to create another Pull Request for each correction as long as you continue pushing relevant commits to the same source branch.
Example
git switch feature/login
Make the requested changes, then:
git add . git commit -m "Update login validation" git push
The new commit can appear in the existing Pull Request.
Draft Pull Request
A draft Pull Request can be useful when you want to share work early for discussion or visibility but the changes are not yet ready for final review or merging.
Work in Progress ↓ Create Draft PR ↓ Discussion / Early Feedback ↓ Continue Development ↓ Ready for Review ↓ Normal Review ↓ Merge
Pull Request vs Direct Merge ⭐

Pull Request WorkflowDirect Merge Workflow
Changes are proposed firstChanges are merged directly
Review can happen before mergeMay not include a review step
Discussion and comments can be recordedLess collaboration context
Common in team workflowsCan be useful for simple workflows
Pull Request Propose → Review → Approve → Merge ──────────────────── Direct Merge Merge Immediately
Creating a Pull Request Does Not Merge the Code ⚠️
Create Pull Request ↓ Changes Are Proposed ↓ main Is Still Unchanged ↓ Review ↓ Merge ↓ main Receives Changes
The actual integration happens only when the changes are merged.
Pull Request Branches Can Change While PR Is Open
The source branch can receive additional commits while the Pull Request is open. After you push those commits, the Pull Request comparison can update to include the new changes.
Create PR feature/login → main ↓ PR Open ↓ New Commit on feature/login ↓ git push ↓ PR Includes New Commit
Complete Real-World Example ⭐

1. Switch to main ↓ 2. Create feature/payment ↓ 3. Develop Payment Feature ↓ 4. git add ↓ 5. git commit ↓ 6. git push -u origin feature/payment ↓ 7. Open GitHub ↓ 8. Select: Source: feature/payment Target: main ↓ 9. Review Changes ↓ 10. Add PR Title + Description ↓ 11. Create Pull Request ↓ 12. Code Review ↓ 13. Update if Needed ↓ 14. Approve ↓ 15. Merge
Pull Request Checklist ⭐

Before Creating PR □ Correct feature branch □ Changes committed □ Branch pushed □ Correct source branch □ Correct target branch □ Review changed files □ Check commits □ Clear title □ Useful description □ No unwanted changes
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Create PR before pushing the branch Correct ✅ Push the source branch to the remote first ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Select source and target branches incorrectly Correct ✅ Double-check the PR direction ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Creating a PR automatically merges code Correct ✅ PR proposes changes; merge is separate ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Create a new PR for every requested correction Correct ✅ Push new commits to the same source branch to update the existing PR ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Use an unclear PR title Correct ✅ Describe the actual change clearly ──────────────────── Mistake 6 ❌ Do not review files before submitting Correct ✅ Check commits and changed files before creating the PR
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
CREATE BRANCH Start Separate Work COMMIT Save Work Locally PUSH Send Branch to GitHub PULL REQUEST Ask to Review and Merge MERGE Integrate Changes into Target Branch
Quick Summary

StepAction
1Push your feature branch
2Open the repository on GitHub
3Select source and target branches
4Review commits and file changes
5Add a clear title
6Add a useful description
7Create the Pull Request
8Review, update if needed, approve, and merge

Final Definition: Creating a Pull Request means proposing changes from a source branch to a target branch through a repository hosting platform. The changes can then be reviewed, discussed, updated, approved, and merged.
practice: Use a repository connected to GitHub where you have permission to create branches and Pull Requests.
Step 1: Check your current branch:
git branch
Step 2: Create and switch to a practice feature branch:
git switch -c feature/pr-create-practice
Step 3: Make a small change to your project.
Step 4: Check the change:
git status
Step 5: Stage the changes:
git add .
Step 6: Create a commit:
git commit -m "Add Pull Request practice"
Step 7: Push the new branch to GitHub:
git push -u origin feature/pr-create-practice
Step 8: Open the repository on GitHub and start creating a Pull Request.
Step 9: Select the branches:
Source / Compare Branch feature/pr-create-practice ↓ Pull Request ↓ Target / Base Branch main
Step 10: Review the commits and changed files.
Step 11: Use a clear title, for example:
Add Pull Request practice change
Step 12: Add a short description explaining what you changed.
Step 13: Create the Pull Request.
Step 14: While the PR is still open, make another small change on the same feature branch.
Step 15: Commit and push the new change:
git add . git commit -m "Update Pull Request practice" git push
Observe how the existing Pull Request can update with the new commit.
Create Branch ↓ Make Change ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Create PR ↓ PR Open ↓ Make Another Change ↓ Commit + Push ↓ Same PR Updates
Final Understanding Check:

1. What should normally happen before creating a PR? 2. Which branch is the source in feature/login → main? 3. Which branch is the target in feature/login → main? 4. Does creating a PR automatically merge the changes? 5. What should you check before submitting a PR? 6. What happens if you push another commit to the same PR branch? 7. What is the purpose of a PR title? 8. Complete: Commit → Push → ______ → Review → Merge.

Practice Goal: You should be able to push a feature branch, create a Pull Request from that branch to main, verify the branch direction and proposed changes, add a clear title and description, and understand how new commits can update an existing Pull Request.

qna.q: Q1. What does creating a Pull Request mean?
qna.a: It means proposing changes from a source branch to a target branch for review, discussion, and possible merging.

qna.q: Q2. What should normally happen before creating a Pull Request?
qna.a: The feature branch changes should be committed and the branch should normally be pushed to the remote repository.

qna.q: Q3. In feature/login → main, which is the source branch?
qna.a: feature/login

qna.q: Q4. In feature/login → main, which is the target branch?
qna.a: main

qna.q: Q5. Does creating a Pull Request automatically merge the changes?
qna.a: No. Creating a Pull Request proposes the changes for review. Merging is a separate step.

qna.q: Q6. What should you review before creating a Pull Request?
qna.a: You should review the source branch, target branch, commits, and changed files.

qna.q: Q7. What should a good Pull Request title do?
qna.a: It should clearly describe the main change being proposed.

qna.q: Q8. What is the purpose of a Pull Request description?
qna.a: It helps reviewers understand what changed and why.

qna.q: Q9. What happens when you push a new commit to the same source branch while the PR is open?
qna.a: The existing Pull Request can update to include the new commit.

qna.q: Q10. Do you normally need to create a new Pull Request for every correction requested during review?
qna.a: No. You can usually commit and push the corrections to the same source branch, and the existing Pull Request will update.

qna.q: Q11. What is a draft Pull Request?
qna.a: It is a Pull Request used to share work that is still in progress and not yet ready for final review or merging.

qna.q: Q12. Complete the workflow: Create Branch → Make Changes → Commit → Push → ______ → Review → Merge.
qna.a: Create Pull Request.

items.title: Review Changes
explanation: Simple Meaning
After creating a Pull Request, reviewing changes means checking the proposed code and file changes before approving and merging them into the target branch.
Feature Branch Contains Changes ↓ Pull Request ↓ Review Changes ⭐ ↓ Check Code + Files + Commits ↓ Approve OR Request Changes ↓ Merge
Simple Definition: Reviewing changes means examining the commits and file differences in a Pull Request to verify that the changes are correct, complete, and appropriate before merging.
Where Does Review Fit in the Workflow? ⭐
Create Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ REVIEW CHANGES ⭐ ↓ Approve / Request Changes ↓ Merge
Why Review Changes?
A review helps identify mistakes, unwanted changes, missing functionality, or potential problems before the code is merged into the target branch.
Without Review ❌ Change ↓ Merge Immediately ↓ Possible Errors in main ──────────────────── With Review ✅ Change ↓ Check Changes ↓ Find Issues ↓ Fix Issues ↓ Merge
What Do You Review? ⭐
When reviewing a Pull Request, you normally examine multiple things.

Review AreaWhat to Check
Pull Request TitleDoes it clearly describe the change?
DescriptionDoes it explain what and why?
Source BranchIs the correct branch providing changes?
Target BranchAre changes going to the correct branch?
CommitsAre the commits relevant?
Changed FilesAre only expected files changed?
Code ChangesIs the implementation correct?
Pull Request ↓ Check Title ↓ Check Description ↓ Check Branch Direction ↓ Check Commits ↓ Check Changed Files ↓ Check Code Changes ↓ Decision
Step 1: Check the Pull Request Direction ⭐
First, verify that the Pull Request is comparing the correct branches.
Correct Example ✅ feature/login ↓ Proposed Changes ↓ main Source: feature/login Target: main
Make sure the feature branch contains the changes and the correct target branch will receive them.
Check: Where are changes coming from? ↓ Source Branch Where should changes go? ↓ Target Branch
Step 2: Check the Pull Request Title
The title should give a clear summary of the proposed change.
Good ✅ Add login validation Fix payment calculation issue Update user profile page Poor ❌ Changes Update Fix Test
A clear title helps reviewers quickly understand the purpose of the Pull Request.
Step 3: Read the Description
The description should provide useful context about the change.

Example Pull Request:
Title: Add login validation

Description:
Added validation for empty username and password fields and improved error messages.
As a reviewer, check whether the description matches the actual changes.
Description Says: Add login validation ↓ Review Code ↓ Does the Code Actually Add Login Validation? Yes ✅ → Continue No ❌ → Ask Questions / Request Changes
Step 4: Review the Commits ⭐
Check the commits included in the Pull Request to understand how the changes were developed.
Pull Request Commits ● Add login page ● Add password validation ● Fix validation error ↓ Review Each Commit ↓ Are They Related to the PR?
Look for unrelated or unexpected commits.
Expected PR: Login Feature Commits: ✓ Add login page ✓ Add validation ✓ Fix login error Unexpected: ❌ Delete unrelated files ❌ Change payment logic ❌ Add unrelated feature
Step 5: Review Changed Files ⭐
Check which files were modified, added, or deleted.
Changed Files ✓ login.html ✓ login.js ✓ validation.js Question: Are these files expected for this PR?
If the Pull Request is only about login functionality but contains unrelated files, investigate why they were included.
