PR: Add Login Feature Expected ✅ login.html login.js validation.js Unexpected ❌ payment.js salary_report.xlsx unrelated_config_file
Step 6: Review the Actual Code Changes ⭐
Now examine the differences line by line where necessary.
Old Code ↓ - Removed Lines New Code ↓ + Added Lines ↓ Compare ↓ Understand What Changed
Ask yourself:
Does the code solve the intended problem? Is the logic correct? Are there possible errors? Is anything unnecessary? Are important cases missing? Does the change affect other functionality?
Example: Review a Small Code Change
Suppose the purpose is to prevent empty usernames.
if (username === "") { showError("Username is required"); }
During review, you might check:
Requirement Prevent Empty Username ↓ Code Check username === "" ↓ Does It Match the Requirement? ↓ Check Other Cases Whitespace? Null? Undefined? ↓ Give Review Feedback
Reviewing Additions and Deletions
A code comparison generally shows what was removed and what was added.
Example - oldFunction(); + newFunction(); - means removed + means added
The reviewer should understand why the old behavior was changed and whether the new behavior is correct.
Step 7: Look for Unwanted Changes ⚠️
Sometimes a developer accidentally includes files or changes that do not belong to the Pull Request.
Feature PR Add Login Validation Expected Changes ✓ login.js ✓ validation.js Accidentally Included ❌ debug.log ❌ temporary-file.txt ❌ unrelated-payment-change
Reviewing changed files and differences helps catch these issues before merging.
Step 8: Test or Verify the Changes
Depending on the project and workflow, review may also include checking whether the changes behave as expected through available tests, builds, or manual verification.
Review Code ↓ Run Available Checks ↓ Test Expected Behavior ↓ Does It Work? Yes → Continue Review No → Request Changes
Three Common Review Decisions ⭐

DecisionMeaning
ApproveThe reviewer is satisfied with the proposed changes
Request ChangesThe reviewer wants changes before approval
CommentThe reviewer provides feedback or asks a question

Review Complete ↓ Choose Decision ├── Approve ✅ │ ↓ │ Ready for Merge │ ├── Request Changes 🔄 │ ↓ │ Developer Updates Code │ ↓ │ Commit + Push │ ↓ │ Review Again │ └── Comment 💬 ↓ Discussion / Clarification
Approve Changes
Approve when the changes meet the expected requirements according to your review.
Review ↓ Everything Looks Correct ↓ APPROVE ↓ Ready for Next Merge Step
Approval does not itself mean that the code has already been merged.
Request Changes ⭐
Request changes when important issues need to be corrected before the Pull Request should proceed.
Review Finds Problem ↓ Request Changes ↓ Developer Fixes Code ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ git push ↓ Pull Request Updates ↓ Review Again
Leave Comments
Comments can be used to ask questions, explain concerns, or suggest improvements.

Example Review Comments:

Could you explain why this condition is required?

Can this variable name be more descriptive?

Please handle the empty value case here.

This file appears unrelated to the login feature. Should it be included?
Good Review Feedback ⭐
Useful review feedback should clearly explain the concern and, when possible, the expected improvement.

Less Useful ❌ This is wrong. Fix this. Bad code. ──────────────────── Better ✅ This condition may fail when the value is null. Could we handle that case? This variable name is difficult to understand. Can we use a name that describes its purpose?
Review Loop
Developer Creates PR ↓ Reviewer Checks Changes ↓ Issues Found? NO ↓ Approve ↓ Merge YES ↓ Request Changes ↓ Developer Fixes ↓ Commit + Push ↓ Reviewer Checks Again
Reviewing a PR Does Not Change Your Local Branch
Reviewing changes on a Pull Request is about examining the proposed comparison. Simply reviewing the Pull Request does not automatically merge the changes into your local branch.
Review Pull Request ↓ Examine Changes ↓ Approve / Comment / Request Changes Does NOT Automatically: ❌ Merge the PR ❌ Change your local branch ❌ Delete the feature branch
Review Changes vs Approve ⭐

Review ChangesApprove
Process of checking the PRA review decision
Examine files, commits, and codeIndicates satisfaction with the changes
Can result in comments or requested changesMay allow the PR to proceed toward merge
Review Changes ↓ Understand + Verify ↓ Make Decision ↓ Approve OR Request Changes OR Comment
Complete Review Checklist ⭐

□ Correct source branch? □ Correct target branch? □ Clear PR title? □ Description matches changes? □ Commits are relevant? □ Changed files are expected? □ No unwanted files? □ Code solves the intended problem? □ Logic looks correct? □ Important cases handled? □ Available checks or tests pass? □ No obvious impact on unrelated functionality?
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Only read the PR title Correct ✅ Review commits, files, and actual changes ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Approve without checking branch direction Correct ✅ Verify source and target branches ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Assume all changed files belong to the feature Correct ✅ Check for unrelated or accidental changes ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Request changes without explaining the issue Correct ✅ Give clear and useful feedback ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Think approval automatically merges the PR Correct ✅ Approval and merging are separate actions ──────────────────── Mistake 6 ❌ Create a new PR after every correction Correct ✅ Push new commits to the same source branch to update the existing PR
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
BRANCHES Check Direction COMMITS Check What Was Added FILES Check What Changed CODE Check Logic TEST Verify Behavior DECISION Approve / Request Changes / Comment
Quick Summary

StepWhat to Do
1Check source and target branches
2Read the PR title and description
3Review commits
4Check changed files
5Review actual code differences
6Look for unwanted changes or problems
7Verify behavior with available checks or tests
8Approve, request changes, or leave comments

Final Definition: Reviewing changes is the process of examining a Pull Request's branches, commits, files, and code differences to verify the proposed work before deciding to approve it, request changes, or provide feedback.
practice: Use an existing Pull Request, preferably one created from your own practice feature branch.
Step 1: Open the Pull Request.
Step 2: Check the Pull Request direction:
Source Branch feature/practice ↓ Pull Request ↓ Target Branch main
Step 3: Read the Pull Request title and ask whether it clearly describes the change.
Step 4: Read the description and compare it with the actual purpose of the Pull Request.
Step 5: Review the commits included in the Pull Request.
Step 6: Check every changed file and identify whether it belongs to the feature.
Step 7: Review the important code differences.
For each change, ask:
What changed? Why did it change? Does it solve the requirement? Could it create a problem? Is any important case missing?
Step 8: Check whether there are unwanted or unrelated changes.
Step 9: If available, run or verify the relevant checks and tests.
Step 10: Leave at least one practice comment, for example:
Could you explain why this condition is needed?
Step 11: Choose the appropriate review result based on your findings:
Everything Looks Good ↓ Approve Issue Found ↓ Request Changes Need Clarification ↓ Leave Comment
Step 12: If changes are requested, update the same feature branch and push another commit:
git add . git commit -m "Address review feedback" git push
Then review the updated Pull Request again.
Open PR ↓ Review ↓ Issue Found ↓ Request Changes ↓ Fix Code ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Review Again ↓ Approve ↓ Merge
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is the first branch-related thing you should check in a PR? 2. What should you compare with the PR description? 3. Why should you review changed files? 4. What do + and - generally represent in a code comparison? 5. Name the three common review decisions. 6. Does approving automatically merge the Pull Request? 7. What can happen when new commits are pushed to the PR's source branch? 8. Complete: Review → ______ / Request Changes / Comment.

Practice Goal: You should be able to systematically review a Pull Request by checking its branch direction, title, description, commits, changed files, and code differences, then provide useful feedback or choose an appropriate review decision.

qna.q: Q1. What does reviewing changes mean?
qna.a: It means examining the proposed branches, commits, files, and code differences in a Pull Request before deciding whether the changes are ready to proceed.

qna.q: Q2. What should you check first about the Pull Request branches?
qna.a: You should verify the correct source branch and target branch.

qna.q: Q3. Why should you review the Pull Request description?
qna.a: To understand the intended change and verify whether the actual changes match that purpose.

qna.q: Q4. Why should you review changed files?
qna.a: To verify that expected files were changed and to identify unwanted or unrelated files.

qna.q: Q5. What do + and - generally represent in a code comparison?
qna.a: + generally represents an added line, while - generally represents a removed line.

qna.q: Q6. Name three common review decisions.
qna.a: Approve, Request Changes, and Comment.

qna.q: Q7. Does approving a Pull Request automatically merge it?
qna.a: No. Approval and merging are separate actions.

qna.q: Q8. What should you do if you find an important issue during review?
qna.a: Request changes and clearly explain the issue.

qna.q: Q9. What can happen if a new commit is pushed to the source branch while the Pull Request is open?
qna.a: The existing Pull Request can update to include the new commit.

qna.q: Q10. What makes review feedback useful?
qna.a: It clearly explains the concern and, when possible, describes the expected improvement or asks a specific question.

qna.q: Q11. What is the difference between reviewing changes and approving?
qna.a: Reviewing is the process of examining the changes, while approving is one possible decision after the review.

qna.q: Q12. Complete: Check Branches → Check Commits → Check Files → Check Code → ______.
qna.a: Make a review decision such as Approve, Request Changes, or Comment.

items.title: Merge a Pull Request
explanation: Simple Meaning
After a Pull Request has been reviewed and is ready, merging the Pull Request combines the changes from the source branch into the target branch.
feature/login Contains New Changes ↓ Pull Request ↓ Review + Approval ↓ MERGE PULL REQUEST ⭐ ↓ main Receives the Changes
Simple Definition: Merging a Pull Request integrates the approved changes from the Pull Request's source branch into its target branch.
Where Does Merge Fit in the Workflow? ⭐
Create Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Review Changes ↓ Approve / Ready to Merge ↓ MERGE PULL REQUEST ⭐
Example Before Merging
Suppose a Pull Request was created from feature/login into main.
main ● A ● B feature/login ● A ● B ● C Add login page ● D Add validation ● E Fix login issue
The Pull Request proposes bringing the feature branch changes into main.
feature/login ● C ● D ● E ↓ Pull Request ↓ main
Before Merging a Pull Request ⭐
Before merging, check that the Pull Request is ready according to your project's workflow.
Check Before Merge ✓ Correct source branch ✓ Correct target branch ✓ Changes reviewed ✓ Required changes completed ✓ Required checks completed ✓ Ready to integrate
Step 1: Open the Pull Request
Open the Pull Request that contains the changes you want to merge.
Repository ↓ Pull Requests ↓ Select Pull Request ↓ Review Final Status
Step 2: Verify the Branch Direction ⭐
Always check where the changes are coming from and where they will go.
Source Branch feature/login ↓ MERGE ↓ Target Branch main

Branch TypeExamplePurpose
Source Branchfeature/loginContains the proposed changes
Target BranchmainReceives the merged changes
Step 3: Review the Final Changes
Before merging, perform a final check of the commits and changed files to make sure the Pull Request contains the intended work.
Final Check ↓ Commits ↓ Changed Files ↓ Code Differences ↓ Expected Result? Yes → Continue No → Fix Before Merge
Step 4: Merge the Pull Request ⭐
When the Pull Request is ready, choose the merge action available for the repository and confirm the merge.
Pull Request Ready ↓ Choose Merge ↓ Confirm Merge ↓ Source Changes Integrated ↓ Target Branch Updated
What Happens After Merge?
The target branch receives the changes included in the Pull Request according to the selected merge method.
Before Merge main ● A ● B feature/login ● A ● B ● C ● D ↓ MERGE After Merge main ● A ● B ● C ● D
The Pull Request Is Now Merged
After a successful merge, the Pull Request is typically shown as merged, and the proposed changes are now part of the target branch.
Pull Request OPEN ↓ Review ↓ Ready ↓ MERGED ✅
Merge Does Not Mean the Feature Branch Must Always Remain
After the changes have been successfully integrated, a temporary feature branch may no longer be needed. Depending on the workflow, it can be deleted after merging.
feature/login ↓ Merged into main ↓ Feature Complete ↓ Branch May Be Deleted
Delete the Feature Branch After Merge
If the branch is no longer needed, it can be deleted from the remote repository through the repository interface. You can also later remove the local branch when appropriate.
Before main feature/login ↓ Merge feature/login ↓ After main feature/login Optional: Delete if no longer needed
Merge Pull Request vs Create Pull Request ⭐

Create Pull RequestMerge Pull Request
Proposes changesIntegrates changes
Starts the review processCompletes integration into the target branch
Source and target are comparedApproved changes are combined
Target branch is not yet updated by creating the PR aloneTarget branch receives the merged changes
Create PR ↓ Propose Changes ──────────────────── Merge PR ↓ Integrate Changes
Merge Pull Request vs Approve ⭐

ApproveMerge
Review decisionIntegration action
Indicates the reviewer is satisfiedCombines changes into the target branch
Does not itself change the target branchUpdates the target branch with the merged changes
Review ↓ Approve ↓ Ready to Merge ↓ Merge ↓ Target Branch Updated
Common Merge Methods

Depending on repository settings, a Pull Request may offer different merge methods. The main purpose is the same: integrate the Pull Request changes into the target branch, but the commit history can be recorded differently.

Merge MethodGeneral Result
Merge CommitCombines histories and creates a merge commit
Squash and MergeCombines the Pull Request changes into a single commit before integration
Rebase and MergeApplies the Pull Request commits onto the target branch history without a merge commit
Pull Request ↓ Choose Merge Method ├── Merge Commit ├── Squash and Merge └── Rebase and Merge ↓ Target Branch Updated
Merge Commit
A merge commit method creates a separate commit that records the merge of the branch histories.
Before main ● A ● B \ ● C feature/login ● D ↓ Merge Commit main ● A ● B \ \ \ ● C \ ● D ● M Merge Commit
Squash and Merge
Squash and merge combines the Pull Request changes into one commit on the target branch.
Feature Branch ● C Add login page ● D Add validation ● E Fix login bug ↓ Squash main ● A ● B ● S Add login feature
This can produce a simpler target branch history by representing the Pull Request work as one commit.
Rebase and Merge
Rebase and merge places the Pull Request commits onto the target branch history without creating a merge commit.
Before main ● A ● B feature/login ● A ● B ● C ● D ↓ Rebase and Merge main ● A ● B ● C ● D
Which Merge Method Should You Use?
Follow your project's repository rules and team workflow. Different teams may prefer merge commits, squash merges, or rebase-based workflows for different reasons.
Important: Do not choose a merge method only because it looks simpler. Understand the repository's workflow and use the method expected by the project.
What If There Is a Merge Conflict? ⚠️
If the source and target branches contain incompatible changes, Git may require the conflict to be resolved before the Pull Request can be merged.
Pull Request ↓ Attempt Merge ↓ Conflict? NO → Merge Successfully ✅ YES → Resolve Conflict ↓ Commit Resolution ↓ Push ↓ Merge Again
A merge conflict does not automatically mean the Pull Request is wrong. It means Git needs help deciding how conflicting changes should be combined.
What If New Changes Are Added Before Merge?

If additional commits are pushed to the Pull Request's source branch before merging, the Pull Request can update to include those commits. Review requirements may need to be satisfied again depending on the repository rules.
PR Ready ↓ New Commit Added ↓ git push ↓ PR Updates ↓ Review Again if Required ↓ Merge
Important: Merge Updates the Target Branch ⭐
If you merge feature/login into main, the main branch receives the integrated changes.
feature/login ↓ MERGE ↓ main Result: main now includes login feature changes
This is different from simply pushing the feature branch.
git push feature/login ↓ Updates Remote Feature Branch ──────────────────── Merge Pull Request ↓ Updates Target Branch
After Merging: Update Your Local main
If you have a local repository, you may need to switch to your local target branch and pull the latest remote changes after the Pull Request is merged.
git switch main git pull
Pull Request Merged on GitHub ↓ Remote main Updated ↓ Your Local main May Be Behind ↓ git switch main ↓ git pull ↓ Local main Updated
Complete Example Workflow ⭐

1. Create feature/login ↓ 2. Make Changes ↓ 3. Commit Changes ↓ 4. Push Branch ↓ 5. Create Pull Request ↓ 6. Review Changes ↓ 7. Request Changes if Needed ↓ 8. Update + Push Again ↓ 9. Approve / Ready to Merge ↓ 10. Merge Pull Request ↓ 11. main Updated ↓ 12. Update Local main ↓ 13. Delete Feature Branch if No Longer Needed
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Creating a PR means the code is already in main Correct ✅ The code reaches the target branch after merging ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Approval and merge are the same action Correct ✅ Approval is a review decision; merge integrates changes ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Push feature branch = merge into main Correct ✅ Pushing updates the feature branch; merging updates the target branch ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Merge without checking branch direction Correct ✅ Verify source and target branches first ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Local main automatically updates after merging on GitHub Correct ✅ Update your local main, for example by switching to it and pulling ──────────────────── Mistake 6 ❌ Every feature branch must be deleted immediately Correct ✅ Delete it when it is no longer needed according to the project workflow
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
PUSH Send Feature Branch to GitHub PULL REQUEST Propose Changes REVIEW Check Changes APPROVE Review Decision MERGE ⭐ Integrate into Target Branch PULL Update Local Branch
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
Merge Pull RequestIntegrate source branch changes into the target branch
Source BranchContains the proposed changes
Target BranchReceives the merged changes
ApproveReview decision; does not itself merge
MergeIntegrates the changes
Merge ConflictRequires conflicting changes to be resolved before integration
After MergeUpdate your local target branch if needed
Final Definition: Merging a Pull Request integrates the approved changes from the source branch into the target branch. After a successful merge, the target branch contains the Pull Request changes.
practice: Use a practice Pull Request that you are allowed to merge. Do not merge changes into an important shared branch unless you are authorized to do so.
Step 1: Open your Pull Request.
Step 2: Verify the branch direction:
Source feature/merge-practice ↓ Pull Request ↓ Target main
Step 3: Review the final commits and changed files.
Step 4: Check that the Pull Request is ready to merge according to the repository workflow.
Step 5: Select the appropriate merge action and confirm the merge.
Step 6: Verify that the Pull Request is marked as merged.
Step 7: Check that the target branch now contains the intended changes.
Step 8: Update your local target branch:
git switch main git pull
Step 9: Verify the merged changes locally:
git log --oneline
Step 10: If the feature branch is no longer needed and your workflow allows it, delete the branch.
Open PR ↓ Check Source + Target ↓ Review Final Changes ↓ Ready? ↓ Merge ↓ PR Marked Merged ↓ Target Branch Updated ↓ Update Local main ↓ Delete Feature Branch if No Longer Needed
Final Understanding Check:

1. What does merging a Pull Request do? 2. In feature/login → main, which branch receives the changes? 3. Is approving the same as merging? 4. What is the difference between pushing a feature branch and merging a Pull Request? 5. What may need to happen if a merge conflict exists? 6. Name one common merge method. 7. What command sequence can update your local main after a PR is merged remotely? 8. Complete: Pull Request → Review → Approve → ______.

Practice Goal: You should be able to verify a Pull Request, merge it into the correct target branch, understand the difference between approval and merging, update your local branch afterward, and understand that a feature branch may be deleted when it is no longer needed.

qna.q: Q1. What does merging a Pull Request do?
qna.a: It integrates the changes from the Pull Request's source branch into the target branch.

qna.q: Q2. In feature/login → main, which branch is the source branch?
qna.a: feature/login

qna.q: Q3. In feature/login → main, which branch receives the merged changes?
qna.a: main

qna.q: Q4. Is approving a Pull Request the same as merging it?
qna.a: No. Approval is a review decision, while merging integrates the changes into the target branch.

qna.q: Q5. What happens to main after feature/login is successfully merged into it?
qna.a: main receives and contains the integrated changes from feature/login.

qna.q: Q6. What is the difference between pushing a feature branch and merging a Pull Request?
qna.a: Pushing updates the remote feature branch, while merging integrates the Pull Request changes into the target branch.

qna.q: Q7. What may be required if a merge conflict prevents merging?
qna.a: The conflicting changes need to be resolved before the Pull Request can be successfully merged.

qna.q: Q8. Name three common merge methods.
qna.a: Merge Commit, Squash and Merge, and Rebase and Merge.

qna.q: Q9. What command sequence can commonly update your local main after a PR is merged remotely?
qna.a: git switch main followed by git pull.

qna.q: Q10. Does merging a Pull Request automatically mean the feature branch must remain forever?
qna.a: No. If the branch is no longer needed, it may be deleted according to the project workflow.

qna.q: Q11. What should you verify before merging?
qna.a: Verify the correct source and target branches, review status, required changes or checks, and that the Pull Request is ready to integrate.

qna.q: Q12. Complete: Create Branch → Commit → Push → Pull Request → Review → Approve → ______.
qna.a: Merge.

items.title: Resolve Conflicts in a Team Workflow
explanation: Simple Meaning
In a team workflow, a merge conflict can happen when two or more developers change overlapping parts of the same code and Git cannot automatically decide which change should be kept.
Developer A Changes Same Code ↓ ├── Merge / Pull Request ──┐ │ ↓ Developer B Git Cannot Decide Changes Same Code ↓ CONFLICT ⚠️ ↓ Team Resolves It ↓ Merge

Simple Definition: Resolving conflicts in a team workflow means coordinating with other developers, understanding overlapping changes, choosing the correct final code, resolving the Git conflict, testing the result, and then completing the merge.
Where Does This Happen in a Team Workflow? ⭐

Developer Creates Branch ↓ Makes Changes ↓ Commit + Push ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Other Changes Also Reach Target Branch ↓ Merge Conflict? ⚠️ ↓ YES → Resolve Conflict ↓ Review Final Result ↓ Test ↓ Merge
Why Are Team Conflicts Different?
When working alone, you usually know why every change was made. In a team, another developer's change may contain important logic that you should not accidentally remove.
Your Change ↓ Understand Purpose Team Member's Change ↓ Understand Purpose ↓ Compare Both ↓ Choose Correct Final Code ↓ Resolve Conflict
The goal is not simply to make the conflict markers disappear. The goal is to preserve the correct intended behavior from the team's changes.
Example Team Situation ⭐
Suppose two developers start from the same version of main.
main ● A ● B ↓ ┌───┴───┐ ↓ ↓ Dev A Dev B ↓ ↓ feature/login feature/security
Developer A changes a validation function while Developer B changes the same part of that function.
Developer A function validate() { checkUsername(); } ──────────────────── Developer B function validate() { checkPassword(); }
Git may be unable to automatically determine the correct combined result.
Step 1: Do Not Immediately Choose Ours or Theirs ⚠️
When a conflict appears, do not automatically keep your version or automatically keep the other version.
Conflict Found ↓ Do NOT Guess ❌ ↓ Understand Both Changes ⭐ ↓ Why Was Your Change Made? Why Was Their Change Made? ↓ Choose Correct Final Result
Both changes may be needed.
Your Change checkUsername(); Their Change checkPassword(); Possible Final Result checkUsername(); checkPassword();
Step 2: Identify Who Made the Other Change
Before changing important code, understand the context of the conflicting change. Check the commit, Pull Request, or ask the team member if the purpose is unclear.
Conflict ↓ Check Commit History ↓ Check Pull Request Context ↓ Understand Purpose ↓ Still Unclear? ↓ Ask Developer / Team
Communication is especially important when the conflict affects business logic, shared functionality, database changes, or critical production code.
Step 3: Communicate With the Team ⭐
If you do not understand why the conflicting code exists, ask before removing or changing it.

Example Message:

Hi, I am resolving a conflict between my login validation changes and your recent changes in validation.js. I see that you changed this condition for password validation. Is this logic required for your feature? I want to make sure both changes are preserved correctly.
A good conflict-resolution message should identify the file or area, explain the conflict, and ask about the purpose of the change.
Step 4: Update Your Branch With the Latest Target Branch
In a Pull Request workflow, conflicts often appear because the target branch has changed after your feature branch was created.
feature/login Created ↓ main Changes Later ↓ feature/login Is Behind main ↓ Pull Request ↓ Possible Conflict
One common approach is to bring the latest target branch changes into your local branch before resolving the conflict.
git switch feature/login git fetch origin git merge origin/main
This example merges the latest remote main changes into your current feature branch.
Before origin/main ● A ● B ● C New Team Change feature/login ● A ● B ● D Your Change ↓ Merge origin/main into feature/login ↓ Conflict? ↓ Resolve if Required
Step 5: Read the Conflict Carefully ⭐
Git marks the conflicting sections so you can compare both versions.
<<<<<<< HEAD checkUsername(); ======= checkPassword(); >>>>>>> origin/main

SectionMeaning
<<<<<<< HEADBeginning of the current version being compared
Before =======One side of the conflicting changes
After =======The other side of the conflicting changes
>>>>>>>End of the conflict section

Important: The exact labels shown in conflict markers can depend on the Git operation being performed. Read the surrounding context instead of assuming that one label always means the same branch in every situation.
Step 6: Decide the Correct Final Code
There are usually three possibilities.

DecisionMeaning
Keep your changeYour version is the correct final behavior
Keep their changeThe other version is the correct final behavior
Combine both ⭐Both changes are needed in the final result
Conflict ↓ Understand Requirement ↓ ├── Keep Yours ├── Keep Theirs └── Combine Both ⭐ ↓ Final Correct Code
Example: Combining Both Changes ⭐
Suppose the conflict is:
<<<<<<< HEAD checkUsername(); ======= checkPassword(); >>>>>>> origin/main
After discussing the requirements, you discover that both validations are required.
The final code can become:
checkUsername(); checkPassword();
Then remove all conflict markers.
Step 7: Check for Remaining Conflict Markers ⚠️
Before continuing, make sure the file does not still contain unresolved conflict markers.
Wrong ❌ <<<<<<< HEAD ======= >>>>>>> ──────────────────── Correct ✅ Clean Final Code No Conflict Markers
Leaving conflict markers in the code can break the application or cause invalid source code.
Step 8: Check Git Status
Use git status to see which files still need attention.
git status
git status ↓ Check Unmerged / Resolved Files ↓ Resolve All Required Files ↓ Continue
Step 9: Test the Combined Result ⭐
Conflict resolution can produce code that is syntactically valid but logically incorrect. Test the result after resolving the conflict.
Resolve Conflict ↓ Code Looks Clean ↓ Run Tests / Build ↓ Manual Verification if Needed ↓ Both Features Still Work? YES → Continue NO → Fix Again
In a team workflow, verify that your changes and the other developer's changes still work together.
Step 10: Stage the Resolved Files
After resolving and checking the files, stage them.
git add validation.js
Or, if appropriate for the changes you are resolving:
git add .
Step 11: Complete the Merge
If you are resolving a conflict during a normal merge, after all conflicts are resolved and staged, complete the merge with a commit.
git commit
Git may open a default merge commit message that you can review and save.
Conflict ↓ Resolve Files ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ Merge Completed
Step 12: Push the Resolved Changes
After the merge is successfully completed on your feature branch, push the updated branch.
git push
Local Feature Branch Conflict Resolved ↓ Merge Completed ↓ git push ↓ Remote Feature Branch Updated ↓ Pull Request Updates
Complete Team Workflow Example ⭐

Developer A Creates feature/login ↓ Makes Changes ↓ Commit + Push ↓ Creates PR to main Meanwhile... Developer B Merges Changes into main ↓ main Changes ↓ Developer A's PR Has Conflict ↓ Developer A Checks Latest main ↓ Brings Latest main Into feature/login ↓ Conflict Appears ↓ Understand Both Changes ↓ Communicate if Needed ↓ Resolve Correctly ↓ Test ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ git push ↓ PR Updated ↓ Review ↓ Merge
Do Not Resolve Conflicts Blindly ⚠️
The fastest-looking solution is not always the correct solution.

Conflict ↓ Delete One Side Quickly ❌ Could Accidentally Remove: • Another Feature • Important Bug Fix • Security Logic • Database Logic • Team Member's Work ──────────────────── Better ⭐ Understand ↓ Communicate ↓ Resolve ↓ Test
When Should You Ask Another Developer?

Ask for Help When: ✓ You do not understand the other change ✓ Both changes affect the same business logic ✓ Database changes conflict ✓ Production-critical code is affected ✓ Security-related code is affected ✓ Tests fail after combining changes ✓ You are unsure which behavior is correct
Who Should Resolve the Conflict?

There is no single answer for every team. Often, the developer responsible for the Pull Request resolves conflicts in their branch because they need to update the proposed changes. For complex conflicts, the developers who made the conflicting changes may work together.
Simple Conflict ↓ PR Author May Resolve ──────────────────── Complex Shared Logic ↓ Developers Discuss Together ↓ Resolve + Test
Merge Conflict vs Logical Conflict ⭐

Merge ConflictLogical Conflict
Git cannot automatically combine the changesGit combines changes successfully, but the combined behavior is wrong
Git stops and asks for resolutionMay not show any Git warning
Conflict markers can appearTesting and review are needed to detect it
Merge Conflict Git Says: I Need Help ↓ Resolve Markers ──────────────────── Logical Conflict Git Says: Merge Successful ↓ But Combined Code May Be Wrong ↓ Review + Test Required ⭐
Example of a Logical Conflict

Developer A changes a function to return values in rupees while Developer B changes another part to expect values in paise. Git might merge both changes without conflict, but the application logic can still become incorrect.
Git Merge Successful ✅ ↓ Application Logic Incorrect ❌ ↓ Why? Changes Did Not Conflict Textually, But They Conflict Functionally
This is why team communication, code review, and testing are important even when Git reports no merge conflict.
Conflict Prevention in a Team ⭐

1. Pull / Sync Regularly ↓ 2. Keep Branches Short-Lived ↓ 3. Communicate Who Is Changing Shared Files ↓ 4. Make Small Focused Changes ↓ 5. Create Smaller Pull Requests ↓ 6. Merge Reviewed Changes Regularly ↓ 7. Review Before Merge ↓ 8. Test Combined Changes
Useful Team Communication Example

Example:

Hi team, I am currently updating inventory.js around the stock calculation function. Please let me know if anyone is changing the same section so we can coordinate before merging.
This type of communication can reduce the chance of two developers independently changing the same critical code area.
Merge-Based Conflict Resolution Workflow
git switch feature/login git fetch origin git merge origin/main
If a conflict occurs:
Resolve Files Manually ↓ Test Changes ↓ git add <resolved-files> ↓ git commit ↓ git push
Abort If You Need to Start Again ⚠️
If you are in the middle of a merge and decide you should stop and return to the state before that merge attempt, Git provides a merge abort command.
git merge --abort
Use this carefully and only when you intend to cancel the current merge operation.
Merge Started ↓ Conflict Too Complex? ↓ Need to Recheck Requirements? ↓ git merge --abort ↓ Stop Current Merge Attempt ↓ Discuss / Plan ↓ Try Again Later
Important Team Rule 🧠
CONFLICT ≠ DELETE CODE CONFLICT ↓ UNDERSTAND BOTH CHANGES ↓ COMMUNICATE IF NEEDED ↓ CHOOSE CORRECT RESULT ↓ REMOVE MARKERS ↓ TEST ↓ COMMIT ↓ PUSH
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Always keep your code Correct ⭐ Understand whether both changes are needed ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Always keep the other developer's code Correct ⭐ Understand the requirement before choosing ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Remove conflict markers without checking logic Correct ⭐ Verify the final combined code ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Resolve conflict but do not test Correct ⭐ Test that all affected functionality works together ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Delete another developer's work because it causes a conflict Correct ⭐ Discuss the change if its purpose is unclear ──────────────────── Mistake 6 ❌ Think no Git conflict means no problem Correct ⭐ Review and test for logical conflicts too
Quick Summary

StepAction
1Identify the conflict
2Understand your change and the other change
3Check commit or PR context
4Communicate with the team if unclear
5Choose the correct final code
6Remove all conflict markers
7Check git status
8Test the combined result
9Stage resolved files
10Complete the merge
11Push the updated branch

Final Definition: Resolving conflicts in a team workflow means carefully combining overlapping changes by understanding both developers' intentions, communicating when necessary, producing the correct final code, testing it, and then completing and sharing the resolved merge.
practice: Practice this in a test repository or practice branch. Do not intentionally create conflicts in an important shared branch.
Step 1: Create a practice branch:
git switch -c feature/conflict-team-practice
Step 2: Make a small change to a practice file and commit it:
git add . git commit -m "Add team conflict practice change"
Step 3: Push the branch:
git push -u origin feature/conflict-team-practice
Step 4: Simulate a teammate changing the same area through another branch or repository clone.
Step 5: Merge that teammate change into main.
Step 6: Return to your practice branch and get the latest remote information:
git switch feature/conflict-team-practice git fetch origin
Step 7: Bring the latest main changes into your branch:
git merge origin/main
Step 8: If a conflict occurs, do not immediately choose one version. Read both changes and decide whether to keep one or combine both.
Step 9: Edit the file and remove all conflict markers.
Step 10: Check the repository state:
git status
Step 11: Test the final combined code.
Step 12: Stage the resolved file:
git add <file-name>
Step 13: Complete the merge:
git commit
Step 14: Push the resolved branch:
git push
Step 15: Verify that the Pull Request or remote branch now contains the resolved result.
Practice Branch ↓ Your Change ↓ Team Change Reaches main ↓ git fetch origin ↓ git merge origin/main ↓ Conflict ↓ Understand Both Changes ↓ Combine Correctly ↓ Test ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ git push
Communication Practice: Imagine the other change is unclear. Write a message asking the teammate why the conflicting logic was added before changing or removing it.

Practice Goal: You should be able to resolve a team conflict without blindly deleting code, understand both sides of the conflict, communicate when required, create the correct combined result, test it, commit the resolution, and push the updated branch.

qna.q: Q1. Why is resolving a conflict in a team workflow more than simply removing conflict markers?
qna.a: Because you must understand the purpose of both developers' changes and produce the correct final behavior, not just make Git accept the file.

qna.q: Q2. What should you do before deleting another developer's conflicting code?
qna.a: Understand why the code was added. Check the commit or Pull Request context and ask the developer or team if the purpose is unclear.

qna.q: Q3. What are three possible decisions when resolving a conflict?
qna.a: Keep your change, keep the other change, or combine both changes.

qna.q: Q4. Why might combining both changes be the correct solution?
qna.a: Because both developers' changes may be required for the final application behavior.

qna.q: Q5. What command can show which files still need attention during conflict resolution?
qna.a: git status

qna.q: Q6. Why should you test after resolving a conflict?
qna.a: Because the final combined code may be logically incorrect even after the conflict markers are removed.

qna.q: Q7. What is a logical conflict?
qna.a: It is when Git combines the code successfully but the combined behavior is incorrect or incompatible.

qna.q: Q8. What is one common approach to bring the latest remote main changes into a feature branch?
qna.a: git fetch origin followed by git merge origin/main while working on the feature branch.

qna.q: Q9. What should happen after resolving the files during a normal merge conflict?
qna.a: Stage the resolved files, complete the merge with a commit, and push the updated branch.

qna.q: Q10. When should you communicate with another developer during conflict resolution?
qna.a: When you do not understand the other change or when the correct final behavior is unclear.

qna.q: Q11. What command can cancel an in-progress merge if you need to stop the current merge attempt?
qna.a: git merge --abort

qna.q: Q12. Complete: Understand → Communicate if needed → Resolve → ______ → Commit → Push.
qna.a: Test.

items.title: Issues
explanation: Simple Meaning
A GitHub Issue is used to record, discuss, plan, and track work in a repository. Issues can be used for bugs, new features, tasks, ideas, feedback, and other work that needs to be tracked.
Problem / Task / Idea ↓ Create Issue ⭐ ↓ Discuss + Track Work ↓ Assign Developer ↓ Work on Solution ↓ Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Merge ↓ Close Issue
Simple Definition: A GitHub Issue is a place in a repository where a team can record and track a bug, task, feature request, idea, or other piece of work.
Where Do Issues Fit in a Team Workflow? ⭐
Bug / Requirement / Task ↓ Create Issue ↓ Discuss + Plan ↓ Assign Work ↓ Create Feature Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit + Push ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Merge ↓ Close Issue
Issues help teams organize work before and during development. GitHub describes Issues as a way to track ideas, feedback, tasks, and bugs. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
Example: Bug Report ⭐
Suppose users cannot log in when they enter a valid username and password.

Issue Title:
Login fails with valid credentials

Description:
Users are unable to log in even when valid credentials are entered.

Expected Result:
User should successfully log in.

Actual Result:
An error message is displayed.
Bug Found ↓ Create Issue #25 ↓ Developer Investigates ↓ Create Branch fix/login-error ↓ Fix Problem ↓ Pull Request ↓ Merge ↓ Close Issue #25
Common Types of Issues

Issue TypeExample
BugLogin button does not work
Feature RequestAdd dark mode
TaskUpdate project documentation
EnhancementImprove search performance
QuestionShould this API support pagination?
IdeaAdd notification settings
Issue Number ⭐
Every Issue has its own number inside the repository.
Repository Issues #21 Fix login error #22 Add dark mode #23 Update README #24 Improve search speed
The number makes it easy to reference a specific Issue in discussions, commits, and Pull Requests.
Fixes #21
This means the work or Pull Request is referring to Issue number 21.
How to Create an Issue ⭐
Open Repository ↓ Click Issues ↓ Click New Issue ↓ Select Template if Available ↓ Add Title ↓ Add Description ↓ Add Details if Needed ↓ Submit Issue

In GitHub's repository interface, you can open the Issues section, create a new issue, provide a title and description, and optionally add information such as assignees, labels, milestones, issue type, or project details depending on your permissions and repository setup. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
1. Write a Clear Issue Title ⭐
The title should clearly explain the problem or work item.
Good Titles ✅ Fix login error when password contains spaces Add dark mode to user settings Improve inventory report loading speed ──────────────────── Poor Titles ❌ Bug Issue Problem Fix this
2. Add a Useful Description ⭐
The description should provide enough information for someone else to understand the Issue and work on it.

Example Bug Issue:

Problem: Inventory report shows incorrect quantity.

Steps to Reproduce:
1. Open Inventory Report
2. Select store BM11
3. Search the report

Expected Result:
Correct quantity should be displayed.

Actual Result:
Quantity is different from the expected value.
For bug reports, useful details can include how to reproduce the problem, the expected result, and the actual result. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
3. Add Labels
Labels help categorize and organize Issues.
Issue ↓ Labels bug feature documentation help wanted high priority

Label ExamplePossible Meaning
bugSomething is not working correctly
featureNew functionality is requested
documentationDocumentation-related work
high priorityWork requires higher attention
The exact labels depend on how the repository or team organizes its work.
4. Assign the Issue
An Issue can be assigned to a developer or team member so everyone can understand who is responsible for working on it.
Issue #25 Fix Login Error ↓ Assigned To ↓ Developer A ↓ Developer A Works on Issue
Assignees are used to clarify who is working on a particular Issue or Pull Request. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
5. Add a Milestone
A milestone can be used to group related work around a larger goal or target.
Milestone: Version 2.0 Issues: ✓ #21 Login Fix ✓ #22 Dark Mode ✓ #23 API Update ✓ #24 Documentation
GitHub supports milestones for tracking progress across groups of Issues and Pull Requests. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}
Issue Templates
Some repositories provide Issue templates or forms to help users submit information in a consistent format.
New Issue ↓ Choose Template ├── Bug Report ├── Feature Request ├── Documentation └── Other
A template may ask for specific information such as the problem, steps to reproduce, expected behavior, and actual behavior.
Example Team Workflow ⭐

Tester Finds Bug ↓ Creates Issue #45 ↓ Team Discusses Problem ↓ Issue Assigned to Developer ↓ Developer Creates Branch fix/issue-45-login ↓ Developer Fixes Bug ↓ Commit Changes ↓ Push Branch ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Review Changes ↓ Merge Pull Request ↓ Issue Resolved ↓ Close Issue
Issues and Branches
A team may include the Issue number in a branch name to make the branch purpose easier to identify.
fix/issue-45-login
Issue #45 Fix Login Error ↓ Branch fix/issue-45-login ↓ Development Work
This naming style is a team convention, not a mandatory Git rule.
Issues and Commits
Commit messages can also reference an Issue number.
git commit -m "Fix login validation #45"
The exact conventions for linking commits and Issues can depend on the team's workflow.
Issues and Pull Requests ⭐
An Issue describes or tracks work, while a Pull Request proposes the code changes made to complete that work.

IssuePull Request
Tracks a problem or piece of workProposes code changes
Can describe a bug or requirementContains commits and changed files
Used for planning and discussionUsed for review and merging
Can exist before development startsUsually follows development work
ISSUE What needs to be done? ↓ Developer Works ↓ PULL REQUEST How was it changed? ↓ Review ↓ Merge
Linking an Issue and Pull Request
A Pull Request can reference the Issue it addresses. This helps the team understand why the code changes were made.
Issue #45 Fix Login Error ↓ Pull Request Fixes #45 ↓ Merged ↓ Issue Can Be Closed According to Workflow
Always verify the repository workflow and GitHub behavior for the exact closing keywords and branch settings being used.
Issue Status
At a basic level, an Issue can be open while work or discussion is ongoing and closed when the team considers it completed or no longer applicable.
OPEN Issue Created ↓ Discussion / Work ↓ Fix / Complete Work ↓ CLOSED
Closing an Issue
An Issue can be closed when the problem has been resolved, the requested work is complete, or the team decides that the Issue should not continue.
Issue Open ↓ Work Completed ↓ Verify Result ↓ Close Issue
Closing an Issue should follow the team's workflow rather than automatically meaning that every discussion has been solved.
Reopening an Issue
If an Issue was closed but the problem still exists or additional work is required, it can be reopened.
Issue Closed ↓ Problem Still Exists? YES → Reopen Issue ↓ Continue Work NO → Keep Closed
Comments and Discussion
Team members can use an Issue for discussion and updates.
Issue Created ↓ Comment: I can reproduce this problem ↓ Comment: Root cause found ↓ Comment: Fix is ready in PR #52 ↓ Review + Merge ↓ Close Issue
This keeps important context about the work in one place.
Sub-Issues

Large pieces of work can be broken into smaller sub-issues so the team can track individual tasks separately. GitHub supports hierarchical relationships between parent issues and sub-issues. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
Parent Issue Add Payment Feature ├── Sub-Issue #101 │ Create Payment API │ ├── Sub-Issue #102 │ Create Payment UI │ └── Sub-Issue #103 Add Payment Tests
Issue Dependencies
Some work cannot start until another task is completed. GitHub Issues can also represent dependencies between pieces of work. :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}
Issue #20 Create Database Table ↓ Must Complete First ↓ Issue #21 Create Database API ↓ Must Complete First ↓ Issue #22 Create User Interface
Issue vs Commit vs Pull Request ⭐

ConceptMain Purpose
IssueTrack and discuss work
BranchWork separately on changes
CommitSave a snapshot of changes
Pull RequestPropose and review changes
MergeIntegrate changes into the target branch
Issue What needs to be done? ↓ Branch Where work happens ↓ Commit Save progress ↓ Pull Request Propose changes ↓ Review Check changes ↓ Merge Integrate changes ↓ Close Issue Work completed
Good Issue Checklist ⭐

□ Clear title □ Explain the problem or task □ Add reproduction steps if it is a bug □ Mention expected result □ Mention actual result if applicable □ Add useful labels □ Assign the correct person if needed □ Add milestone if needed □ Add related context or references □ Keep discussion relevant
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Use a vague title like 'Bug' Correct ✅ Describe the actual problem ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Create an Issue without enough details Correct ✅ Explain what happened and provide useful context ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Think an Issue contains the code changes Correct ✅ Issues track work; Pull Requests propose code changes ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Close an Issue without verifying the work Correct ✅ Verify that the problem or task is actually completed ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Use one large Issue for every small task Correct ✅ Break large work into smaller trackable tasks when useful ──────────────────── Mistake 6 ❌ Ignore comments and team discussion Correct ✅ Use the Issue to preserve useful context about the work
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
ISSUE What is the problem or task? BRANCH Where do I work separately? COMMIT Save my changes PULL REQUEST Ask to review my changes MERGE Add changes to target branch CLOSE ISSUE Work is completed
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
IssueTracks a bug, task, idea, feature, or other work
Issue NumberUnique reference number within the repository
LabelHelps categorize an Issue
AssigneeShows who is responsible for work
MilestoneGroups work around a larger goal or target
OpenWork or discussion is ongoing
ClosedWork is completed or no longer needs to continue
Sub-IssueSmaller work item under a larger Issue
Pull RequestProposes the code changes for review

Final Definition: A GitHub Issue is a tool for recording, discussing, planning, assigning, and tracking work such as bugs, tasks, features, ideas, and feedback throughout a project's development workflow.
practice: Use a practice repository where Issues are enabled and where you have permission to create an Issue.
Step 1: Open your repository.
Step 2: Open the Issues section.
Step 3: Click New Issue.
Step 4: Create a practice Issue with a clear title:
Add practice dark mode button
Step 5: Add a useful description explaining what needs to be done.

Example Description:

Add a button that allows users to switch between light mode and dark mode. The selected mode should be applied to the page correctly.
Step 6: Add a label if your repository provides suitable labels.
Step 7: Assign the Issue if appropriate and permitted.
Step 8: Submit the Issue and note its Issue number.
Example Issue #10 Add practice dark mode button
Step 9: Create a branch related to the Issue:
git switch -c feature/issue-10-dark-mode
Step 10: Make a small practice change.
Step 11: Commit the changes:
git add . git commit -m "Add dark mode button for issue 10"
Step 12: Push the branch:
git push -u origin feature/issue-10-dark-mode
Step 13: Create a Pull Request and reference the related Issue according to your repository workflow.
Step 14: Review and merge the Pull Request when appropriate.
Step 15: Verify that the Issue work is complete and close the Issue according to the team's workflow.
Create Issue ↓ Issue #10 ↓ Create Branch feature/issue-10-dark-mode ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Merge ↓ Verify Work ↓ Close Issue
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is the main purpose of an Issue? 2. Name three types of work that can be tracked using Issues. 3. What should a good Issue title do? 4. What information is useful in a bug report? 5. What is the difference between an Issue and a Pull Request? 6. What is an assignee? 7. What is the purpose of labels? 8. Complete: Issue → Branch → Commit → Pull Request → Review → Merge → ______.

Practice Goal: You should be able to create a clear GitHub Issue, add useful details, understand labels and assignees, connect the Issue to development work, create a related branch and Pull Request, and close the Issue after the work is completed and verified.

qna.q: Q1. What is a GitHub Issue?
qna.a: It is a place in a repository used to record, discuss, plan, and track work such as bugs, tasks, features, ideas, or feedback.

qna.q: Q2. Name three things that can be tracked using Issues.
qna.a: Examples include bugs, feature requests, tasks, ideas, enhancements, and feedback.

qna.q: Q3. What should a good Issue title do?
qna.a: It should clearly describe the problem, task, or work item.

qna.q: Q4. What information is useful in a bug Issue?
qna.a: Useful information can include the problem, steps to reproduce it, the expected result, and the actual result.

qna.q: Q5. What is the difference between an Issue and a Pull Request?
qna.a: An Issue tracks or describes work, while a Pull Request proposes the code changes made for that work.

qna.q: Q6. What is an Issue number?
qna.a: It is the unique number used to identify an Issue within a repository.

qna.q: Q7. What is the purpose of labels?
qna.a: Labels help categorize and organize Issues.

qna.q: Q8. What is an assignee?
qna.a: An assignee is a person identified as responsible for working on an Issue or Pull Request.

qna.q: Q9. What is a milestone?
qna.a: A milestone can group related Issues and Pull Requests around a larger goal or target.

qna.q: Q10. What is a sub-issue?
qna.a: It is a smaller Issue connected under a larger parent Issue to break work into more manageable tasks.

qna.q: Q11. What is the difference between an open and closed Issue?
qna.a: An open Issue is still being discussed or worked on, while a closed Issue has been completed or is no longer being tracked.

qna.q: Q12. Complete: Issue → Branch → Commit → Pull Request → Review → Merge → ______.
qna.a: Close Issue.

items.title: Labels
explanation: Simple Meaning
GitHub Labels are tags used to categorize and organize Issues and Pull Requests. They help a team quickly understand the type, priority, status, or area of work.
Issue / Pull Request ↓ Add Label ↓ Understand Quickly 🐛 bug ✨ feature 📚 documentation 🔥 high priority ❓ question
Simple Definition: A GitHub Label is a tag attached to an Issue or Pull Request to help categorize and organize it.
Why Are Labels Used? ⭐
A repository may contain many Issues and Pull Requests. Labels make it easier to group and filter related work.

Without Labels ❌ #21 Login Error #22 Add Dark Mode #23 Update README #24 Slow Search #25 API Question Harder to Group ──────────────────── With Labels ✅ #21 🐛 bug #22 ✨ feature #23 📚 documentation #24 🐛 bug + 🔥 high priority #25 ❓ question
Common Types of Labels

LabelMeaning
bugSomething is not working correctly
featureNew functionality or feature
enhancementImprove existing functionality
documentationDocumentation-related work
questionRequires clarification or discussion
high priorityNeeds faster attention
help wantedAdditional help is needed
The exact labels used depend on the repository and the team's workflow.
Example: Bug Label ⭐
Issue #21 Login fails with valid credentials Labels: 🐛 bug 🔥 high priority
By looking at the labels, a developer can quickly understand that the Issue is a bug and needs higher attention.
One Issue Can Have Multiple Labels ⭐
An Issue or Pull Request is not limited to one label. Multiple labels can describe different aspects of the same work.
Issue #30 Improve Inventory Report Labels: 🐛 bug 📊 reports 🔥 high priority
Here, the labels describe the type of problem, the affected area, and the priority.
Labels Can Represent Different Categories

LABEL CATEGORIES 1. Type 🐛 bug ✨ feature 📚 documentation 2. Priority 🔥 high priority 🟡 medium priority 🟢 low priority 3. Area frontend backend database reports 4. Status / Workflow in progress needs review blocked
Teams can create their own label system. The important point is to use clear and consistent naming.
Example Team Workflow ⭐

Bug Found ↓ Create Issue #45 ↓ Add Labels 🐛 bug 🔥 high priority ↓ Assign Developer ↓ Developer Creates Branch ↓ Fixes Bug ↓ Creates Pull Request ↓ Add / Update Labels if Needed ↓ Review ↓ Merge ↓ Close Issue
How to Add a Label
Open Issue or Pull Request ↓ Find Labels Section ↓ Select Existing Label ↓ Label Added
If you have the required repository permissions, you may also be able to manage the repository's available labels.
Example Labels for a Project

IssueLabels
Login button not workingbug, frontend, high priority
Add export to Excelfeature, reports
Update READMEdocumentation
Improve SQL query performanceenhancement, backend
API response questionquestion, backend
Labels Help With Filtering ⭐
Labels can help you find related Issues or Pull Requests more easily.
All Issues ↓ Filter: bug ↓ Only Bug-Related Issues ──────────────────── All Issues ↓ Filter: high priority ↓ Only High-Priority Issues
This becomes especially useful when a repository has many open Issues.
Labels vs Assignees

LabelsAssignees
Describe or categorize the workShow who is responsible for the work
Example: bugExample: Developer A
Can have multiple labelsDepends on repository workflow
Help filter and organize workHelp clarify responsibility
Issue #45 Fix Login Error Label → What type of work is this? 🐛 bug 🔥 high priority Assignee → Who is working on it? Developer A
Labels vs Milestones

LabelsMilestones
Categorize the workGroup work around a larger goal
Example: bugExample: Version 2.0
Can describe type, priority, or areaUsually represents a target or larger release goal
Issue #45 Label: 🐛 bug Milestone: Version 2.0
Labels vs Issue Types
Labels are flexible tags chosen by the repository, while issue types, where enabled and used, provide a more structured way to classify work. A team may use both depending on its workflow.
Issue Type Structured Classification Example: Bug / Task / Feature ──────────────────── Label Flexible Tag Example: high priority / frontend / blocked
Good Label Naming ⭐
Good ✅ bug high priority frontend needs review Clear and Consistent ──────────────────── Poor ❌ issue1 urgent123 misc stuff check later maybe
A good label should make sense to the whole team without requiring someone to guess its meaning.
Create a Consistent Label System
TYPE bug feature enhancement documentation PRIORITY high priority medium priority low priority AREA frontend backend database reports STATUS in progress needs review blocked
A consistent system prevents duplicate or confusing labels such as having both bug and bugs when they mean the same thing.
Example: Using Labels to Find Work
Team Lead Needs High-Priority Bugs ↓ Filter Issues By: 🐛 bug AND 🔥 high priority ↓ Relevant Work Appears
Labels help teams quickly focus on a particular category of work.
Labels on Pull Requests
Labels can also be used on Pull Requests to help categorize the proposed changes.
Pull Request Add Dark Mode Labels: ✨ feature frontend needs review
This can help reviewers understand the general type and area of the changes.
Important: Labels Do Not Change Git Code
Label Added ↓ Git Branch? No Change Git Commit? No Change Git Files? No Change Labels Only Help Organize and Track Work ⭐
Labels are part of the repository's work-management workflow. They do not modify your Git commits or source code.
Example Complete Workflow

Problem Found ↓ Create Issue ↓ Add Labels 🐛 bug backend 🔥 high priority ↓ Assign Developer ↓ Create Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Create Pull Request ↓ Add PR Labels if Needed ↓ Review ↓ Merge ↓ Close Issue
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Think Labels change the code Correct ✅ Labels only categorize and organize work ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Create too many confusing labels Correct ✅ Use a clear and consistent label system ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Use labels as the assignee Correct ✅ Labels describe work; assignees show responsibility ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Use only one label for everything Correct ✅ Use multiple labels when they describe different aspects ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Create duplicate labels with the same meaning Correct ✅ Keep naming consistent across the repository
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
LABEL = WHAT KIND OF WORK? 🐛 What type? → bug 🔥 What priority? → high priority 💻 Which area? → backend 🚧 What status? → blocked
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
LabelA tag used to categorize Issues and Pull Requests
Type LabelDescribes the type of work, such as bug or feature
Priority LabelShows relative urgency or importance
Area LabelShows the affected part, such as frontend or database
Status LabelCan describe workflow state, such as blocked
Multiple LabelsOne Issue or Pull Request can have multiple labels
FilteringLabels help find related work

Final Definition: GitHub Labels are flexible tags used to categorize, organize, filter, and quickly understand Issues and Pull Requests based on information such as type, priority, affected area, or workflow status.
practice: Use a practice repository where you have permission to create or edit Issues and labels.
Step 1: Open an existing Issue or create a new practice Issue.
Step 2: Create an Issue with this example title:
Login button does not respond after clicking
Step 3: Add the label:
bug
Step 4: Add another label to describe the affected area, if available:
frontend
Step 5: If the problem requires urgent attention, add a priority label such as:
high priority
Practice Issue Login button does not respond Labels: 🐛 bug 💻 frontend 🔥 high priority
Step 6: Open the Issues list and try filtering by the bug label.
Step 7: Try filtering by another label and observe how the list changes.
Step 8: If you have permission to manage labels, review the repository's existing labels and check whether any have duplicate or unclear meanings.
Step 9: Create a practice Pull Request and add suitable labels to it.
Issue 🐛 bug 💻 frontend 🔥 high priority ↓ Filter By Label ↓ Find Related Work Quickly
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is the main purpose of a Label? 2. Can one Issue have multiple Labels? 3. What is the difference between a Label and an Assignee? 4. Give one example of a type label. 5. Give one example of a priority label. 6. Give one example of an area label. 7. Do Labels change your Git code or commits?

Practice Goal: You should be able to use Labels to categorize Issues and Pull Requests, apply multiple labels when useful, understand the difference between Labels and Assignees, and filter repository work using labels.

qna.q: Q1. What is a GitHub Label?
qna.a: A Label is a tag used to categorize and organize Issues and Pull Requests.

qna.q: Q2. Can one Issue have multiple Labels?
qna.a: Yes. Multiple Labels can describe different aspects such as type, priority, area, or status.

qna.q: Q3. Give three examples of common labels.
qna.a: Examples include bug, feature, documentation, enhancement, question, and high priority.

qna.q: Q4. What is the difference between a Label and an Assignee?
qna.a: A Label categorizes or describes the work, while an Assignee identifies who is responsible for working on it.

qna.q: Q5. What is the purpose of a priority label?
qna.a: It helps indicate the relative urgency or importance of the work.

qna.q: Q6. How do Labels help when a repository has many Issues?
qna.a: They allow related work to be grouped and filtered more easily.

qna.q: Q7. Do Labels change Git commits or source code?
qna.a: No. Labels only help organize and track work; they do not change your Git code or commits.

qna.q: Q8. What is an area label?
qna.a: It identifies the part of the project related to the work, such as frontend, backend, database, or reports.

qna.q: Q9. What is a good rule for naming labels?
qna.a: Use clear, meaningful, and consistent names that the whole team can understand.

qna.q: Q10. Can Labels be used on Pull Requests?
qna.a: Yes. Labels can be used on both Issues and Pull Requests.

qna.q: Q11. Complete: Label = What kind of ______?
qna.a: Work.

qna.q: Q12. Which is better: creating duplicate labels with the same meaning or maintaining one consistent label system?
qna.a: Maintaining one clear and consistent label system is better.

items.title: Milestones
explanation: Simple Meaning
A GitHub Milestone is used to group related Issues and Pull Requests around a larger goal, release, project phase, or target date.
Large Goal ⭐ ↓ Create Milestone ↓ Group Related Work Issue #21 ─┐ Issue #22 ─┼── Version 2.0 Issue #23 ─┤ Pull Request #24 ─┘
Simple Definition: A GitHub Milestone is a way to group related Issues and Pull Requests so a team can track progress toward a larger goal.
Why Are Milestones Used? ⭐
Large projects usually contain many separate tasks. A Milestone helps organize those tasks under one bigger objective.

Without Milestone ❌ #21 Fix Login #22 Add Dark Mode #23 Update API #24 Update README Separate Work Items ──────────────────── With Milestone ✅ Milestone: Version 2.0 #21 Fix Login #22 Add Dark Mode #23 Update API #24 Update README All Working Toward One Goal
Common Examples of Milestones

MilestonePurpose
Version 1.0Track work required for the first release
Version 2.0Track work planned for the next major release
Website LaunchTrack tasks required before launch
Q4 ReleaseGroup work planned for a release period
Payment FeatureTrack all work related to a larger feature
Example: Version Release ⭐
Milestone: Version 2.0 Progress: 2 / 5 Complete ✓ #21 Fix Login Bug ✓ #22 Update Documentation □ #23 Add Dark Mode □ #24 Improve API □ #25 Add Tests
The Milestone gives the team one place to view the related work and understand overall progress.
Milestone Workflow ⭐
Define Large Goal ↓ Create Milestone ↓ Add Related Issues / Pull Requests ↓ Team Works on Items ↓ Issues and PRs Get Completed ↓ Track Progress ↓ Goal Completed ↓ Close Milestone
Example: Website Launch
Milestone: Website Launch □ Create Home Page □ Create Login Page □ Connect Database □ Add User Registration □ Test Application □ Update README □ Deploy Application
Each item may be worked on separately, but all of them contribute to the larger goal of launching the website.
Milestone Progress ⭐
As related Issues and Pull Requests are completed, the Milestone can show progress toward the larger goal.
Milestone: Version 2.0 Start 0% Complete │ ├── Fix Login ✓ ├── Add Dark Mode ✓ ├── Update API ✓ ├── Add Tests □ └── Update Docs □ Progress 60% Complete
This helps the team understand how much work is finished and how much remains.
Milestone vs Label ⭐

MilestoneLabel
Groups work around a larger goalCategorizes work
Example: Version 2.0Example: bug
Shows progress toward a targetHelps filter and organize work
Usually represents a bigger objectiveDescribes type, priority, area, or status
Issue #45 Fix Login Error Milestone → What larger goal? Version 2.0 Label → What kind of work? 🐛 bug 🔥 high priority
Milestone vs Issue

MilestoneIssue
Represents a larger goalRepresents one piece of work
Groups related workTracks a specific task, bug, or feature
Example: Website LaunchExample: Create Login Page
MILESTONE Website Launch ├── Issue #10 │ Create Home Page │ ├── Issue #11 │ Create Login Page │ ├── Issue #12 │ Connect Database │ └── Issue #13 Test Application
Milestone vs Project

MilestoneProject
Groups work around a specific goal or targetProvides broader planning and work-management capabilities
Often used for releases or major objectivesCan organize and track work in different views and workflows
Example: Version 2.0Example: Product Development Board
Project Product Development ↓ Milestone: Version 1.0 ├── Issue #1 ├── Issue #2 └── Issue #3 Milestone: Version 2.0 ├── Issue #4 ├── Issue #5 └── Issue #6
Adding an Issue to a Milestone
Open Issue ↓ Find Milestone Section ↓ Select Milestone ↓ Issue Added to Milestone
An Issue can be associated with a Milestone to show that the work contributes to that larger target.
Example: Team Workflow ⭐

Team Goal: Release Version 2.0 ↓ Create Milestone Version 2.0 ↓ Create Issues #21 Fix Login #22 Add Dark Mode #23 Improve API #24 Add Tests ↓ Add All Related Issues To Milestone ↓ Assign Developers ↓ Developers Work on Issues ↓ Create Pull Requests ↓ Review + Merge ↓ Issues Completed ↓ Milestone Progress Updates ↓ All Work Complete ↓ Close Milestone
Milestones Can Have a Target Date
A Milestone can be associated with a due date so the team has a target for completing the larger goal.
Milestone Version 2.0 Target: 30 September Related Work: ✓ Fix Login ✓ Add Dark Mode □ Add Tests □ Update API
A due date is a planning target; teams should still manage actual work and dependencies based on their workflow.
When Should You Use a Milestone? ⭐

Use a Milestone When: ✓ Multiple Issues belong to one release ✓ Multiple tasks are needed for one major goal ✓ You want to track progress toward a target ✓ You are planning a project phase ✓ Related Pull Requests and Issues need grouping
When a Milestone May Not Be Needed
Single Small Task ↓ No Larger Grouping Needed ↓ Issue Alone May Be Enough
Milestones are most useful when several pieces of work need to be viewed as progress toward a larger objective.
Example: Inventory Report Improvement
Milestone: Inventory Report Version 2 □ Fix quantity mismatch □ Improve SQL performance □ Add store-level validation □ Improve Excel export □ Add error handling □ Complete testing
Each task can have its own Issue, while the Milestone tracks progress for the complete report improvement.
Milestones and Pull Requests
Related Pull Requests can also be associated with a Milestone so development changes can be tracked alongside the larger goal.
Milestone: Version 2.0 Issue #21 → Fix Login Pull Request #31 → Login Fix Issue #22 → Add Dark Mode Pull Request #32 → Dark Mode Issue #23 → Add Tests Pull Request #33 → Test Updates
Complete Development Flow ⭐

LARGE GOAL Release Version 2.0 ↓ MILESTONE Version 2.0 ↓ ISSUES What needs to be done? ↓ LABELS What type / priority / area? ↓ ASSIGNEE Who is responsible? ↓ BRANCH Where development happens ↓ COMMIT Save changes ↓ PULL REQUEST Propose changes ↓ REVIEW Check changes ↓ MERGE Integrate changes ↓ ISSUE CLOSED Work completed ↓ MILESTONE CLOSED Large goal completed
Milestone Status
A Milestone is generally open while the related goal is still being worked on and can be closed when the team considers the larger objective complete or no longer active.
OPEN MILESTONE Related Work Still In Progress ↓ Complete / Finish Goal ↓ CLOSED MILESTONE
Reopening a Milestone
If additional work becomes necessary after a Milestone is closed, a team may reopen it depending on its workflow and repository permissions.
Milestone Closed ↓ More Work Needed? YES → Reopen Milestone ↓ Continue Tracking Work NO → Keep Closed
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Think Milestone means one task Correct ✅ A Milestone represents a larger goal containing related work ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Use a Milestone instead of an Issue for every small task Correct ✅ Use Issues for individual work and Milestones for larger goals ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Confuse Labels and Milestones Correct ✅ Label = What kind of work? Milestone = What larger goal? ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Close the Milestone before checking remaining work Correct ✅ Review progress and verify the larger goal ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Put unrelated work into one Milestone Correct ✅ Group work that contributes to the same larger objective
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
MILESTONE = WHAT BIG GOAL? ISSUE = WHAT NEEDS TO BE DONE? LABEL = WHAT KIND OF WORK? ASSIGNEE = WHO WILL DO IT?
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
MilestoneGroups related work around a larger goal
IssueTracks one specific piece of work
LabelCategorizes the work
AssigneeShows who is responsible
Due DateA target date for the Milestone
ProgressShows how much related work is complete
Open MilestoneLarge goal is still being worked on
Closed MilestoneLarge goal is completed or no longer active
Final Definition: A GitHub Milestone is used to group related Issues and Pull Requests and track progress toward a larger goal such as a release, project phase, feature, or target.
practice: Use a practice repository where you have permission to create and manage Milestones.
Step 1: Think of one larger goal for your practice project.

Example Goal:
Complete Version 1.0 of my practice website.
Step 2: Create a Milestone with this title:
Version 1.0
Step 3: Add a description explaining the goal of the Milestone.

Example:
This Milestone contains all important work required before releasing Version 1.0.
Step 4: Add a target date if your practice workflow requires one.
Step 5: Create several related Issues.
Issue #1 Create Home Page Issue #2 Create Login Page Issue #3 Connect Database Issue #4 Add Basic Tests Issue #5 Update README
Step 6: Associate the related Issues with the Version 1.0 Milestone.
Milestone: Version 1.0 □ #1 Create Home Page □ #2 Create Login Page □ #3 Connect Database □ #4 Add Basic Tests □ #5 Update README
Step 7: Add suitable Labels to the individual Issues.
#1 → feature, frontend #2 → feature, frontend #3 → feature, backend #4 → testing #5 → documentation
Step 8: Complete one or more Issues through your normal development workflow.
Issue ↓ Create Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Merge ↓ Close Issue
Step 9: Return to the Milestone and observe how completed work contributes to overall progress.
Step 10: After all required work is completed and verified, close the Milestone.
Version 1.0 5 / 5 Issues Complete 100% ↓ Verify Goal ↓ Close Milestone
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is the main purpose of a Milestone? 2. What is the difference between a Milestone and an Issue? 3. What is the difference between a Milestone and a Label? 4. Give one example of a Milestone name. 5. What happens to Milestone progress as related work is completed? 6. When should you use a Milestone? 7. Complete: Milestone = What ______ goal?

Practice Goal: You should be able to create a Milestone, define a larger project goal, group related Issues under it, understand the difference between Milestones, Issues, and Labels, track progress, and close the Milestone when the larger goal is completed.

qna.q: Q1. What is a GitHub Milestone?
qna.a: A Milestone groups related Issues and Pull Requests around a larger goal.

qna.q: Q2. Give three examples of Milestones.
qna.a: Examples include Version 1.0, Website Launch, Version 2.0, Q4 Release, and Payment Feature.

qna.q: Q3. What is the difference between a Milestone and an Issue?
qna.a: A Milestone represents a larger goal, while an Issue tracks one specific task, bug, feature, or piece of work.

qna.q: Q4. What is the difference between a Milestone and a Label?
qna.a: A Milestone answers what larger goal the work belongs to, while a Label categorizes the type, priority, area, or status of the work.

qna.q: Q5. What is the purpose of Milestone progress?
qna.a: It helps show how much of the related work has been completed toward the larger goal.

qna.q: Q6. Can a Milestone have a target date?
qna.a: Yes. A Milestone can have a due date used as a target for completing the larger goal.

qna.q: Q7. When should you use a Milestone?
qna.a: Use one when multiple related Issues or Pull Requests contribute to a larger release, feature, project phase, or goal.

qna.q: Q8. What should happen before closing a Milestone?
qna.a: The team should review the remaining work and verify that the larger goal is completed according to its workflow.

qna.q: Q9. Can unrelated Issues be grouped into one Milestone?
qna.a: They can technically be associated, but good practice is to group work that contributes to the same larger objective.

qna.q: Q10. Complete: Milestone = What ______ goal?
qna.a: Larger or bigger.

qna.q: Q11. Complete: Issue = What needs to be ______?
qna.a: Done.

qna.q: Q12. Complete: Label = What kind of ______?
qna.a: Work.

items.title: Releases & Tags
explanation: Simple Meaning

A Git Tag is a named reference that usually marks an important point in Git history, such as a version. A GitHub Release is a published version that is typically created from a tag and can include release notes and downloadable files.
Development ↓ Commit ↓ Commit ↓ Commit ↓ Tag: v1.0.0 ⭐ ↓ GitHub Release ↓ Published Version

Simple Definition:

Tag: Marks a specific commit, usually for an important version or point in history.

Release: A published GitHub version, normally associated with a Git tag, with information such as release notes.
Why Are Tags Used? ⭐
Projects continue receiving new commits. A tag makes it easy to identify an important commit later, especially when marking versions.
Commit History A ─── B ─── C ─── D ─── E ↑ v1.0.0 The Tag Points to An Important Commit ⭐
For example, instead of remembering a commit ID, you can use a meaningful tag name such as v1.0.0.
Example Without a Tag
Commit History A ─── B ─── C ─── D ─── E Which Commit Was Version 1.0? Harder to Remember ❌
Example With a Tag
Commit History A ─── B ─── C ─── D ─── E ↑ v1.0.0 Version 1.0 Commit Easy to Identify ✅
What Is a GitHub Release? ⭐
A GitHub Release represents a published version of your project. It is associated with a Git tag and can contain release notes describing changes in that version.
Git Tag v1.0.0 ↓ Create GitHub Release ↓ Release Title ↓ Release Notes ↓ Publish ↓ Users Can See Version 1.0.0
Tag vs Release ⭐

Git TagGitHub Release
Part of Git historyGitHub published release information
Marks a specific point or commitRepresents a published version
Usually used for versionsUsually based on a tag
Created using Git or GitHubCreated on GitHub
Can exist without a ReleaseUses a tag as its reference point
TAG Marks a Commit v1.0.0 ↓ Commit C ──────────────────── RELEASE Publishes Information About That Version Version 1.0.0 Release Notes Downloadable Files
Important Relationship ⭐
Commit ↓ Tag v1.0.0 ↓ Release Version 1.0.0
A tag can exist by itself. Creating a GitHub Release adds a published release around a selected tag.
Common Tag Naming
Examples: v1.0.0 v1.0.1 v1.1.0 v2.0.0 Other Possible Names: release-2026 production-ready project-launch
Many software projects use version-style tag names such as v1.0.0, but Git does not force one naming convention.
Understanding Version Numbers ⭐
v1.2.3 │ │ │ │ │ └── Patch │ └──── Minor └────── Major

VersionTypical Meaning
v1.0.0First major release
v1.0.1Small fix or patch
v1.1.0New backward-compatible features
v2.0.0Next major version, often with significant changes
This major.minor.patch format is commonly associated with semantic versioning, but a project should follow its own documented versioning rules.
Creating a Lightweight Tag
A lightweight tag is the simplest form of tag. It points directly to a specific commit.
git tag v1.0.0
HEAD ↓ Latest Commit ↓ Create Tag v1.0.0 ↓ Tag Points to This Commit
If no commit is specified, the tag is created for the current HEAD commit.
Creating an Annotated Tag ⭐
An annotated tag stores additional tag information, such as a message and tagger details.
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release version 1.0.0"
Commit ↑ Annotated Tag Name: v1.0.0 Message: Release version 1.0.0 Tag Information Included ⭐
Lightweight vs Annotated Tag

Lightweight TagAnnotated Tag
Simple reference to a commitStores additional tag information
Created with git tag nameCreated with git tag -a name -m "message"
Useful for simple temporary markersCommonly preferred for important releases
Good Practice: For important public release points, many teams prefer annotated tags because they include additional metadata and a message.
View All Tags ⭐
git tag
Repository Tags v1.0.0 v1.0.1 v1.1.0 v2.0.0
This lists the tags available in your local repository.
View Information About a Tag
git show v1.0.0
This can display information associated with the tag and the commit it references.
Create a Tag for an Older Commit
