You can create a tag for a specific earlier commit by providing its commit reference.
git tag v1.0.0 a1b2c3d
A ─── B ─── C ─── D ↑ v1.0.0 Tag Created For Older Commit B
Tags Are Not Automatically Pushed ⭐
Creating a tag locally does not automatically send that tag to your remote repository.
Local Repository Create Tag v1.0.0 ↓ Only Local Initially ──────────────────── Push Tag ↓ Remote Repository GitHub
Push One Tag
git push origin v1.0.0
Local Tag v1.0.0 ↓ git push origin v1.0.0 ↓ GitHub / Remote v1.0.0
Push All Tags
git push origin --tags
Use this carefully because it pushes all local tags that are not already present on the remote.
Delete a Local Tag
git tag -d v1.0.0
Local Tags v1.0.0 v1.1.0 Delete v1.0.0 ↓ Local Tags v1.1.0
Delete a Remote Tag
git push origin --delete v1.0.0
This removes the specified tag from the remote repository. Be careful when deleting tags used by other developers or release processes.
Tags and Branches Are Different ⭐

BranchTag
Usually moves forward as new commits are addedUsually marks a fixed point in history
Used for ongoing developmentUsed to mark important commits or versions
Example: mainExample: v1.0.0
HEAD can move as commits are madeNormally used as a stable reference
Branch: main A ─── B ─── C ─── D ─── E ↑ main Tag: v1.0.0 A ─── B ─── C ─── D ─── E ↑ v1.0.0
Important: Do Not Treat Tags Like Branches

After creating a release tag, teams generally treat it as a stable marker for that version. If a release contains a problem, a common approach is to create a new commit and a new version tag instead of silently changing the meaning of an existing published version tag.
v1.0.0 Release Published ↓ Bug Found ↓ Fix Code ↓ New Commit ↓ Create New Tag v1.0.1 ↓ Create New Release
Creating a GitHub Release ⭐
Open GitHub Repository ↓ Open Releases ↓ Create New Release ↓ Choose Existing Tag OR Create New Tag ↓ Add Release Title ↓ Add Release Notes ↓ Publish Release
A release can provide users with a clear published version and information about what changed.
Example Release

Tag: v1.0.0

Release Title: Version 1.0.0

Release Notes:
• Added user login
• Added registration
• Added dark mode
• Fixed inventory report issue
• Updated documentation
What Are Release Notes? ⭐
Release notes explain what is included, changed, improved, or fixed in a particular release.
Release: v1.1.0 What's New: ✓ Added search feature ✓ Added Excel export Improvements: ✓ Improved report performance Bug Fixes: ✓ Fixed login validation
Good release notes help users and developers understand the differences between versions.
Draft Releases
A release can be prepared as a draft before publishing, allowing release information to be reviewed before it becomes publicly published.
Create Release ↓ Add Tag + Notes ↓ Save as Draft ↓ Review Information ↓ Ready? ↓ Publish Release
Pre-Releases
A project can also publish a pre-release for testing or early access before the final stable release.
Development ↓ v2.0.0-beta.1 Pre-Release ↓ Testing ↓ Fix Problems ↓ v2.0.0 Stable Release ⭐
Common examples include names such as alpha, beta, or rc depending on the project's versioning convention.
Complete Release Workflow ⭐

Development ↓ Create Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Merge to main ↓ Version Ready? ↓ Create Tag v1.0.0 ↓ Push Tag ↓ Create GitHub Release ↓ Add Release Notes ↓ Publish ⭐
Example: Website Version Workflow

Version 1.0 Development Issue #1 → Home Page Issue #2 → Login Issue #3 → Registration Issue #4 → Database ↓ All Work Complete ↓ Merge to main ↓ Create Tag v1.0.0 ↓ Push Tag ↓ Create Release Version 1.0.0 ↓ Publish
Releases & Milestones ⭐
Milestone Version 1.0 ↓ Track Related Issues ↓ All Required Work Complete ↓ Create Tag v1.0.0 ↓ Create Release Version 1.0.0
A Milestone helps plan and track the work toward a larger goal, while a Tag and Release can mark and publish the resulting version.
Milestone vs Tag vs Release

ConceptMain Purpose
MilestoneTrack progress toward a larger goal
TagMark a specific point in Git history
ReleasePublish a version and its release information
Milestone Plan the Goal ↓ Issues Complete the Work ↓ Tag Mark the Version Commit ↓ Release Publish the Version
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Think a Tag and Release are exactly the same Correct ✅ Tag marks a Git point; Release publishes information around a version ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Forget to push the Tag Correct ✅ Local tags are not automatically pushed ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Think git push automatically pushes every tag Correct ✅ Push tags explicitly when needed ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Use a Branch as a version marker Correct ✅ Branches are for development; Tags are commonly used for version points ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Change or delete a published release tag carelessly Correct ✅ Treat published version tags carefully because others may depend on them ──────────────────── Mistake 6 ❌ Create a Release without explaining changes Correct ✅ Add useful Release Notes
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
COMMIT Save code TAG Mark version point RELEASE Publish version information ──────────────────── v1.0.0 = TAG Version 1.0.0 page = RELEASE
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
TagA named reference marking a specific point in Git history
Lightweight TagSimple reference to a commit
Annotated TagTag with additional metadata and a message
ReleaseA published GitHub version associated with a tag
Release NotesInformation about changes in that version
Draft ReleaseRelease prepared before publishing
Pre-ReleaseEarly/testing version before a stable release
BranchUsed for ongoing development
TagUsually marks a fixed important point or version

Final Definition: A Git Tag marks an important specific point in repository history, commonly a version, while a GitHub Release publishes that version with information such as release notes and associated downloadable files.
practice: Use a practice repository so you can safely create commits, tags, and releases.
Step 1: Check your current repository status:
git status
Step 2: Create or use an existing commit that you want to mark as a practice version.
git add . git commit -m "Prepare version 1.0.0"
Step 3: Create an annotated tag:
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release version 1.0.0"
Step 4: View your tags:
git tag
Expected Result:
v1.0.0
Step 5: View the tag information:
git show v1.0.0
Step 6: Push the tag to your remote repository:
git push origin v1.0.0
Step 7: Open your repository on GitHub and confirm that the tag is available.
Step 8: Open the Releases section and create a new release using the v1.0.0 tag.
Step 9: Use this practice release title:
Version 1.0.0
Step 10: Add practice release notes:

What's New:
• Added practice feature
• Updated documentation

Bug Fixes:
• Fixed practice issue
Step 11: Publish the release.
Commit ↓ Tag v1.0.0 ↓ Push Tag ↓ GitHub ↓ Create Release ↓ Add Notes ↓ Publish
Optional Practice: Make another small change and create a patch version.
git add . git commit -m "Fix small issue" git tag -a v1.0.1 -m "Release version 1.0.1" git push origin v1.0.1
Final Understanding Check:

1. What does a Git Tag mark? 2. What is the difference between a Tag and a Release? 3. Are local tags automatically pushed to GitHub? 4. Which command lists tags? 5. Which command creates an annotated tag? 6. Which command pushes one tag? 7. What are Release Notes? 8. What is the difference between a Branch and a Tag? 9. Complete: Commit → Tag → ______ → Publish Version 10. What might v1.0.1 represent compared with v1.0.0?

Practice Goal: You should be able to create and view Git tags, understand lightweight and annotated tags, push tags to a remote repository, explain the difference between Tags and GitHub Releases, and publish a release with useful release notes.

qna.q: Q1. What is a Git Tag?
qna.a: A Git Tag is a named reference that marks a specific point in repository history, commonly an important version commit.

qna.q: Q2. What is a GitHub Release?
qna.a: A GitHub Release is a published version associated with a tag that can include release notes and other release information.

qna.q: Q3. What is the main difference between a Tag and a Release?
qna.a: A Tag marks a specific point in Git history, while a Release publishes information about a version based on a tag.

qna.q: Q4. Are tags automatically pushed when you create them locally?
qna.a: No. A locally created tag must be pushed explicitly when you want it available on the remote.

qna.q: Q5. Which command lists all local tags?
qna.a: git tag

qna.q: Q6. Which command creates an annotated tag?
qna.a: git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release version 1.0.0"

qna.q: Q7. Which command pushes one specific tag to origin?
qna.a: git push origin v1.0.0

qna.q: Q8. What is a lightweight tag?
qna.a: It is a simple tag that directly references a commit without the additional metadata of an annotated tag.

qna.q: Q9. What is an annotated tag?
qna.a: It is a tag that stores additional metadata and can include a message.

qna.q: Q10. What do Release Notes explain?
qna.a: They explain changes, improvements, features, or fixes included in a particular release.

qna.q: Q11. What is the difference between a Branch and a Tag?
qna.a: A Branch is used for ongoing development and normally moves as new commits are added, while a Tag usually marks a specific stable point in history.

qna.q: Q12. Complete: Commit → Tag → ______.
qna.a: Release.

qna.q: Q13. In a common major.minor.patch version format, what might v1.0.1 represent after v1.0.0?
qna.a: A small patch or bug-fix release, depending on the project's versioning rules.

items.title: GitHub Profile README
explanation: Simple Meaning

A GitHub Profile README is a special README.md file displayed on your GitHub profile. It allows you to introduce yourself and showcase information such as your skills, projects, interests, and achievements.
GitHub Account ↓ Create Special Repository ↓ Repository Name = Your GitHub Username ↓ Add README.md ↓ README Appears on Your Profile ⭐
Simple Definition: A GitHub Profile README is a special README.md file that appears on your GitHub profile and helps you introduce yourself to visitors.
Why Is It Special? ⭐
Normally, a repository README appears inside that repository. A Profile README is special because GitHub displays it directly on your profile when it is created using the required repository setup.
Normal Repository my-project └── README.md README appears inside my-project repository ──────────────────── Special Profile Repository username └── README.md README appears on GitHub Profile ⭐
How Does GitHub Know It Is a Profile README?
You create a public repository whose name exactly matches your GitHub username. Then you add a README.md file to that repository.
GitHub Username nethaji123 Repository Name nethaji123 Both Names Match ⭐ ↓ README.md Can Be Used As Profile README
Important Rule: The repository name must exactly match your GitHub username for GitHub to recognize it as your profile repository.
Example
Username: john-dev Create Repository: john-dev Inside Repository: john-dev/ └── README.md ↓ README appears on john-dev's profile
Creating a Profile README ⭐

Step 1 Open Your GitHub Profile ↓ Step 2 Check Your Exact Username ↓ Step 3 Create New Repository ↓ Step 4 Repository Name = Username ↓ Step 5 Keep Repository Public ↓ Step 6 Initialize / Add README.md ↓ Step 7 Write Your Profile Content ↓ Step 8 Commit Changes ↓ Profile README Appears ⭐
What Can You Add to a Profile README?
PROFILE README 👋 Introduction 💻 Skills 📚 Currently Learning 🚀 Projects 🎯 Goals 📫 Contact Information 🏆 Achievements 🌐 Portfolio / Other Links
You can choose what to include based on what you want visitors to know about you.
Basic Example ⭐

# Hi, I'm John 👋 ## About Me I am a software developer interested in web development and Python. ## Skills - Python - SQL - HTML - CSS - JavaScript ## Currently Learning - Data Structures and Algorithms - Git and GitHub ## Projects - Inventory Management System - Portfolio Website
How It Looks Conceptually

GitHub Profile ──────────────────── Profile Information John Software Developer ──────────────────── PROFILE README ⭐ Hi, I'm John 👋 Skills Python | SQL | JavaScript Currently Learning DSA | Git | GitHub Projects Inventory System Portfolio Website ──────────────────── Repositories
Markdown Is Used ⭐
Profile READMEs are written using Markdown, usually in a file named README.md.

MarkdownPurpose
# TitleLarge heading
## TitleSection heading
**text**Bold text
- ItemBullet point
[Text](link)Link
![Alt Text](image-url)Image
Recommended Profile README Structure ⭐
1. Introduction ↓ 2. About Me ↓ 3. Skills ↓ 4. Currently Learning ↓ 5. Projects ↓ 6. Goals ↓ 7. Contact / Links
Introduction Section
# Hi 👋 I'm John Welcome to my GitHub profile!
Keep the introduction simple and clear. Visitors should quickly understand who you are or what you are interested in.
About Me Section
## About Me - 💻 Interested in software development - 📚 Currently learning Python and DSA - 🌱 Improving my programming skills every day - 🚀 Building practical projects
Skills Section
## Skills - Python - SQL - HTML - CSS - JavaScript - Git - GitHub
Currently Learning Section
## Currently Learning - Data Structures and Algorithms - Python Full Stack Development - Advanced SQL - Git and GitHub
Projects Section ⭐
## Projects ### Inventory Management System A project for managing inventory data and reports. ### Portfolio Website A personal website showcasing my skills and projects.
You can also link to repositories or live projects when appropriate.
Profile README vs Repository README ⭐

Profile READMERepository README
Introduces the developer or profileExplains a specific project
Appears on the GitHub profileAppears inside a repository
Repository name matches usernameRepository can have any valid name
Example: About Me and SkillsExample: Installation and Usage

PROFILE README Who am I? What are my skills? What am I learning? What projects do I build? ──────────────────── PROJECT README What is this project? How do I install it? How do I use it? What technologies are used?
Profile Repository vs Normal Repository
Normal Repository Repository: inventory-app README.md Purpose: Explain inventory-app ──────────────────── Profile Repository Repository: username README.md Purpose: Introduce the GitHub profile ⭐
Adding Project Links
You can link to projects from your Profile README so visitors can quickly explore your work.
## My Projects - [Inventory Management System](https://github.com/username/inventory-project) - [Portfolio Website](https://github.com/username/portfolio)
Replace username and repository names with your actual GitHub information.
Adding Contact Information
## Connect With Me - GitHub: https://github.com/username - LinkedIn: Your LinkedIn Profile - Portfolio: Your Portfolio Website
Privacy Tip: Only add contact information that you are comfortable making publicly visible on your GitHub profile.
Adding Images and Badges
Markdown can also be used to display images, badges, and other visual elements. These are optional and should support the information in your profile rather than make it difficult to read.
Simple Profile Name About Me Skills Projects ↓ Good Foundation ⭐ ──────────────────── Optional Additions Badges Images Statistics Animations Use Only If Useful
Good Profile README Practices ⭐

✓ Keep it clear ✓ Use meaningful sections ✓ Show real skills and projects ✓ Keep project descriptions short ✓ Update it when your skills change ✓ Use readable formatting ✓ Link useful public projects ✓ Avoid unnecessary personal information
Avoid This ⚠️

❌ Very long introduction ❌ Too many unnecessary animations ❌ Listing skills you cannot explain ❌ Broken project links ❌ Outdated information ❌ Publicly sharing sensitive information ❌ Making the README difficult to read
Example Professional Profile README ⭐

# Hi 👋 I'm John ## About Me I am interested in software development and enjoy building practical applications. ## Skills - Python - SQL - HTML - CSS - JavaScript - Git & GitHub ## Currently Learning - Data Structures and Algorithms - Full Stack Development ## Projects - Inventory Management System - Portfolio Website ## Goals - Build more real-world projects - Improve problem-solving skills - Become a better software developer
Profile README Is a Git Repository ⭐
Your Profile README still exists inside a GitHub repository. This means you can use normal Git concepts to update it.
Profile Repository ↓ Clone Repository ↓ Edit README.md ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ git push ↓ GitHub Profile Updates
Updating Your Profile README
git clone https://github.com/username/username.git cd username # Edit README.md git add README.md git commit -m "Update profile README" git push
After pushing the changes to the profile repository, the updated README can be reflected on your GitHub profile.
Complete Workflow ⭐

Choose What to Show ↓ Check Exact GitHub Username ↓ Create Public Repository Name = Username ↓ Add README.md ↓ Write Using Markdown ↓ Commit Changes ↓ GitHub Displays README On Your Profile ↓ Update Over Time ⭐
Example for a Developer Journey

Profile README 👋 Introduction I am learning software development 💻 Skills Python | SQL | HTML | CSS 📚 Learning DSA | Git | GitHub 🚀 Building Web Projects Database Projects 🎯 Goal Become a Full Stack Developer
Important: Keep It Updated
Your skills, projects, and learning goals can change over time. Updating the Profile README helps keep your GitHub profile relevant to your current work.
Old Profile ❌ Learning: Basic Python No Projects ──────────────────── Current Profile ✅ Skills: Python, SQL, Git Projects: Inventory System Learning: DSA, Full Stack Keep Information Current ⭐
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Repository name does not match username Correct ✅ Repository name = exact GitHub username ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Create the repository without a README Correct ✅ Add README.md ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Think every repository README appears on the profile Correct ✅ Only the special profile repository README is used for this purpose ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Write outdated information Correct ✅ Update skills, projects, and goals regularly ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Add too much unnecessary information Correct ✅ Keep the profile focused and readable ──────────────────── Mistake 6 ❌ Share sensitive personal information publicly Correct ✅ Only publish information you are comfortable making public
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
USERNAME = REPOSITORY NAME + README.md ↓ PROFILE README ⭐
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
Profile READMEA special README displayed on your GitHub profile
Repository NameMust match your GitHub username exactly
README.mdContains your profile content
MarkdownUsed to format the README
SkillsTechnologies you know
ProjectsWork you want to showcase
UpdateEdit and push changes as your profile develops

Final Definition: A GitHub Profile README is a special public repository README displayed on your GitHub profile when the repository name exactly matches your GitHub username. It can be used to introduce yourself, showcase skills, projects, learning goals, and other public professional information.
practice: Step 1: Open your GitHub profile and note your exact GitHub username.
Step 2: Create a new repository using exactly the same name as your GitHub username.
GitHub Username YOUR_USERNAME Repository Name YOUR_USERNAME Must Match Exactly ⭐
Step 3: Create the repository as a public repository and add a README.md file.
Step 4: Add this basic practice content to README.md:
# Hi 👋 I'm Your Name ## About Me I am learning software development. ## Skills - Python - SQL - Git - GitHub ## Currently Learning - DSA - Full Stack Development ## Projects - My Practice Project
Step 5: Commit the README changes.
Step 6: Open your GitHub profile and check whether the Profile README appears.
Step 7: Add at least three skills that you can genuinely explain or demonstrate.
Step 8: Add one real project you have worked on or are currently building.
Step 9: Add a Currently Learning section.
Step 10: Review the README and remove information that is outdated, unnecessary, or too personal for a public profile.
Profile README Practice Introduction ✓ About Me ✓ Skills ✓ Currently Learning ✓ Projects ✓ Goals ✓ Public-Safe Information ✓ ↓ Clear GitHub Profile ⭐
Optional Practice: Clone your profile repository locally and update the README using Git commands.
git clone https://github.com/username/username.git cd username # Edit README.md git add README.md git commit -m "Improve profile README" git push
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is a GitHub Profile README? 2. What must the repository name match? 3. What is the required README file name? 4. Where does the Profile README appear? 5. Name three things you can add to it. 6. What language/format is commonly used to write it? 7. What is the difference between a Profile README and a Project README? 8. Complete: Username = ______ Name 9. Should you add sensitive information to a public Profile README? 10. Why should you update your Profile README over time?

Practice Goal: You should be able to create a GitHub Profile README repository, ensure the repository name matches your username, write and format README.md using Markdown, add meaningful skills and projects, and update your public developer profile over time.

qna.q: Q1. What is a GitHub Profile README?
qna.a: It is a special README.md file that is displayed on your GitHub profile.

qna.q: Q2. What must the profile repository name match?
qna.a: It must exactly match your GitHub username.

qna.q: Q3. What file is used for the Profile README?
qna.a: README.md

qna.q: Q4. Where does a Profile README appear?
qna.a: It appears on your GitHub profile.

qna.q: Q5. Name four things you can include in a Profile README.
qna.a: Examples include an introduction, skills, currently learning, projects, goals, and useful public contact or portfolio links.

qna.q: Q6. What format is commonly used to write a README?
qna.a: Markdown.

qna.q: Q7. What is the difference between a Profile README and a Repository README?
qna.a: A Profile README introduces the developer and appears on the GitHub profile, while a Repository README explains a specific project.

qna.q: Q8. Complete: GitHub Username = Repository ______.
qna.a: Name.

qna.q: Q9. Should you share sensitive personal information in a public Profile README?
qna.a: No. Only add information you are comfortable making publicly visible.

qna.q: Q10. Can you update your Profile README later?
qna.a: Yes. You can edit README.md and commit or push the updated changes.

qna.q: Q11. Does every repository README automatically appear on your GitHub profile?
qna.a: No. The special profile repository setup is required.

qna.q: Q12. Why is it useful to keep a Profile README updated?
qna.a: It helps your profile reflect your current skills, projects, learning progress, and professional interests.

items.title: Repository Visibility & Settings
explanation: Simple Meaning
GitHub repository visibility controls who can find and access a repository, while repository settings control how the repository is configured and managed.
GitHub Repository ↓ Repository Settings ├── Visibility ├── Access / Collaboration ├── Branch Settings ├── Features └── General Configuration

Simple Definition:

Visibility = Who can access the repository.

Settings = Configuration options used to manage how the repository works.
Repository Visibility ⭐
The main visibility options are Public, Private, and, depending on the GitHub plan and organization setup, Internal.
REPOSITORY VISIBILITY 🌍 Public Anyone can view 🔒 Private Only authorized people can access 🏢 Internal Organization members can access (when available)
Public Repository
A public repository can be viewed by anyone on GitHub. It is commonly used for open-source projects, portfolios, learning projects, and code you want to share publicly.
PUBLIC REPOSITORY 🌍 GitHub Users ↓ Anyone Can View Repository Code Examples: ✓ Open-source project ✓ Portfolio project ✓ Learning project ✓ Public library
Private Repository
A private repository is restricted to people who have been granted access. It is useful when source code, business work, or project information should not be publicly visible.
PRIVATE REPOSITORY 🔒 Repository ↓ Authorized Users Only ✓ Owner ✓ Collaborators ✓ Approved Team Members Others Cannot Access
Internal Repository
An internal repository is generally used within supported organization environments where access is available to organization members without making the repository public to everyone.
INTERNAL REPOSITORY 🏢 GitHub Organization ↓ Organization Members Can Access Public Internet Cannot Access
Public vs Private vs Internal ⭐

VisibilityWho Can Access?Typical Use
PublicAnyone who can access the repository publiclyOpen source, portfolios, public projects
PrivateAuthorized users onlyPersonal private work, company projects, confidential development
InternalOrganization members, where supportedInternal organization projects
Example
My Projects portfolio-website → Public 🌍 company-inventory-system → Private 🔒 organization-coding-guidelines → Internal 🏢
Changing Repository Visibility ⭐

Repository owners or users with the required permissions can change repository visibility through the repository settings. This should be done carefully because changing visibility can affect who can access the repository.
Repository ↓ Settings ↓ General ↓ Danger Zone / Visibility Option ↓ Change Visibility ↓ Confirm Change

Important: Before changing a repository from Private to Public, check that the repository does not contain secrets, passwords, API keys, confidential files, or other information that should not be publicly exposed.
Private → Public Example ⚠️

Private Repository 🔒 config file API information Internal code ↓ Before Making Public: ✓ Review files ✓ Remove secrets ✓ Check commit history ✓ Review sensitive information ✓ Confirm public sharing is intended ↓ Make Public 🌍
Repository Settings ⭐

The repository Settings area contains options for managing different aspects of a repository. Available options can vary based on repository ownership, permissions, organization policies, and GitHub features.
REPOSITORY SETTINGS General Access / Collaborators Branches / Rules Features Security Options Integrations Other Repository Configuration
General Settings
General settings are used for basic repository configuration.
GENERAL SETTINGS Repository Name Description Website URL Default Branch Repository Features Visibility Archive / Transfer / Delete (Available options may vary)
Repository Name
You can manage the repository name through repository settings when you have the required permission.
Before: my-project ↓ Rename ↓ After: my-awesome-project
If you rename a repository, check and update any documentation, integrations, local remotes, or external references that depend on the old repository name.
Repository Description

Example:
A web application for managing inventory, stock movement, and reports.
A clear description helps visitors and collaborators quickly understand the purpose of the repository.
Default Branch ⭐

The default branch is the main branch GitHub uses as the primary branch for actions such as viewing repository code and opening certain pull requests. Its name is often main, although repositories can use another branch name.
Repository main ← Default Branch ⭐ │ ├── feature-login ├── feature-report └── bugfix-quantity
The default branch should be managed carefully because team workflows and integrations may depend on it.
Collaborators and Access
Repository settings can be used to manage access for collaborators and teams, depending on whether the repository belongs to a personal account or an organization.
Repository Owner ↓ Manage Access ↓ Add Authorized Users ↓ Collaborators Can Work Based on Their Permissions
Example Access Concept

UserPossible Role / Access
Repository OwnerManages the repository and settings
Maintainer / AdminMay manage repository configuration depending on permissions
DeveloperWorks with code according to granted permissions
ViewerCan view information when access allows it
The exact roles and permissions depend on the account, organization, repository configuration, and access model.
Repository Features
Repositories can enable or disable features based on the project workflow and available GitHub options.
Possible Repository Features Issues Pull Requests Projects Discussions Wiki Other Available Features
Example
Small Learning Repository ✓ Issues ✓ Pull Requests ✗ Discussions ✗ Wiki Enable What You Need
Branch Settings and Protection ⭐
Repository settings can include rules or protection settings for important branches. These controls help teams manage how changes reach branches such as main.
Developer ↓ Feature Branch ↓ Pull Request ↓ Review Required? ↓ Checks Pass? ↓ Merge into main
Rules can help prevent unwanted direct changes and support a controlled team workflow.
Example Branch Rule
main Branch 🔒 Direct Push? ❌ Not Allowed by Rule ↓ Create Feature Branch ↓ Make Changes ↓ Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Checks ↓ Merge ✅
Repository Security Settings
GitHub provides security-related settings and features that may help identify or manage security concerns. The exact available features can depend on the repository, account, organization, and plan.
SECURITY MANAGEMENT Review Access ↓ Protect Important Branches ↓ Manage Security Features ↓ Review Alerts / Dependencies When Available ↓ Keep Repository Secure
Never Store Secrets in Source Code ⚠️
Do NOT Commit ❌ Passwords API Keys Access Tokens Private Credentials ──────────────────── Use Secure Configuration And Appropriate Secret Management ✅
Repository visibility is not a replacement for proper secret management. Sensitive credentials should be handled carefully even when a repository is private.
Archive a Repository
Archiving is useful when a repository is no longer actively developed but you want to preserve it for reference.
Active Project ↓ Development Ends ↓ Archive Repository ↓ Preserve for Reference ↓ No Normal Active Development Workflow
Before archiving, make sure the team understands that the project is no longer intended for normal active development.
Transfer a Repository
Repository ownership can be transferred in supported situations when moving a project to another user or organization.
Current Owner ↓ Transfer Repository ↓ New Owner / Organization ↓ Repository Managed There
Check access, integrations, links, and project dependencies before transferring an important repository.
Delete a Repository ⚠️
Deleting a repository is a major action. Before deleting, verify that the repository and its important data are no longer needed and follow the confirmation process carefully.
Repository ↓ Settings ↓ Delete Option ↓ Review Carefully ⚠️ ↓ Confirm Required Information ↓ Delete
Good Practice: Before deleting an important repository, verify backups, team dependencies, documentation links, and whether the project may still be needed.
Repository Settings and Team Workflow ⭐
Repository Settings ↓ Configure Visibility ↓ Manage Access ↓ Set Default Branch ↓ Configure Branch Rules ↓ Enable Needed Features ↓ Team Development Workflow ↓ Safer and More Organized Collaboration
Example: Team Repository
Repository: inventory-management-system Visibility: Private 🔒 Default Branch: main Workflow: Feature Branch ↓ Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Checks ↓ Merge to main
Visibility vs Access ⭐

VisibilityAccess Permissions
Controls the general audience of the repositoryControls what authorized users can do
Example: PublicExample: Who can push or manage settings
Example: PrivateExample: Who can review or administer
Visibility Who Can Generally Access? Public / Private / Internal ──────────────────── Permissions What Can Each Authorized User Do? View / Work / Manage Depending on Granted Access
Repository Settings vs Git Commands

Repository SettingsGit Commands
Manage GitHub repository configurationManage Git repository history and files
Example: Change visibilityExample: git commit
Example: Manage collaboratorsExample: git branch
Example: Branch rulesExample: git merge
GIT Local Repository Work add commit branch merge rebase ──────────────────── GITHUB SETTINGS Repository Management visibility access branch rules features configuration
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Make a repository Public without reviewing its contents Correct ✅ Check for secrets and confidential information first ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Think Private means secrets can be committed safely Correct ✅ Use proper secret management and avoid committing credentials ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Give unnecessary users high-level permissions Correct ✅ Grant only the access needed for their work ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Change the default branch without checking the workflow Correct ✅ Review Pull Requests, automation, documentation, and team dependencies ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Delete a repository without checking whether it is still needed Correct ✅ Review dependencies and important data before deleting ──────────────────── Mistake 6 ❌ Think repository settings and Git commands are the same Correct ✅ Git manages repository history; GitHub settings manage repository configuration
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
VISIBILITY = WHO CAN ACCESS? SETTINGS = HOW IS THE REPOSITORY CONFIGURED? ACCESS PERMISSIONS = WHAT CAN AUTHORIZED USERS DO?
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
PublicRepository is publicly accessible
PrivateRepository access is restricted to authorized users
InternalOrganization-level visibility where supported
SettingsRepository configuration and management options
Default BranchMain branch selected as the repository's default
AccessControls authorized collaborators and permissions
Branch RulesControls or requirements for important branches
ArchivePreserves a repository no longer actively developed
TransferMoves repository ownership in supported situations
DeleteRemoves the repository and should be handled carefully

Final Definition: GitHub repository visibility determines who can access a repository, while repository settings provide configuration and management controls for areas such as repository information, access, branches, features, security, archiving, transferring, and other repository operations.
practice: Use a practice repository where you have permission to view and manage repository settings.
Step 1: Open one of your GitHub repositories.
Step 2: Open the repository Settings section.
Repository ↓ Settings ↓ Explore Available Options
Step 3: Check the repository's current visibility.
Ask Yourself: Is it Public? 🌍 Is it Private? 🔒 Is Internal available for this repository? 🏢
Step 4: Review the repository name and description.
Step 5: Check which branch is configured as the default branch.
Example: Default branch: main
Step 6: Review who currently has access to the repository, where your repository type and permissions allow you to view this information.
Step 7: Review available branch rules or protection settings. Do not change important rules unless you understand the effect on your workflow.
Step 8: Check which repository features are enabled.
Issues Enabled / Disabled Pull Requests Enabled / Available Projects Enabled / Disabled Discussions Enabled / Disabled Review Your Actual Repository Setup
Step 9: If you want to test visibility changes, use a separate practice repository rather than an important project.

Safety Check Before Private → Public:
✓ No passwords
✓ No API keys
✓ No access tokens
✓ No confidential files
✓ No sensitive information in files you intend to publish
Step 10: Write down the difference between visibility, permissions, and repository settings.
Visibility → Who can generally access? Permissions → What can authorized users do? Settings → How is the repository configured?
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is repository visibility? 2. What is the difference between Public and Private? 3. When might Internal visibility be used? 4. What should you check before making a repository Public? 5. What is a default branch? 6. What is the difference between visibility and permissions? 7. Why are branch rules useful? 8. What is repository archiving used for? 9. What should you check before deleting a repository? 10. Complete: Visibility = Who can ______? Settings = How is the repository ______?

Practice Goal: You should be able to explain Public, Private, and Internal repository visibility, understand the purpose of repository settings, distinguish visibility from access permissions, identify the default branch, review repository features and branch rules, and safely manage important repository configuration.

qna.q: Q1. What does repository visibility control?
qna.a: It controls the general audience that can access the repository.

qna.q: Q2. What is a Public repository?
qna.a: A Public repository is publicly accessible and can be viewed by anyone who can access it.

qna.q: Q3. What is a Private repository?
qna.a: A Private repository restricts access to authorized users.

qna.q: Q4. What is an Internal repository?
qna.a: It is an organization-level repository visibility option available in supported environments for organization members without making the repository public to everyone.

qna.q: Q5. What should you check before making a repository Public?
qna.a: Check for passwords, API keys, access tokens, confidential files, and other sensitive information.

qna.q: Q6. What is the difference between visibility and permissions?
qna.a: Visibility controls who can generally access a repository, while permissions control what authorized users are allowed to do.

qna.q: Q7. What is the default branch?
qna.a: It is the primary branch configured as the repository's default, often named main.

qna.q: Q8. Why are branch rules or protection settings useful?
qna.a: They help control how changes reach important branches and can enforce workflow requirements such as reviews or checks.

qna.q: Q9. Does a Private repository mean it is safe to commit passwords and API keys?
qna.a: No. Sensitive credentials should still be handled with proper secret management and should not be committed carelessly.

qna.q: Q10. What is repository archiving used for?
qna.a: It is used to preserve a repository that is no longer intended for active development.

qna.q: Q11. What is the difference between Git commands and GitHub repository settings?
qna.a: Git commands manage repository files and history, while GitHub settings manage repository configuration and access-related options.

qna.q: Q12. Complete: Visibility = Who can ______?
qna.a: Access.

qna.q: Q13. Complete: Settings = How is the repository ______?
qna.a: Configured.

items.title: HTTPS vs SSH
explanation: Simple Meaning
HTTPS and SSH are two common ways to connect your local Git repository with a remote repository such as GitHub.
Your Computer ↓ Git Authentication Method ↓ HTTPS 🔐 OR SSH 🔑 ↓ Remote Repository ↓ GitHub

Simple Definition:

HTTPS connects to GitHub using an HTTPS repository URL and supported authentication credentials such as a Personal Access Token.

SSH connects using an SSH repository URL and SSH key-based authentication.
Why Do We Need HTTPS or SSH? ⭐
Your local Git repository needs a way to communicate with the remote repository when performing operations such as git clone, git pull, git fetch, and git push.
Local Repository Your Computer ↓ How Do We Connect? ↓ HTTPS 🔐 SSH 🔑 ↓ GitHub Repository
HTTPS
HTTPS uses a repository URL that begins with https://.
https://github.com/username/my-project.git
Local Computer ↓ Git Command ↓ HTTPS Connection 🔐 ↓ Authentication When Required ↓ GitHub Repository
Example: Clone Using HTTPS ⭐
git clone https://github.com/username/my-project.git
Git downloads the repository using the HTTPS remote URL.
HTTPS Authentication

For operations that require authentication, GitHub can use supported authentication methods. Depending on your setup, credentials may be handled through a credential manager, browser-based authentication, GitHub CLI, or a Personal Access Token instead of your account password.
git push ↓ HTTPS Remote ↓ Authentication Required? ↓ Supported Authentication Credential Manager PAT 🔑 Browser / Device Flow Other Configured Method ↓ GitHub Verifies Access
SSH
SSH uses a repository URL that typically looks different from an HTTPS URL.
git@github.com:username/my-project.git
Local Computer ↓ Git Command ↓ SSH Connection 🔑 ↓ SSH Key Authentication ↓ GitHub Repository
How SSH Authentication Works ⭐
SSH uses a key pair consisting of a private key and a public key.
YOUR COMPUTER Private Key 🔒 Never Share ↓ SSH Authentication ↓ GITHUB ACCOUNT Public Key 🔑 Added to GitHub
Important: Your private SSH key must remain private. You can add the corresponding public key to your GitHub account.
SSH Key Pair Example
SSH KEY PAIR Private Key 🔒 Stays on Your Computer ──────────────────── Public Key 🔑 Added to GitHub ──────────────────── Both Work Together For Authentication ⭐
Example: Clone Using SSH ⭐
git clone git@github.com:username/my-project.git
Git connects to the repository using SSH and authenticates using your configured SSH key.
HTTPS vs SSH Repository URLs ⭐

HTTPSSSH
https://github.com/username/project.gitgit@github.com:username/project.git
Uses HTTPS connectionUses SSH connection
Can use token or other supported authenticationUses SSH key-based authentication
Full Comparison ⭐

FeatureHTTPSSSH
Repository URLStarts with https://Typically starts with git@
AuthenticationSupported credentials such as PAT or credential managerSSH key pair
Initial SetupUsually simpler for beginnersRequires SSH key setup
Clonegit clone https://...git clone git@github.com:...
Private SecretPAT or other stored credential must be protectedPrivate SSH key must be protected
Daily UsageCan be convenient with credential managementConvenient after SSH setup
HTTPS Workflow
1. Get HTTPS Repository URL ↓ 2. Clone Repository ↓ 3. Make Changes ↓ 4. git add ↓ 5. git commit ↓ 6. git push ↓ 7. Authenticate When Required ↓ 8. GitHub Receives Changes
git clone https://github.com/username/project.git cd project # Make changes git add . git commit -m "Update project" git push
SSH Workflow

1. Generate SSH Key Pair ↓ 2. Keep Private Key Secure ↓ 3. Add Public Key to GitHub ↓ 4. Get SSH Repository URL ↓ 5. Clone Repository ↓ 6. Make Changes ↓ 7. git add ↓ 8. git commit ↓ 9. git push ↓ 10. SSH Key Authenticates You
git clone git@github.com:username/project.git cd project # Make changes git add . git commit -m "Update project" git push
HTTPS: Advantages
HTTPS 👍 ✓ Simple repository URL ✓ Often easier for beginners ✓ Works with common credential managers ✓ Can use Personal Access Tokens ✓ Usually convenient in restricted networks
HTTPS: Considerations
HTTPS ⚠️ Authentication may be required PAT must be protected Credential setup depends on system and Git configuration
SSH: Advantages
SSH 👍 ✓ Key-based authentication ✓ Convenient after initial setup ✓ No need to manually enter a token for every operation when configured properly ✓ Common for frequent Git users
SSH: Considerations
SSH ⚠️ Requires initial key setup Private key must remain secret SSH configuration may be more difficult for complete beginners
Which One Should a Beginner Use? ⭐
BEGINNER Want Simple Initial Setup? ↓ HTTPS 👍 ──────────────────── Using Git Frequently? Comfortable Setting Up Keys? ↓ SSH 👍
Both are valid options. HTTPS is often easier when you are learning GitHub, while SSH can be very convenient once you understand SSH key authentication.
HTTPS and PAT Connection ⭐
HTTPS ↓ Authentication Required ↓ Personal Access Token 🔑 Can Be One Supported Credential ↓ GitHub Verifies Access
A PAT is not the same as HTTPS. HTTPS is the connection method and URL type, while a PAT is a credential that can be used for supported authentication.
SSH and SSH Key Connection ⭐
SSH ↓ Authentication Method ↓ Private Key on Computer 🔒 + Public Key on GitHub 🔑 ↓ GitHub Verifies Identity
Easy Comparison 🧠
HTTPS Connection: https://... Authentication: PAT / Credential Manager Or Other Supported Method ──────────────────── SSH Connection: git@github.com:... Authentication: SSH Key Pair
Can You Change HTTPS to SSH Later? ⭐
Yes. You can change the remote URL of an existing local repository from HTTPS to SSH, or from SSH to HTTPS.
Current Remote HTTPS ↓ Change Remote URL ↓ SSH OR Current Remote SSH ↓ Change Remote URL ↓ HTTPS
View Current Remote
git remote -v
Example Output origin https://github.com/username/project.git (fetch) origin https://github.com/username/project.git (push) ↓ Current Method = HTTPS
Change HTTPS Remote to SSH
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:username/project.git
Change SSH Remote to HTTPS
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/username/project.git
Verify After Changing
git remote -v
Change Remote ↓ git remote -v ↓ Check Fetch URL Check Push URL ↓ Correct URL? ✅
HTTPS vs SSH Is Not About Git Commands
The main Git commands remain the same. Usually, the difference is the remote URL and authentication method.
HTTPS git clone git pull git push git fetch ──────────────────── SSH git clone git pull git push git fetch Same Git Commands ⭐ Different Connection / Authentication
Example: Same Repository
Repository: my-project HTTPS URL: https://github.com/username/my-project.git ──────────────────── SSH URL: git@github.com:username/my-project.git Same Repository ⭐ Different Connection Methods
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Think HTTPS and SSH are different Git systems Correct ✅ They are different ways to connect and authenticate with the same remote repository ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Share a Personal Access Token Correct ✅ Treat it like a password ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Share your SSH private key Correct ✅ Only share the public key when required ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Use an SSH URL without configuring an SSH key Correct ✅ Set up and add your public key first ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Think Git commands change completely Correct ✅ Most commands remain the same ──────────────────── Mistake 6 ❌ Forget which remote URL is configured Correct ✅ Use git remote -v to check
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
HTTPS = URL + Token / Supported Credentials 🔐 SSH = URL + SSH Key Pair 🔑 Both = Connect Local Git To GitHub ⭐
Quick Summary

ConceptHTTPSSSH
URL Examplehttps://github.com/...git@github.com:...
AuthenticationPAT, credential manager, or another supported methodSSH key pair
Beginner SetupOften simplerRequires key configuration
Secret to ProtectPAT or stored authentication credentialsPrivate SSH key
Commandsgit clone, pull, push, fetchgit clone, pull, push, fetch
Can Change Later?YesYes

Final Definition: HTTPS and SSH are two common methods for connecting a local Git repository to GitHub. HTTPS uses an https:// remote URL and supported credentials such as a PAT, while SSH uses an SSH-style remote URL and public/private key authentication. Both can be used with the same Git commands and repository.
practice: Step 1: Open one of your existing local Git repositories.
Step 2: Check the current remote URL.
git remote -v
Step 3: Identify the connection type.
Starts with: https:// ↓ HTTPS 🔐 ──────────────────── Starts with: git@github.com: ↓ SSH 🔑
Step 4: Write down your current remote URL type: HTTPS or SSH.
Step 5: Practice recognizing the two URL formats.
HTTPS: https://github.com/username/project.git SSH: git@github.com:username/project.git
Step 6: If you have a separate practice repository and already understand SSH setup, practice changing the remote URL.
# Change to SSH git remote set-url origin git@github.com:username/project.git # Verify git remote -v
Step 7: Practice changing it back to HTTPS if needed.
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/username/project.git # Verify git remote -v
Step 8: Explain the difference between a PAT and an SSH key.
PAT 🔑 Secret Token Credential ──────────────────── SSH Key Pair 🔐 Private Key → Keep Secret Public Key → Add to GitHub
Step 9: Remember the security rule: never share a real PAT or your SSH private key.
Step 10: Explain why the following commands can work with both connection methods:
git clone git fetch git pull git push
Answer: The Git commands are generally the same. The remote URL and authentication method are what change.
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is HTTPS used for in GitHub? 2. What is SSH used for in GitHub? 3. How does an HTTPS repository URL usually begin? 4. How does an SSH repository URL usually look? 5. What credential can be used with HTTPS authentication? 6. What type of authentication does SSH use? 7. Which SSH key must remain secret? 8. Can you change a remote from HTTPS to SSH? 9. Which command shows configured remotes? 10. Complete: HTTPS = https://... SSH = ______@github.com:...

Practice Goal: You should be able to identify HTTPS and SSH repository URLs, explain their authentication differences, protect PATs and SSH private keys, check your current remote using git remote -v, and change a practice repository remote between HTTPS and SSH.

qna.q: Q1. What are HTTPS and SSH used for in GitHub?
qna.a: They are common methods for connecting a local Git repository to a remote GitHub repository.

qna.q: Q2. How does an HTTPS repository URL usually begin?
qna.a: https://

qna.q: Q3. What does an SSH GitHub repository URL commonly look like?
qna.a: It commonly uses a format such as git@github.com:username/repository.git.

qna.q: Q4. What can be used for supported HTTPS authentication?
qna.a: A Personal Access Token, credential manager, or another supported authentication method.

qna.q: Q5. What authentication does SSH use?
qna.a: SSH uses public/private key authentication.

qna.q: Q6. Which SSH key must remain secret?
qna.a: The private SSH key.

qna.q: Q7. Can you share your SSH public key?
qna.a: Yes. The public key is designed to be added to services such as GitHub, while the private key must remain secret.

qna.q: Q8. Are HTTPS and SSH different Git systems?
qna.a: No. They are different connection and authentication methods that can be used with Git repositories.

qna.q: Q9. Do git push and git pull commands change completely when switching from HTTPS to SSH?
qna.a: No. The commands generally remain the same; the remote URL and authentication method change.

qna.q: Q10. Which command shows the configured remote URLs?
qna.a: git remote -v

qna.q: Q11. How can you change an HTTPS remote to an SSH remote?
qna.a: Use git remote set-url origin followed by the SSH repository URL.

qna.q: Q12. Complete: HTTPS = https://..., SSH = ______@github.com:...
qna.a: git

qna.q: Q13. Which method is often easier for beginners?
qna.a: HTTPS is often easier for beginners because it usually requires less initial key configuration.

items.title: Personal Access Token (PAT) Basics
explanation: Simple Meaning

A Personal Access Token (PAT) is a secret credential that can be used to authenticate with GitHub instead of using your account password in certain situations, such as Git operations over HTTPS or accessing GitHub APIs.
Your Computer ↓ Git / Application ↓ Needs Authentication ↓ GitHub ↑ Personal Access Token (PAT) 🔑

Simple Definition: A Personal Access Token is a secret value generated from your GitHub account that can be used to authenticate requests and access resources based on the permissions granted to that token.
Why Is a PAT Needed? ⭐
GitHub authentication methods vary depending on what you are doing. A PAT can be used when a command-line Git operation over HTTPS or an application/API request requires token-based authentication.
You Want To Access GitHub ↓ Authentication Required ↓ Choose Supported Authentication ↓ Examples: PAT 🔑 SSH Key 🔐 GitHub CLI Authentication Other Supported Methods
Important: PAT Is Not Your Password ⚠️
GitHub Password Used to Sign In To Your Account ──────────────────── Personal Access Token 🔑 Used as a Secret Credential For Specific Authentication And Access Purposes
A PAT should be treated like a password because someone who obtains it may be able to use the permissions associated with that token.
Example: Git Push Using HTTPS ⭐
Your Local Repository ↓ git push ↓ GitHub HTTPS Authentication ↓ Username / Account Identity + PAT 🔑 ↓ GitHub Verifies Access ↓ Push Allowed or Denied
The exact authentication prompt can depend on your operating system, Git credential manager, GitHub configuration, and authentication method.
What Does a PAT Look Like?
A Personal Access Token is a long secret string generated by GitHub. You should never publish or share a real token.
Example only — NOT a real token: github_pat_example_ABC123XYZ456
Security Rule: Never use a real Personal Access Token in screenshots, public repositories, README files, source code, chat messages, or documentation.
How PAT Permissions Work ⭐
A token can be created with permissions that determine what the token is allowed to access or perform. You should grant only the permissions required for the task.
Personal Access Token 🔑 ↓ Permissions ↓ What Can This Token Do? Read Repository Data Write Repository Data Access Specific Resources Other Allowed Actions Only What Is Granted ⭐
Principle of Least Privilege ⭐
Task: Push Code to One Repository ❌ Give More Permissions Than Needed ──────────────────── ✅ Give Only Required Permissions Least Privilege = Safer Access ⭐
When creating a token, avoid granting broad or unnecessary permissions if a smaller set of permissions is sufficient.
Types of Personal Access Tokens

GitHub provides different PAT models, including fine-grained personal access tokens and tokens with broader permission scopes. The available options and permission choices can depend on the current GitHub interface and account or organization policies.

PERSONAL ACCESS TOKENS Fine-Grained Token ⭐ → Can be restricted more specifically → Can be limited to selected resources Broader Scoped Token → Uses broader permission scopes → May provide wider access depending on configuration
For learning purposes, remember the main idea: always understand what a token can access before creating or using it.
Fine-Grained Token Concept
Token 🔑 Access To: Selected Repository A ✅ Selected Repository B ❌ Selected Repository C ❌ Permissions: Read Contents ✅ Write Contents ✅ Other Unneeded Access ❌
Creating a PAT — Basic Flow ⭐
GitHub Account ↓ Account Settings ↓ Developer Settings ↓ Personal Access Tokens ↓ Choose Token Type ↓ Configure Access ↓ Set Permissions ↓ Create Token ↓ Copy and Store Securely 🔐
The exact menu names and screens can change over time, but the general process is to create a token, choose the required access, configure permissions, and securely store the generated secret.
Token Expiration ⭐
Tokens can be configured with an expiration period depending on the token type and available options. An expiration date limits how long a token remains usable.
Create Token ↓ Token Works 🔑 ↓ Expiration Reached ↓ Token No Longer Works ↓ Create / Use New Authorized Token If Needed
Using an appropriate expiration period can reduce the risk of an old token remaining active indefinitely.
Example Scenario

You Work On: my-project You Need: Push Changes Through HTTPS Git Requires Authentication ↓ Use Supported Authentication ↓ PAT Can Be Used 🔑 ↓ GitHub Checks: Is Token Valid? Has It Expired? Does It Have Required Access? ↓ Allow / Deny Request
PAT and GitHub API
A PAT can also be used to authenticate certain GitHub API requests. The permissions attached to the token determine what authenticated actions and resources are available.
Application / Script ↓ API Request ↓ Authorization: PAT 🔑 ↓ GitHub ↓ Check Token Permissions ↓ Return Allowed Response
Store Your Token Securely ⚠️

SAFE PLACES ✓ Secure credential manager ✓ Appropriate secret manager ✓ Secure environment configuration ──────────────────── UNSAFE PLACES ❌ Public GitHub repository ❌ Hard-coded source code ❌ README.md ❌ Screenshots ❌ Public chat ❌ Shared documents without protection
Never Hard-Code a Token
❌ Bad: TOKEN = "your_real_secret_token"
Conceptually better: TOKEN = read_from_secure_configuration()
The main principle is to keep secrets outside publicly shared source code and use an appropriate secure credential or secret-management method.
What If You Accidentally Expose a Token? 🚨
Token Accidentally Exposed ↓ Revoke / Disable It Immediately 🚨 ↓ Create a Replacement If Needed ↓ Update Applications / Credentials ↓ Review What Access It Had ↓ Check for Unauthorized Activity
Important: Removing a token from a file later may not be enough if it was already committed or shared. Treat an exposed token as compromised and revoke it promptly.
Revoke vs Delete
When you no longer need a token, disable, revoke, or delete it using the available GitHub account controls. The important result is that the old secret should no longer be usable.
Old Token 🔑 No Longer Needed OR Possibly Exposed ↓ Revoke / Delete / Disable ↓ Old Token Cannot Be Used
PAT vs SSH Key ⭐

Personal Access TokenSSH Key
Secret token credentialPublic/private key authentication
Commonly used with HTTPS authentication and API accessCommonly used for Git authentication through SSH
Permissions and expiration can be configuredUses key-pair based authentication
Should be kept secretPrivate key must be kept secret
HTTPS Workflow Git ↓ HTTPS ↓ PAT 🔑 ──────────────────── SSH Workflow Git ↓ SSH ↓ SSH Key 🔐
PAT vs GitHub Password ⭐

GitHub PasswordPersonal Access Token
Used for account sign-inUsed as a separate authentication credential
Protects account loginCan be limited by permissions and access
Do not shareDo not share
Account-level secretSeparate revocable credential
PAT vs Repository Visibility
Repository Visibility Who Can Generally Access? Public / Private / Internal ──────────────────── PAT How Does a Request Authenticate? What Permissions Does the Token Have?
Repository visibility and PAT permissions are different concepts. A token may still need the correct access and permissions for the requested operation.
Common PAT Workflow ⭐

Need to Authenticate ↓ Determine Required Access ↓ Create Token ↓ Grant Minimum Required Permissions ↓ Set Appropriate Expiration ↓ Copy Token Securely ↓ Use Token for Supported Authentication ↓ Revoke When No Longer Needed
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Treat PAT like normal text Correct ✅ Treat it like a password ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Give every available permission Correct ✅ Grant only required permissions ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Create a token and forget about it Correct ✅ Review and remove unused tokens ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Commit a token to Git Correct ✅ Keep secrets out of source code ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Share a token in a screenshot Correct ✅ Hide or redact secret values ──────────────────── Mistake 6 ❌ Only remove an exposed token from the current file Correct ✅ Revoke the exposed token immediately ──────────────────── Mistake 7 ❌ Assume a Private repository makes exposed secrets safe Correct ✅ Use proper secret management regardless of visibility
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
PAT = 🔑 A Secret Credential Access Depends On: VALIDITY + PERMISSIONS + RESOURCE ACCESS + EXPIRATION Keep It Secret 🔐
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
PATPersonal Access Token used as an authentication credential
SecretMust be protected like a password
PermissionsControl what the token can access or do
Least PrivilegeGrant only the access required
ExpirationCan limit how long a token remains usable
Fine-GrainedCan allow more specific resource and permission restrictions
Exposed TokenShould be treated as compromised and revoked promptly
Unused TokenShould be removed, disabled, or revoked when no longer needed

Final Definition: A GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) is a secret authentication credential that can be used for supported GitHub operations and API access. Its permissions and access determine what it can do, so it should be granted only the minimum required privileges, stored securely, and revoked if exposed or no longer needed.
practice: Step 1: Understand the difference between your GitHub account password and a Personal Access Token.
Account Password → Sign in to your account PAT 🔑 → Separate authentication credential → Used for supported operations
Step 2: Open your GitHub account settings and locate the Personal Access Token area. The exact menu structure may change over time.
Step 3: Review the available token types before creating one.
Choose Token Type ↓ Understand Resource Access ↓ Understand Permissions ↓ Choose Only What You Need
Step 4: For practice, imagine you need access only to one repository. Ask yourself: should the token have access to every repository or only the required repository?
Answer: Follow the principle of least privilege and grant only the access required for the task.
Step 5: Review available permissions and understand what each permission allows before selecting it.
Step 6: Choose an appropriate expiration period based on the task and security requirements.
Step 7: If you create a real token, store it securely. Do not paste the real token into this course, a README, source code, screenshots, or a public repository.
Practice Safety Rule: Never send me your real PAT. You can practice with a fake example value only.
Step 8: Practice identifying unsafe code:
TOKEN = "real_secret_token_here"
Question: Why is this unsafe?
Answer: Because secrets stored directly in source code can be accidentally committed, shared, exposed, or copied.
Step 9: Practice the correct response to an exposed token.
Token Exposed ↓ Treat as Compromised ↓ Revoke Immediately ↓ Create Replacement If Needed ↓ Update Authorized Applications
Step 10: Explain this workflow in your own words:
Need Authentication ↓ Determine Required Access ↓ Create PAT ↓ Minimum Permissions ↓ Store Securely ↓ Use for Supported Authentication ↓ Revoke When Finished
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is a PAT? 2. Why should it be kept secret? 3. Is a PAT the same as your GitHub password? 4. What does least privilege mean? 5. What controls what a PAT can do? 6. Why is token expiration useful? 7. Where should you NOT store a PAT? 8. What should you do if a token is exposed? 9. What is one difference between a PAT and an SSH key? 10. Complete: PAT = Secret ______ Credential

Practice Goal: You should understand what a Personal Access Token is, when it can be used, why it must be protected, how permissions and least privilege work, why expiration matters, and what to do immediately if a token is exposed.

qna.q: Q1. What is a Personal Access Token (PAT)?
qna.a: It is a secret authentication credential that can be used for supported GitHub operations and API access.

qna.q: Q2. Is a PAT the same as your GitHub account password?
qna.a: No. It is a separate secret credential with its own access and permission configuration.

qna.q: Q3. Why should a PAT be kept secret?
qna.a: Because someone who obtains it may be able to use the permissions associated with the token.

qna.q: Q4. What determines what a PAT can do?
qna.a: Its validity, configured permissions, resource access, and whether it has expired.

qna.q: Q5. What does the principle of least privilege mean?
qna.a: Grant only the minimum permissions and access required for the task.

qna.q: Q6. Why can token expiration be useful?
qna.a: It limits how long a token remains usable and can reduce the risk of old credentials remaining active.

qna.q: Q7. Can you safely put a PAT in a public GitHub repository?
qna.a: No. A PAT should never be exposed in public repositories or other public locations.

qna.q: Q8. What should you do if a PAT is accidentally exposed?
qna.a: Treat it as compromised and revoke or disable it promptly, then replace and update it if necessary.

qna.q: Q9. Is simply deleting an exposed token from the current file always enough?
qna.a: No. It may already have been shared or committed, so the exposed token should be revoked.

qna.q: Q10. Name one common use of a PAT.
qna.a: It can be used for supported Git operations over HTTPS or for authenticated GitHub API requests.

qna.q: Q11. What is one difference between a PAT and an SSH key?
qna.a: A PAT is a secret token credential commonly used for HTTPS and API authentication, while SSH authentication uses a public/private key pair.

qna.q: Q12. Complete: PAT = Secret ______ Credential.
qna.a: Authentication.

items.title: SSH Key Basics
explanation: Simple Meaning

An SSH key is used for secure authentication between your computer and a remote service such as GitHub. For GitHub, SSH keys allow Git to authenticate you without using a Personal Access Token for every HTTPS-based authentication workflow.
Your Computer 💻 ↓ SSH Authentication ↓ SSH Key Pair 🔑 ↓ GitHub Repository
Simple Definition: An SSH key pair consists of a private key, which stays secret on your computer, and a public key, which can be added to your GitHub account to verify authentication.
Why Are SSH Keys Used? ⭐
When you use an SSH remote URL, Git needs a secure way to prove your identity to GitHub. SSH key authentication provides that method.
git push ↓ SSH Remote URL ↓ Who Is Connecting? ↓ SSH Key Authentication 🔐 ↓ GitHub Verifies Access ↓ Push Allowed / Denied
The SSH Key Pair ⭐
SSH authentication uses two related keys.
SSH KEY PAIR 1. Private Key 🔒 Stays Secret on Your Computer + 2. Public Key 🔑 Added to GitHub ↓ Used Together for Authentication
Private Key 🔒
The private key is the secret part of your SSH key pair. It should remain on your computer and should never be shared publicly.
PRIVATE KEY 🔒 ✓ Keep on your computer ✓ Keep secure ✓ Protect with appropriate security ❌ Do not upload publicly ❌ Do not send to others ❌ Do not commit to Git ❌ Do not share in screenshots
Public Key 🔑
The public key is the part of the key pair that can be added to your GitHub account.
PUBLIC KEY 🔑 Your Computer ↓ Copy Public Key ↓ GitHub Account ↓ SSH Keys Settings ↓ Add Public Key

Easy Rule:

Private Key = Never Share 🔒
Public Key = Can Be Added to GitHub 🔑
How SSH Authentication Works ⭐
YOUR COMPUTER 💻 Private Key 🔒 ↓ Proves Identity Securely ↓ GITHUB Public Key 🔑 ↓ Verifies Authentication ↓ Access Allowed / Denied
You do not need to send your private key to GitHub. The private key remains under your control on your computer.
SSH and GitHub Remote URLs ⭐
When using SSH, the GitHub repository remote URL typically looks like this:
git@github.com:username/my-project.git
git@github.com ↓ SSH Connection username/my-project.git ↓ Repository Location
HTTPS vs SSH Connection

HTTPSSSH
https://github.com/username/project.gitgit@github.com:username/project.git
Uses HTTPSUses SSH
Can use PAT or other supported credentialsUses SSH key authentication
Token/credentials must be protectedPrivate key must be protected
Common SSH Key Files
When you generate an SSH key pair, you normally get two related files: one private key file and one public key file.
Example Concept id_ed25519 → Private Key 🔒 id_ed25519.pub → Public Key 🔑
The exact key name and location can vary depending on the operating system and the options chosen when creating the key.
Why Does the Public Key Often End With .pub? ⭐
id_ed25519 ↓ Private Key 🔒 id_ed25519.pub ↓ Public Key 🔑
The .pub file conventionally contains the public portion of the SSH key pair.
Creating an SSH Key — Basic Concept ⭐
Open Terminal ↓ Generate SSH Key Pair ↓ Private Key Created 🔒 Public Key Created 🔑 ↓ Keep Private Key Secure ↓ Add Public Key to GitHub ↓ Use SSH Repository URL
Example Command
A common modern SSH key algorithm is Ed25519.
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
This command is used to generate an Ed25519 SSH key pair. During the process, your system may ask where to save the key and whether to use a passphrase.
Note: Replace your_email@example.com with your own email address when practicing. Do not use another person's email address.
What Is a Passphrase? 🔐
A passphrase can provide additional protection for your private SSH key. If your private key file is accessed by someone else, the passphrase can add another layer of protection.
Private SSH Key 🔒 + Passphrase 🔐 ↓ Additional Protection
Choose and protect a strong passphrase according to your security requirements. Do not share it.
Typical SSH Key Location
On many systems, SSH keys are stored inside the user's .ssh directory.
~/.ssh/
Home Directory ↓ .ssh ├── id_ed25519 🔒 Private Key └── id_ed25519.pub 🔑 Public Key
The exact file names and locations can vary.
Adding the Public Key to GitHub ⭐
Generate SSH Key Pair ↓ Find Public Key ↓ Copy Public Key Content ↓ GitHub Account Settings ↓ SSH Keys ↓ Add New SSH Key ↓ Save
Only the public key should be copied to GitHub for this setup.
Example Public Key Concept
ssh-ed25519 AAAA...example... user@example.com
This is only an example format. Do not copy a random example key as your own authentication key. Generate your own key pair.
After Adding the SSH Key
Private Key 🔒 On Your Computer + Public Key 🔑 On GitHub ↓ SSH Authentication Ready ↓ Use SSH Remote URL
Test the SSH Connection
After configuring your key and adding the public key to GitHub, you can test SSH authentication.
ssh -T git@github.com
Run Test Command ↓ SSH Connects to GitHub ↓ GitHub Checks Public Key ↓ Authentication Success? ↓ Success Message / Error Message
The exact output can depend on your operating system, SSH configuration, account setup, and whether the key was configured correctly.
Using SSH With an Existing Repository ⭐
If your existing repository currently uses HTTPS, you can change its remote URL to SSH after configuring your SSH key.
Check Current Remote
git remote -v
Example Output origin https://github.com/username/project.git (fetch) origin https://github.com/username/project.git (push) Current Connection = HTTPS
Change Remote to SSH
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:username/project.git
Verify the New Remote
git remote -v
origin git@github.com:username/project.git (fetch) origin git@github.com:username/project.git (push) Current Connection = SSH 🔑
SSH Workflow ⭐
1. Generate SSH Key Pair ↓ 2. Private Key Stays Secure 🔒 ↓ 3. Add Public Key to GitHub 🔑 ↓ 4. Test SSH Connection ↓ 5. Configure SSH Remote URL ↓ 6. git fetch / pull / push ↓ 7. SSH Authenticates You
Example Daily Git Workflow
git status git add . git commit -m "Update project" git push
After SSH authentication is configured correctly, Git can use the configured SSH authentication mechanism when communicating with an SSH remote.
SSH Key vs Personal Access Token ⭐

SSH KeyPersonal Access Token
Uses public/private key pairUses a secret token
Commonly used with SSH Git URLsCommonly used with HTTPS and API authentication
Private key remains on your computerToken is a secret credential
Public key can be added to GitHubPermissions can control token access
Private key must remain secretToken must remain secret
Easy Comparison 🧠
SSH KEY PAIR Private Key 🔒 Never Share Public Key 🔑 Add to GitHub ──────────────────── PAT 🔐 One Secret Token Keep Secret Use for Supported Authentication
Can You Use Multiple SSH Keys?
Yes. A user may have multiple SSH keys for different devices, accounts, or purposes. Each key should be managed carefully so you know which keys are active and where they are used.
Laptop 💻 → SSH Key A Work Computer 🖥️ → SSH Key B Another Device 💻 → SSH Key C GitHub Account May Have Multiple Authorized Public Keys
Why Use Different Keys for Different Devices?
Using separate keys can make it easier to manage access. If one device is lost or compromised, the corresponding public key can be removed without necessarily affecting keys on other devices.
Device A Lost ⚠️ ↓ Remove / Revoke Its Public Key ↓ Device B Key Still Works Device C Key Still Works
Common SSH Problems

Problem: Permission denied (publickey) Possible Reasons: • Public key not added to GitHub • Wrong SSH key being used • Private key unavailable • Incorrect SSH configuration • Wrong GitHub account / access • Remote URL is incorrect
Basic Troubleshooting Flow
SSH Problem ↓ Check Remote URL ↓ git remote -v ↓ Correct SSH URL? ↓ Test Connection ↓ ssh -T git@github.com ↓ Check Public Key Added ↓ Check Local Private Key ↓ Review SSH Configuration
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Upload Private Key to GitHub Correct ✅ Upload Only Public Key ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Share Private Key Correct ✅ Keep Private Key Secret ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Commit SSH Keys to Git Correct ✅ Keep Key Files Outside Repositories ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Use SSH URL Before Setting Up SSH Key Correct ✅ Generate and configure the key first ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Copy the wrong file Correct ✅ Copy the public key, usually the .pub file ──────────────────── Mistake 6 ❌ Delete an old key without checking where it is used Correct ✅ Review active devices and access before removing it ──────────────────── Mistake 7 ❌ Share a screenshot containing private key content Correct ✅ Never expose private key content
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
PRIVATE KEY 🔒 = YOUR SECRET = STAYS ON YOUR COMPUTER PUBLIC KEY 🔑 = CAN BE ADDED TO GITHUB BOTH TOGETHER = SSH AUTHENTICATION ⭐
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
SSH Key PairA private key and a related public key
Private KeySecret key that must remain protected
Public KeyKey that can be added to GitHub
SSH RemoteUses an SSH-style URL such as git@github.com:...
Key GenerationCreates the related private and public keys
PassphraseCan provide additional protection for the private key
Test Commandssh -T git@github.com
Check Remotegit remote -v
Change Remotegit remote set-url origin ...

Final Definition: An SSH key is part of a public/private key pair used for secure authentication. The private key stays secret on your computer, while the public key can be added to GitHub. Together, they allow Git to authenticate with GitHub when using an SSH repository connection.
practice: Step 1: Open Terminal, Git Bash, or another command-line terminal on your computer.
Step 2: Check whether you already have SSH keys.
ls ~/.ssh
Step 3: Look for key pairs such as:
id_ed25519 id_ed25519.pub
No .ssh Key Yet? ↓ Generate a New Key Pair Key Already Exists? ↓ Understand It Before Creating Another
Step 4: Generate an SSH key for practice if you need one.
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
Step 5: Follow the prompts and choose an appropriate secure location and passphrase based on your requirements.
Step 6: Identify which file is private and which is public.
id_ed25519 → Private 🔒 id_ed25519.pub → Public 🔑
Step 7: Copy the content of the public key file only.
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
Safety Rule: Never run cat on your private key and then share its contents. Only copy the public key ending in .pub when adding it to GitHub.
Step 8: Add the public key to your GitHub account through the SSH key settings.
Step 9: Test the SSH connection.
ssh -T git@github.com
Step 10: Check your repository remote.
git remote -v
Step 11: If you are using a practice repository and SSH is configured correctly, change the remote to an SSH URL.
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:username/project.git
Step 12: Verify the remote again.
git remote -v
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is an SSH key pair? 2. Which key must remain secret? 3. Which key is added to GitHub? 4. What does the .pub file usually contain? 5. What is the purpose of ssh-keygen? 6. What does a passphrase protect? 7. What command can test GitHub SSH authentication? 8. What command shows your remote URL? 9. What does an SSH GitHub URL commonly begin with? 10. Complete: Private Key = Keep ______ Public Key = Add to ______

Practice Goal: You should be able to explain private and public SSH keys, safely generate an SSH key pair, identify the .pub public key, add only the public key to GitHub, test SSH authentication, and configure a Git repository to use an SSH remote URL.

qna.q: Q1. What is an SSH key?
qna.a: It is part of a public/private key pair used for secure authentication.

qna.q: Q2. What are the two parts of an SSH key pair?
qna.a: A private key and a public key.

qna.q: Q3. Which SSH key must remain secret?
qna.a: The private key.

qna.q: Q4. Which SSH key can be added to GitHub?
qna.a: The public key.

qna.q: Q5. What does the .pub file usually contain?
qna.a: The public key.

qna.q: Q6. Should you send your private SSH key to GitHub?
qna.a: No. The private key remains on your computer; only the public key is added to GitHub.

qna.q: Q7. What command can generate an Ed25519 SSH key?
qna.a: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

qna.q: Q8. What is the purpose of an SSH passphrase?
qna.a: It can provide additional protection for the private SSH key.

qna.q: Q9. What command can test SSH authentication with GitHub?
qna.a: ssh -T git@github.com

qna.q: Q10. What does an SSH GitHub repository URL commonly look like?
qna.a: git@github.com:username/repository.git

qna.q: Q11. Which command shows configured Git remotes?
qna.a: git remote -v

qna.q: Q12. Complete: Private Key = Keep ______.
qna.a: Secret.

qna.q: Q13. Complete: Public Key = Add to ______.
qna.a: GitHub.

items.title: Never Commit Secrets
explanation: Simple Meaning

A secret is sensitive information that must not be exposed. You should never add secrets to Git commits because committed data can be stored in repository history and may be shared with other people or services.
Secret 🔐 API Key Password PAT Database Password Private Key Access Token ↓ ❌ NEVER COMMIT TO GIT
Simple Rule: If someone else should not know the value, do not put that real value directly into source code or commit it to Git.
What Are Secrets? ⭐
Secrets are confidential values used for authentication, authorization, or accessing protected systems and services.
COMMON SECRETS 🔐 • Passwords • Personal Access Tokens (PATs) • API Keys • Database Credentials • Private SSH Keys • Access Tokens • Secret Keys • Cloud Credentials
Example of a Secret
API_KEY = "your_real_secret_value"
If this contains a real secret, committing the file can expose that credential.
Why Is Committing Secrets Dangerous? 🚨
Developer Adds Secret to Code ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ Secret Stored in Git History ↓ git push ↓ Repository Shared / Exposed ↓ Someone May Access the Secret 🚨
Even a private repository can have multiple collaborators, backups, copies, logs, or future access changes. A secret should therefore be managed separately from normal source code.
Git History Makes This More Serious ⭐
A common beginner mistake is thinking that deleting a secret from the latest file completely removes it. If the secret was committed earlier, it may still exist in Git history.
Commit 1 API_KEY = "SECRET" 🔐 ↓ Commit 2 Secret Deleted ❌ ↓ Current File Looks Safe BUT Old Commit May Still Contain Secret ⚠️

Important: Removing a secret from the current version of a file does not automatically make an already exposed credential safe. If a real secret is exposed, treat it as compromised and rotate or revoke it as appropriate.
Public Repository Example 🚨
Your Computer ↓ Source Code + Secret ❌ ↓ git commit ↓ git push ↓ Public Repository ↓ Secret Can Be Exposed to Others 🚨
Private Repository Is Not a Safe Place for Hard-Coded Secrets

PRIVATE REPOSITORY Does NOT Mean: "Safe to commit secrets" Why? • Collaborators may access code • Access can change • Repository can be copied • Secrets can enter history • Credentials may be exposed accidentally Best Practice ⭐ Keep Secrets Separate
Common Types of Secrets You Should Never Commit ⭐

Secret TypeExample Purpose
PasswordLogging into a protected service
Personal Access TokenAuthenticating supported GitHub operations or API requests
API KeyAuthenticating an application with an API
Database PasswordConnecting to a protected database
Private SSH KeySSH authentication
Access TokenAuthorizing access to a service
Secret KeyApplication security or signing operations
Bad Example ❌
DB_USER = "admin" DB_PASSWORD = "my_real_password" API_KEY = "my_real_api_key"
